On this Masters course you’ll study second language learning as a core module. You’ll explore the major themes that have emerged from the research on the second-language acquisition process. We’ll encourage you to use your own language learning and teaching experience as you assess these approaches.

Alongside this you’ll explore modern classroom operations, and have the opportunity to observe teachers in practice.

There's also a range of optional modules. Select 30 credits (one module) from: Materials and Course Design; Language, Communication, Identity; Beyond Borders; Intercultural Consultancy Project. Select a further 30 credits (one module) from: Postgraduate Research Methods; Communication and Conflict; Teacher Development and Management.

Modules are subject to change and availability.

Assessment
You will show your understanding of the theoretical issues explored on the course and their practical application through various methods, including portfolios, classroom observation tasks and critical essays. At the end of the course, you will also research and complete a 15,000-word major project.

","CoreModules":[{"Title":"Language Teaching in Context: Theory, Practice, Reflection","Description":"In this module you'll develop a research-informed understanding of how English is learned and taught across a range of TESOL contexts, including young learners, ESP, and both face-to-face and online environments. You'll engage with current scholarship on key principles, approaches, and debates in the field, including Communicative Language Teaching, Global Englishes/EIL, and the implications of teaching in multilingual, multicultural settings. Your learning will also be practical: you are invited to analyse two live or recorded lessons, with particular attention to classroom management and its impact on learning. Alongside this, you'll examine principles and practices related to the learning and teaching of the four skills, grammar, vocabulary, and phonology, as well as the nature and value of feedback. You'll also explore contemporary developments in TESOL, including learner autonomy and the growing role of AI in lesson planning and classroom practice. By the end of the module, you'll be equipped to make principled, evidence-based decisions that support your development as an adaptive, reflective TESOL professional.","Code":"MOD000536","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"fc5aba79-345c-4b30-b79f-9a83ebb0785e"},{"Title":"Second Language Acquisition","Description":"You’ll focus on the major themes that have emerged from literature on second language learning over the last three decades. You’ll examine some of the research on the second-language acquisition process, look critically at reports of second-language research, and examine some of the theories which endeavour to interpret research evidence. You will be encouraged to use your own language learning and teaching experience to assess the relative merits of such materials. The module is taught through weekly seminars, offered in the early evening to accommodate those who are in part- or full-time employment. You may be asked to prepare or analyse material for presentation and discussion in class. Students taking part in distance delivery will work in small groups with support from the tutor by means of the Virtual Learning Environment, with progress monitored through formative tasks. Your assessment will be in the form of an extended written assignment to be submitted at the end of the module.","Code":"MOD000535","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"068507fa-af75-48af-9263-826d9204ffb9"},{"Title":"Into ARU","Description":"Entering higher education is exciting; but it can also be a daunting experience. At ARU, we want all our students to make the most of the opportunities higher education provides, reach your potential, become lifelong learners and find fulfilling careers. However, we appreciate that the shift from secondary education, or a return to formal education is, in itself, quite a journey. This module is designed to ease that transition. You'll be enrolled on it as soon as you receive an offer from ARU so you can begin to learn about university life before your course starts. Through Into ARU, you'll explore a virtual land modelled around ARU values: Courage, Innovation, Community, Integrity, Responsibility, and Ambition. This innovative module is designed as a game, where you collect knowledge and complete mini tasks. You'll proceed at your own pace, though we you to have completed your Into ARU exploration by week 6. If for any reason you're unable to complete by that date, we'll signpost to existing services so that we can be confident that you are supported.","Code":"","HideMdfLink":true,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"fe875ffc-613a-4b26-98b2-b567ca8891ec"}],"OptionalModules":[{"Title":"Materials and Course Design","Description":"You will explore the factors involved in the design of language courses and teaching materials, reflecting on one possible process of course design. You will start with an analysis of the context in which the course will take place, the needs of the learners, and current theories of language and language learning. You will move on to consider how course content can be selected and ordered in a principled way, how assessment relates to course design, and how and when courses should be evaluated. Finally, you will consider the evaluation, adaptation and creation of course materials. The face-to-face seminars will be a combination of teacher input, student input and discussion, both in groups and whole class. Students taking part in distance delivery will work in a small group with support from the tutor by means of the Virtual Learning Environment, with progress monitored through formative tasks. The assessment will be in the form of a portfolio and will give you the opportunity to consider what particular syllabus might be relevant to your own current or future teaching context. The elements of the portfolio will relate to particular units of the module, and the portfolio can therefore be progressively built up as the course proceeds.","Code":"MOD000537","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"597a339c-2c19-4843-afda-08faa5731488"},{"Title":"Language, Identity and Policy","Description":"You will explore the psychological and social intricacies of language and interaction both in general and within the EU. You will examine the question of language within the EU, identifying the points of tension for a community of nations who seek to work together increasingly closely and to achieve intercultural understanding while at the same time making a strong commitment to cultural and linguistic diversity. You will assess how far EU policy confronts the language issues identifiable within its current frontiers and the likely way forward as more countries and more languages join, comparing the situation in Europe with those experienced in other countries. Finally, you will explore how developing language technologies might facilitate future intercultural communication and help to resolve some of the current difficulties.","Code":"MOD000531","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"69205077-101b-48e6-9fbf-1b0d63f40705"},{"Title":"Beyond Borders Intercultural Communication Welfare and Policy","Description":"This module takes an interdisciplinary approach to introducing key topics and ways of working in the social sciences. You'll look at the development of relations, communicative styles and values between individuals and groups of different cultural backgrounds and delve into comparative issues concerning social policy and social welfare in the international and intercultural context. You'll do this by exploring areas such as gender equality, social housing, education and immigration and wider social concepts such as identity, intersectionality and inequality. You'll work with case studies to exemplify these concepts. In this way, you'll develop the foundation for a deeper understanding and appreciation of fundamental topics in the social sciences. You'll also receive guidance on study at Master’s level and the module will guide you towards the academic research and writing skills needed to work independently at this level.","Code":"MOD010759","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"bbb89968-3e72-43f6-86a5-634020d297e9"},{"Title":"Intercultural Consultancy Project","Description":"Working with an external collaborative partner, you will negotiate a 12 week consultancy project that demonstrates and builds upon theoretical and practical skills you have acquired on your course. The module will enable you to work contextually within the framework of work-based learning by facilitating knowledge exchange between the student and their external partner. The project will respond to the opportunities and needs of the external partner as applied to the field of intercultural communications. You will critically engage with how this professional sector operates in context of the wider business environments and how this can be applied to your career development. This module supports you in the development of key skills required in contemporary intercultural work environments, such as face-to-face and asynchronous communications, collaborative and cooperative decision making or intra-team conflict resolution.","Code":"MOD008998","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"828f471c-8924-483e-b522-4be3447c71d2"},{"Title":"Postgraduate Research Methods","Description":"In this module you'll gain the research skills and techniques needed both to critically evaluate the literature you'll be using in your course and to put into practice in your own dissertation. We'll explore the methodologies and methods applied in contemporary social science research to enable you to select an appropriate range for your own needs. You'll have the opportunity to experiment with a variety of methods so that you'll fully understood them and be able to adapt them creatively for your own projects. The module will place research methods in a wider framework of social research strategies at a postgraduate level. We'll examine the research design options available to you at Masters level and explore thoroughly the issues involved in planning a research project and formulating research questions. With the aid of library expertise, you'll have access to and understand current tools for reviewing and researching existing literature. Particular attention will be paid to ethical principles and the politics of social research. A central part of the module will address the practicalities of employing both qualitative and quantitative methodologies. Computer-assisted analysis methods will be introduced.","Code":"MOD000825","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"5b02c3ba-c947-4e80-93fc-9a64099bcba0"},{"Title":"Communication and Conflict","Description":"On this module you'll explore historical and thematic approaches to reporting on conflict and also how communication functions in a crisis. You'll examine the reciprocal relationships between the military, governments and the media, including how the media can be used to legitimise conflict, and the changing role of social media in building consensus and protest, including the use of Twitter and Facebook to organise demonstrations and undermine the power of state-dominated discourses. You’ll also consider more traditional forms of communication, including censorship and propaganda, and whether the state is ever able to retain control of the narrative, as well as the role of the war reporter, and the way in which governments can utilise the independent media and how independent it really is. Other areas of exploration include consent, public interest, ethics and the representation of suffering, looking at whether the dominance of media in the debate in the West means that public interest in conflict is limited by the limitations of the media, and what this means for winning hearts and minds during insurgencies, military interventions and peacekeeping operations. Finally, you'll look at the way war and conflict is portrayed in fictional accounts and the underlying assumptions of such portrayals, and will examine conflicting discourses about war in post-conflict environments and the way the media can contribute to or hamper the process of post-conflict reconstruction. Themes throughout the module will include the question of who owns, defines and propagates the truth, and the implications of this in the context of conflict and war.","Code":"MOD003644","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"a956aeb6-6c48-423b-b081-fb889035e622"},{"Title":"Teacher Development and Management","Description":"In this module you will develop an understanding of the issues and practices concerned with developing and training teachers of English to speakers of other languages. You will examine current and recent research and explore the key concepts and practices in areas such as observing teachers and giving feedback, designing training programmes, leadership in academic management and professionalism within teaching. You will watch live or recorded lessons and develop ideas about what feedback you would give on the lessons to develop the teacher’s skills. You will reflect on your experience of working within teaching organisations. You will be taught through weekly seminars, offered in the early evenings to accommodate those in part-or full-time employment. The seminars will be staff led, and you will be asked to prepare material for presentation and discussion in class. Observation of teachers in practice will be arranged outside the weekly seminar. If you are studying via distance delivery you will work in small groups with support from the tutor via our learning management system, Canvas, with progress monitored through formative tasks.","Code":"MOD008996","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"21e23f3b-b0a1-48f5-a281-e2282412fbf0"}],"Id":"cd0c9de0-3791-4c36-9f0d-48fd4f884601","SelectedModule":false},{"Title":"Year 2","CoreModuleSectionHeading":"Core modules","OptionModuleSectionHeading":"","Summary":"

In Year 2 your focus is on your Major Project. This is an opportunity to explore in detail a topic that reflects your particular interest.

There's also a range of optional modules. Select 30 credits (one module) from: Materials and Course Design; Language, Communication, Identity; Beyond Borders; Intercultural Consultancy Project. Select a further 30 credits (one module) from: Postgraduate Research Methods; Communication and Conflict; Teacher Development and Management.

Modules are subject to change and availability.

Assessment
You will show your understanding of the theoretical issues explored on the course and their practical application through various methods, including portfolios, classroom observation tasks and critical essays. At the end of the course, you will also research and complete a 15,000-word major project.

","CoreModules":[{"Title":"Major Project for Masters Stage","Description":"This module will support you in the preparation and submission of a Masters dissertation, allowing you to explore in-depth a particular topic that reflects your academic interest.","Code":"MOD000545","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"cd0b1b77-e95a-473c-b0db-d28caa707aa9"}],"OptionalModules":[{"Title":"Materials and Course Design","Description":"You will explore the factors involved in the design of language courses and teaching materials, reflecting on one possible process of course design. You will start with an analysis of the context in which the course will take place, the needs of the learners, and current theories of language and language learning. You will move on to consider how course content can be selected and ordered in a principled way, how assessment relates to course design, and how and when courses should be evaluated. Finally, you will consider the evaluation, adaptation and creation of course materials. The face-to-face seminars will be a combination of teacher input, student input and discussion, both in groups and whole class. Students taking part in distance delivery will work in a small group with support from the tutor by means of the Virtual Learning Environment, with progress monitored through formative tasks. The assessment will be in the form of a portfolio and will give you the opportunity to consider what particular syllabus might be relevant to your own current or future teaching context. The elements of the portfolio will relate to particular units of the module, and the portfolio can therefore be progressively built up as the course proceeds.","Code":"MOD000537","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"597a339c-2c19-4843-afda-08faa5731488"},{"Title":"Beyond Borders Intercultural Communication Welfare and Policy","Description":"This module takes an interdisciplinary approach to introducing key topics and ways of working in the social sciences. You'll look at the development of relations, communicative styles and values between individuals and groups of different cultural backgrounds and delve into comparative issues concerning social policy and social welfare in the international and intercultural context. You'll do this by exploring areas such as gender equality, social housing, education and immigration and wider social concepts such as identity, intersectionality and inequality. You'll work with case studies to exemplify these concepts. In this way, you'll develop the foundation for a deeper understanding and appreciation of fundamental topics in the social sciences. You'll also receive guidance on study at Master’s level and the module will guide you towards the academic research and writing skills needed to work independently at this level.","Code":"MOD010759","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"bbb89968-3e72-43f6-86a5-634020d297e9"},{"Title":"Intercultural Consultancy Project","Description":"Working with an external collaborative partner, you will negotiate a 12 week consultancy project that demonstrates and builds upon theoretical and practical skills you have acquired on your course. The module will enable you to work contextually within the framework of work-based learning by facilitating knowledge exchange between the student and their external partner. The project will respond to the opportunities and needs of the external partner as applied to the field of intercultural communications. You will critically engage with how this professional sector operates in context of the wider business environments and how this can be applied to your career development. This module supports you in the development of key skills required in contemporary intercultural work environments, such as face-to-face and asynchronous communications, collaborative and cooperative decision making or intra-team conflict resolution.","Code":"MOD008998","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"828f471c-8924-483e-b522-4be3447c71d2"},{"Title":"Postgraduate Research Methods","Description":"In this module you'll gain the research skills and techniques needed both to critically evaluate the literature you'll be using in your course and to put into practice in your own dissertation. We'll explore the methodologies and methods applied in contemporary social science research to enable you to select an appropriate range for your own needs. You'll have the opportunity to experiment with a variety of methods so that you'll fully understood them and be able to adapt them creatively for your own projects. The module will place research methods in a wider framework of social research strategies at a postgraduate level. We'll examine the research design options available to you at Masters level and explore thoroughly the issues involved in planning a research project and formulating research questions. With the aid of library expertise, you'll have access to and understand current tools for reviewing and researching existing literature. Particular attention will be paid to ethical principles and the politics of social research. A central part of the module will address the practicalities of employing both qualitative and quantitative methodologies. Computer-assisted analysis methods will be introduced.","Code":"MOD000825","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"5b02c3ba-c947-4e80-93fc-9a64099bcba0"},{"Title":"Communication and Conflict","Description":"On this module you'll explore historical and thematic approaches to reporting on conflict and also how communication functions in a crisis. You'll examine the reciprocal relationships between the military, governments and the media, including how the media can be used to legitimise conflict, and the changing role of social media in building consensus and protest, including the use of Twitter and Facebook to organise demonstrations and undermine the power of state-dominated discourses. You’ll also consider more traditional forms of communication, including censorship and propaganda, and whether the state is ever able to retain control of the narrative, as well as the role of the war reporter, and the way in which governments can utilise the independent media and how independent it really is. Other areas of exploration include consent, public interest, ethics and the representation of suffering, looking at whether the dominance of media in the debate in the West means that public interest in conflict is limited by the limitations of the media, and what this means for winning hearts and minds during insurgencies, military interventions and peacekeeping operations. Finally, you'll look at the way war and conflict is portrayed in fictional accounts and the underlying assumptions of such portrayals, and will examine conflicting discourses about war in post-conflict environments and the way the media can contribute to or hamper the process of post-conflict reconstruction. Themes throughout the module will include the question of who owns, defines and propagates the truth, and the implications of this in the context of conflict and war.","Code":"MOD003644","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"a956aeb6-6c48-423b-b081-fb889035e622"},{"Title":"Teacher Development and Management","Description":"In this module you will develop an understanding of the issues and practices concerned with developing and training teachers of English to speakers of other languages. You will examine current and recent research and explore the key concepts and practices in areas such as observing teachers and giving feedback, designing training programmes, leadership in academic management and professionalism within teaching. You will watch live or recorded lessons and develop ideas about what feedback you would give on the lessons to develop the teacher’s skills. You will reflect on your experience of working within teaching organisations. You will be taught through weekly seminars, offered in the early evenings to accommodate those in part-or full-time employment. The seminars will be staff led, and you will be asked to prepare material for presentation and discussion in class. Observation of teachers in practice will be arranged outside the weekly seminar. If you are studying via distance delivery you will work in small groups with support from the tutor via our learning management system, Canvas, with progress monitored through formative tasks.","Code":"MOD008996","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"21e23f3b-b0a1-48f5-a281-e2282412fbf0"},{"Title":"Language, Communication, Identity","Description":"In this module, you will explore the interrelationships between language, culture and society, and identity. Starting by looking at the connection between language and the individual, we examine key concepts of identity and linguistic variation. The notion of ‘self’ and its relationship to language is being investigated in the context of different social and cultural dimensions, including gender, race and ethnicity. The second part of the module moves towards a discussion of language policy from several angles. Using a case-study approach, we explore policy-making, including national language policies and aspects of educational policy in which language play a key role. You are encouraged to critically reflect on how your own lived experience relates to the issues under consideration in the module.","Code":"MOD008999","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"e0669ae4-47dc-498b-ad18-f85b51219d1a"}],"Id":"c48f3f6b-8a15-40f7-9037-ce5ca50ad043","SelectedModule":false}],"UcasCode":"","SITSCode":"","AstraCode":"P0025","ModeOfStudy":{"KisCode":"PartTime","ModeOfStudyCode":"PT","ExcludeFromCourseSummary":false,"Name":"Part-time","Id":"77ee6eb5-cef9-4099-87c0-3c2819c645cd"},"CoreOption":false,"FoundationOption":false,"PlacementOption":false,"ProfessionalExperienceOption":false,"PartTimeOption":false,"Extra1":false,"Extra2":false,"Status":null,"StartDateDisclaimer":null,"DegreeApprenticeship":false,"Award":null,"Qualification":null,"LocationOverride":null,"EntryRequirementYears":[{"Name":"2025","Id":"523e76c8-c5e1-46e9-aec6-efe48fefd779"}],"EntryRequirementsInformation":[{"HeadingTitle":"Standard entry requirements","RichTextContent":[{"RichTextTitle":"","RichTextContent":"

Alongside this you’ll explore modern classroom operations, and have the opportunity to observe teachers in practice.

You will be encouraged to use your own language learning and teaching experience to assess the relative merits of such materials. You may be asked to prepare or analyse material for presentation and discussion in class. You'll engage with current scholarship on key principles, approaches, and debates in the field, including Communicative Language Teaching, Global Englishes/EIL, and the implications of teaching in multilingual, multicultural settings. Your learning will also be practical: you are invited to analyse two live or recorded lessons, with particular attention to classroom management and its impact on learning. Alongside this, you'll examine principles and practices related to the learning and teaching of the four skills, grammar, vocabulary, and phonology, as well as the nature and value of feedback. You'll also explore contemporary developments in TESOL, including learner autonomy and the growing role of AI in lesson planning and classroom practice. As a distance learner, you'll study, or have the option to study all the modules listed below, but at different points in the course depending on whether you start in September or January.

Modules are subject to change and availability.

Assessment
You will show your understanding of the theoretical issues explored on the course and their practical application through various methods, including portfolios, classroom observation tasks and critical essays. At the end of the course, you will also research and complete a 15,000-word major project.

If you study this course by distance learning, you will not need to attend any face-to-face sessions.

","CoreModules":[{"Title":"Second Language Acquisition","Description":"You’ll focus on the major themes that have emerged from literature on second language learning over the last three decades. You’ll examine some of the research on the second-language acquisition process, look critically at reports of second-language research, and examine some of the theories which endeavour to interpret research evidence. You will be encouraged to use your own language learning and teaching experience to assess the relative merits of such materials. The module is taught through weekly seminars, offered in the early evening to accommodate those who are in part- or full-time employment. You may be asked to prepare or analyse material for presentation and discussion in class. Students taking part in distance delivery will work in small groups with support from the tutor by means of the Virtual Learning Environment, with progress monitored through formative tasks. Your assessment will be in the form of an extended written assignment to be submitted at the end of the module.","Code":"MOD000535","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"068507fa-af75-48af-9263-826d9204ffb9"},{"Title":"Language Teaching in Context: Theory, Practice, Reflection","Description":"In this module you'll develop a research-informed understanding of how English is learned and taught across a range of TESOL contexts, including young learners, ESP, and both face-to-face and online environments. You'll engage with current scholarship on key principles, approaches, and debates in the field, including Communicative Language Teaching, Global Englishes/EIL, and the implications of teaching in multilingual, multicultural settings. Your learning will also be practical: you are invited to analyse two live or recorded lessons, with particular attention to classroom management and its impact on learning. Alongside this, you'll examine principles and practices related to the learning and teaching of the four skills, grammar, vocabulary, and phonology, as well as the nature and value of feedback. You'll also explore contemporary developments in TESOL, including learner autonomy and the growing role of AI in lesson planning and classroom practice. By the end of the module, you'll be equipped to make principled, evidence-based decisions that support your development as an adaptive, reflective TESOL professional.","Code":"MOD000536","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"fc5aba79-345c-4b30-b79f-9a83ebb0785e"},{"Title":"Major Project for Masters Stage","Description":"This module will support you in the preparation and submission of a Masters dissertation, allowing you to explore in-depth a particular topic that reflects your academic interest.","Code":"MOD000545","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"cd0b1b77-e95a-473c-b0db-d28caa707aa9"},{"Title":"Into ARU","Description":"Entering higher education is exciting; but it can also be a daunting experience. At ARU, we want all our students to make the most of the opportunities higher education provides, reach your potential, become lifelong learners and find fulfilling careers. However, we appreciate that the shift from secondary education, or a return to formal education is, in itself, quite a journey. This module is designed to ease that transition. You'll be enrolled on it as soon as you receive an offer from ARU so you can begin to learn about university life before your course starts. Through Into ARU, you'll explore a virtual land modelled around ARU values: Courage, Innovation, Community, Integrity, Responsibility, and Ambition. This innovative module is designed as a game, where you collect knowledge and complete mini tasks. You'll proceed at your own pace, though we you to have completed your Into ARU exploration by week 6. If for any reason you're unable to complete by that date, we'll signpost to existing services so that we can be confident that you are supported.","Code":"","HideMdfLink":true,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"fe875ffc-613a-4b26-98b2-b567ca8891ec"}],"OptionalModules":[{"Title":"Materials and Course Design","Description":"You will explore the factors involved in the design of language courses and teaching materials, reflecting on one possible process of course design. You will start with an analysis of the context in which the course will take place, the needs of the learners, and current theories of language and language learning. You will move on to consider how course content can be selected and ordered in a principled way, how assessment relates to course design, and how and when courses should be evaluated. Finally, you will consider the evaluation, adaptation and creation of course materials. The face-to-face seminars will be a combination of teacher input, student input and discussion, both in groups and whole class. Students taking part in distance delivery will work in a small group with support from the tutor by means of the Virtual Learning Environment, with progress monitored through formative tasks. The assessment will be in the form of a portfolio and will give you the opportunity to consider what particular syllabus might be relevant to your own current or future teaching context. The elements of the portfolio will relate to particular units of the module, and the portfolio can therefore be progressively built up as the course proceeds.","Code":"MOD000537","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"597a339c-2c19-4843-afda-08faa5731488"},{"Title":"Teacher Development and Management","Description":"In this module you will develop an understanding of the issues and practices concerned with developing and training teachers of English to speakers of other languages. You will examine current and recent research and explore the key concepts and practices in areas such as observing teachers and giving feedback, designing training programmes, leadership in academic management and professionalism within teaching. You will watch live or recorded lessons and develop ideas about what feedback you would give on the lessons to develop the teacher’s skills. You will reflect on your experience of working within teaching organisations. You will be taught through weekly seminars, offered in the early evenings to accommodate those in part-or full-time employment. The seminars will be staff led, and you will be asked to prepare material for presentation and discussion in class. Observation of teachers in practice will be arranged outside the weekly seminar. If you are studying via distance delivery you will work in small groups with support from the tutor via our learning management system, Canvas, with progress monitored through formative tasks.","Code":"MOD008996","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"21e23f3b-b0a1-48f5-a281-e2282412fbf0"},{"Title":"Postgraduate Research Methods","Description":"In this module you'll gain the research skills and techniques needed both to critically evaluate the literature you'll be using in your course and to put into practice in your own dissertation. We'll explore the methodologies and methods applied in contemporary social science research to enable you to select an appropriate range for your own needs. You'll have the opportunity to experiment with a variety of methods so that you'll fully understood them and be able to adapt them creatively for your own projects. The module will place research methods in a wider framework of social research strategies at a postgraduate level. We'll examine the research design options available to you at Masters level and explore thoroughly the issues involved in planning a research project and formulating research questions. With the aid of library expertise, you'll have access to and understand current tools for reviewing and researching existing literature. Particular attention will be paid to ethical principles and the politics of social research. A central part of the module will address the practicalities of employing both qualitative and quantitative methodologies. Computer-assisted analysis methods will be introduced.","Code":"MOD000825","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"5b02c3ba-c947-4e80-93fc-9a64099bcba0"}],"Id":"0cfbeaa4-2803-45db-9746-ed59b07ff280","SelectedModule":false}],"UcasCode":"","SITSCode":"","AstraCode":"P0025","ModeOfStudy":{"KisCode":"PartTime","ModeOfStudyCode":"PT","ExcludeFromCourseSummary":false,"Name":"Part-time","Id":"77ee6eb5-cef9-4099-87c0-3c2819c645cd"},"CoreOption":false,"FoundationOption":false,"PlacementOption":false,"ProfessionalExperienceOption":false,"PartTimeOption":false,"Extra1":false,"Extra2":false,"Status":null,"StartDateDisclaimer":null,"DegreeApprenticeship":false,"Award":null,"Qualification":null,"LocationOverride":null,"EntryRequirementYears":[{"Name":"2025","Id":"523e76c8-c5e1-46e9-aec6-efe48fefd779"}],"EntryRequirementsInformation":[{"HeadingTitle":"Standard entry requirements","RichTextContent":[{"RichTextTitle":"","RichTextContent":"

Postgraduate MSc Applied Wildlife Conservation Master practical wildlife conservation skills through applied conservation biology, fieldwork and data analysis to tackle real-world global biodiversity challenges. The part-time option takes 28 months (September starts), or 33 months (January starts). 2 years part-time It's possible to study this course part-time. You'll take the same modules as MSc/MA students, but sometimes in a different order or in different years. As a part-time student you'll typically study for twice as long as full-time students. For example if the MSc/MA course takes one year, you can expect to study over two years, though for some courses this may vary. 1st in the region for postgraduates progressing into senior roles. Source: Graduate Outcomes Survey 2026 If you’re passionate about tackling global biodiversity and climate challenges, this innovative Master’s is for you. You'll develop the technical expertise and professional competencies sought by conservation employers worldwide, equipping you to champion nature in a rapidly changing world. You'll combine field-based learning with advanced technical training in biodiversity assessment methods, spatial data analysis including Geographical Information Systems (GIS), conservation communication, conservation biology research and quantitative data analysis to make a meaningful impact in conservation. Hear from our staff and students about studying Applied Wildlife Conservation at ARU. Close full-screen gallery. Hear from our staff and students about studying Applied Wildlife Conservation at ARU. Why ARU? Gain hands-on conservation experience through fieldwork, laboratory work, and real-world projects in your areas of interest Develop in-demand technical and research skills, including GIS and field survey and biodiversity assessment techniques Collaborate with conservation organisations on real-world environmental projects, Live Briefs , and research challenges Conduct your major research project with supervision from leading academics from our Centre for Ecology, Evolution and Environment Enhance your studies with an optional field skills course in France hosted by the Mediterranean Ecology Research Observatory for Practical Skills Master data handling, reporting and communication skills Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers This course gave me a wonderful opportunity to apply my lifelong love of nature to exciting worldwide contexts while challenging my academic ability. Linda Butterfield, Countryside Ranger, Lea Valley Park Prepare for an impactful career protecting wildlife and habitats. You'll graduate with skills in fieldwork, laboratory techniques (eDNA), computational ecology (GIS and R Stats), academic research, and science communication to help you secure your dream role in the conservation sector. Graduation doesn't have to be the end of your time with us. You might decide to continue your academic career and join a research programme at ARU, such as our PhD Biology . Take advantage of our Alumni Scholarship and save £400 on your fees. What can you do with an Applied Wildlife Conservation degree? This course will prepare you for careers in areas such as conservation biology, nature conservation, ecological consultancy, conservation education, PhD research, project management, policy and governance. You may also develop a career within a non-governmental organisation (NGO), charity, zoo, private company, or government body, or in a related field such as ecotourism. Typical graduate destinations include: Wildlife conservation and management Ecological and environmental consultancy Environmental charities and NGOs Governmental organisations, local authorities and the Civil Service Project management and data analysts Conservation research and education Sustainability and environmental policy PhD study or other research work Environmental policy and governance Attending the 2025 Student Conference on Conservation Science Animal Behaviour Applications for Conservation student Afrika shares her experiences of the 2025 Student Conference on Conservation Science (SCCS) in Cambridge. Where have previous Applied Wildlife Conservation graduates worked? Graduates have furthered their careers at an array of organisations including: The Wildlife Trusts Forestry Commission Milton Keynes Parks Trust Benthic Solutions Civil Service UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology Anglian Water International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Joint Nature Conservation Committee (JNCC) Mammal Society Froglife How can ARU help with my employability and career development? We want you to be a step ahead when you graduate, so we offer: courses designed with employers tutors with professional industry knowledge hands-on learning which may include industry-led projects, placements or Professional Experience modules . Alongside your course, there are lots of other opportunities to build your skills and experience: add value to your CV with an ARU Certificate of Professional Development get involved in a thriving volunteering programme develop your brilliant business ideas work with businesses to make a social impact . We’re here to help you develop your CV and find that all-important role after graduation. Our Employability Service offers tailored career appointments, advice on writing your CV, help to complete job applications, and much more. You’ll have 24/7 access to an online Careers Centre too, which is packed with useful resources. The support continues after you graduate, with lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . Find out more about careers support at ARU . Teaching and modules Our MSc students are a regular source of inspiration to me. Some of the best moments of my career have been working on field trips with them. Dr Peter Brown, Associate Professor in Ecology and Conservation Develop the practical skills needed to tackle global biodiversity loss. You'll practise fieldwork, ecological survey techniques, spatial mapping, conservation genetics, research methods and science communication. You’ll apply your learning to real-world conservation challenges, specialise through optional modules, and complete an independent research project on a contemporary conservation issue. Developed with international environmental organisations, this Master's equips you with employer-valued expertise in wildlife and habitat management, data analysis and sustainable conservation, supported by field trips, specialist guest lecturers and strong links with leading conservation organisations. What will I study? MSc 2 years part-time MSc Modules are subject to change and availability, and may vary by location. If you have the choice of optional modules, these are indicated with a *. Year 1 GIS Tools for Biodiversity Mapping and Conservation (15 credits) Distributions, Landscapes and Conservation (15 credits) Current Topics in Wildlife Conservation (15 credits) Behavioural Ecology and Conservation (15 credits) Communication Skills for Conservation (15 credits) Research Methods (15 credits) Masters Research Project (60 credits) Practical Applications of DNA Based Technologies (15 credits) * Study Tour: Understanding Biodiversity and Sustainability (15 credits) * Sustainable Land Management (15 credits) * Applied Animal Behaviour and Animal Welfare * Cognition Evolution and Behaviour * Module details 2 years part-time It's possible to study this course part-time. You'll take the same modules as MSc/MA students, but sometimes in a different order or in different years. As a part-time student you'll typically study for twice as long as full-time students. For example if the MSc/MA course takes one year, you can expect to study over two years, though for some courses this may vary. How is Applied Wildlife Conservation assessed? You'll be continually assessed through Live Briefs , group presentations, report writing, and field and lab reporting. Who teaches Applied Wildlife Conservation at ARU? Our teaching team includes internationally recognised researchers and experienced practitioners working across the fields of conservation, ecology, animal behaviour and environmental sustainability. Dr Jim Littlemore Senior Lecturer Dr Bas Boots Senior Lecturer Dr Peter Brown Associate Professor Professor Dannielle Green Professor Dr Thomas Ings Associate Professor Dr Hannah White Senior Lecturer Facilities Study in our state of the art £40m Science Centre in the heart of Cambridge. You'll have access to specialist facilities supporting animal and environmental biology and use industry-standard GIS and spatial analysis software, well stocked laboratories, field equipment and dedicated teaching spaces including our research labs. You'll learn beyond campus through residential and local field trips across East Anglia, practical training and opportunities to engage with conservation organisations. You'll also benefit from ARU's extensive library and digital learning resources and support services. Take a guided tour and meet our students . Use your art for wellbeing and develop ethical, practical, and inclusive approaches addressing global health and wellbeing challenges. Make a positive contribution to society, healthcare and the planet through ethical and systemic creative interventions. Art for Change through Engagement (ACE) The ACE project has been shortlisted for the 2023/24 University of Cambridge VC Research Impact Awards. This was a collaboration between Cambridge School of Art and Cambridge University's Wellcome-MRC Institute of Metabolic Science - Metabolic Research Laboratories (IMS-MRL). Find out more about the ACE project Designed for creative life Our new £40m Creative Quarter brings together professional environments – studios, workshops, performance and exhibition spaces – where you can collaborate, create and showcase your work. Be part of a creative community built around making, experimentation and innovation, while developing practical skills, strengthening your portfolio and connecting with industry. As an Art Professional, you will develop the leadership skills, understanding and knowledge critical to creating dynamic and inclusive forms of participatory research and practice, community engagement, resilience building, and creative urban culture. ARU has been ranked in the top 20% of universities in the world for Good Health and Wellbeing in the 2023 Times Higher Education (THE) Impact Rankings. You’ll gain a broad understanding of ethical and future health from the perspective of art and will tackle mental, physical, emotional, and social wellbeing issues in a global context. You will be rethinking existing places, environments, and communities including to reduce individual loneliness and isolation, aggression and discrimination, increasing prosocial behaviours, and improving social consciousness. You will be developing as an art professional, while building your profile and having the freedom to use your art for different purposes, such as mental health or community support. Why should I study Art for Health and Wellbeing? In a world that needs people to stay well, recover faster, manage long-term conditions, and experience a better quality of life, art professionals have never played such a central role - tackling physical, mental and social wellbeing as well as considering all forms of human productivity, strengthening local relationships, and building strong communities through art-based interventions and creative approaches that are connected, shared, and intelligent. At ARU, you’ll work closely with students from across the Cambridge School of Art , including the postgraduate students from Human-Centred Design and Interior Design Innovation on an industry-led collaborative project and deliver public-facing events. As an Art, Health, and Wellbeing student in Cambridge , you’ll be able to work in a start-up environment and a relaxed culture in which creativity and creative problem solving are valued and build strong relationships and freely exchange thoughts and ideas. Most importantly, you’ll receive support and guidance from our experienced staff who, as well as running their own studio practice, have worked with companies such as the NHS , Prepared International , Nebama Mind, World Health Organization , and World Humanitarian Forum . The creative freedom offered by the course results in a variety of degree outputs based on art futuring, ideas and methods for creativity as an expanded ethical and professional practice, from social prescribing and increasing human connectivity, to overcoming fear, pain, anxiety, depression and stress. Talks from visiting lecturers and live briefs from industry are built into our course. They focus on areas including participatory research and practice, digital health, social design and sustainability, interactive storytelling and digital technologies, care systems and future health. We'll encourage you to build your profile by entering national and international competitions, as well as taking part in our own competitions such as the Sustainability Art Prize , the Arts and Wellbeing Award, and the British Council Venice Biennale Fellowship award. You'll have the chance to develop a business plan and pitch for start-up funding through our annual competition, The Big Pitch , and you can get involved in our Art & Care series of research talks and other and creative events. This Masters will help you achieve a career within the public, private, and third sector in roles such as: Health and Social Care Researcher Psycho-Social Interventionist (physical/digital) Culture and Community Innovator UX/UI Artist/Researcher Health and Wellbeing Strategist Social Service Artist/Designer Health and Wellbeing Experience Artist/Designer Wellbeing Consultant Creative Health Specialist Health Policy Advisor Wellbeing Artist ARU career support All of our modules integrate professional practice, and you’ll be introduced to different aspects of the creative industry by the teaching team and external guests. This will help you develop an appreciation and awareness of the changing role of creatives and artists, and the increasing responsibilities within potential career paths. Your awareness of current practices and responsibilities will develop at an early stage of your studies, particularly in the Care Ethics and Care Practices modules. You’ll also use the Personal Development Planning (PDP) tool to record, map and review your employability skills and experience across the course, and engage with employability and career development supported by academic and technical staff as well as the ARU Employability Service and ARU Enterprise and Innovation. These in-house centres provide: daily drop-in sessions careers advice and guidance workshops covering job search, making applications, and designing CVs interview preparation Job Fairs, employability events and presentations from employers job opportunities, internships, and work placements. Graduation doesn’t have to be the end of your time with us. You could choose to continue your academic career with a PhD programme at ARU . var configOptions = {"HeroIntroduction":"","HeroImage":null,"CourseInfoDisclosureTitle":"Combining course options","CourseInfoDisclosure":"","StartDateDisclaimer":"","AdditionalInfoSectionTitle":"","AdditionalInfoSectionText":"","AdditionalInfoTitle":"","AdditionalInfo":"","StaffHeader":"","StaffRichText":[],"CourseOptions":[{"Duration":{"Name":"1 year full-time","Id":"0e006fc1-d6c6-476d-b58d-0f7542981c6e"},"StartDate":[{"Name":"September 2027","Id":"12ba467c-68e1-4784-9b56-3b8ccb7cca9f"}],"Location":[{"ShortName":"Cambridge","AstraLocationCode":"cam","DisplayOrder":1,"Id":"e44a5b31-f469-4e5b-93ad-f9219a73fe81"}],"Modules":[{"Title":"Year 1","CoreModuleSectionHeading":"Core modules","OptionModuleSectionHeading":"","Summary":"

Our MA Art, Health, and Wellbeing degree is designed to reflect a wider eco-system of people, processes, systems and places, whilst focussing on your own planned outcomes. Your learning and teaching will include both face-to-face and online modes, where required, and will typically include presentations, lectures, and seminars; learning through thinking, doing, making and drawing; project and collaborative work; prototyping and testing; art theory and practice; research and ideation.

You’ll engage actively in the construction of your own knowledge, which will require higher order thinking and rethinking assumptions, while reflecting on your own learning through disciplinary, interdisciplinary, and multidisciplinary collaborations. ‘Active’ learning will involve you in reading, writing, discussing or being engaged in problem-solving and enquiry-based activities, and represents a shift from teacher-centred to more student-centred teaching approaches. Most importantly, to be actively involved, you must engage in such higher-order thinking tasks as analysis, synthesis and evaluation.

You’ll be assessed through various methods that reflect the skills, knowledge and understanding that you’ll need to work as an ethically-minded practising artist, such as research analysis and translation; creative process, experimentation, concept generation and realisation; portfolio and visual communication; critical understanding and reflective practice; employability skills; place, environment, and communities identified issues and plans of action; backcasting and forecasting skills and approaches.

Modules are subject to change and availability.

","CoreModules":[{"Title":"Critical and Contextual Studies","Description":"This module addresses the theoretical background and aspects of art discipline through the questions: What is art and creativity, and how can they address health and wellbeing issues?; What is the role of art in the 21st century?; and why is creativity and art so important? You will have the opportunity to explore and experiment with the existing art methods and develop new ones, finding ways to articulate your knowledge and skills in practice and in a self-selected project, through a taught process. You will explore the importance of art methods and creative approaches to addressing local and global issues, and examine a range of current concepts, principles, and models of art and creativity, including narrative building, scenario creation, engagement, personas, types of creative methods, creative processes, and tools etc, and their usefulness in tackling social, economic, environmental, and cultural challenges.","Code":"","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"61e5afa4-bd70-4bac-902b-c25ce0cdfeb6"},{"Title":"Care Ethics: Place, Environment, and Community","Description":"In this module you’ll develop the ability to highlight how preoccupations addressed by care ethicists - including caring for animals and the environment, bioethics, and public policy - are also shared through creative and socially engaged approaches and practices that have the potential to impact people’s lives while raising awareness where needed. You’ll be presented with a pool of such practices and research to give a critical context to your own developing ideas and projects. Examining a range of concepts and frameworks of Art, Health, and Wellbeing, you’ll learn to understand the importance of a creative approach in thinking about problems and solutions from the big picture. You’ll not only consider if your creative work is legal, efficient, or cost-effective, but also explore how your decisions and actions will affect others, questioning the motives behind them, taking responsibility for the choices you make, and understanding how to act within a specific set of circumstances. Focusing on the scope, complexity and interconnectedness of place and environment, you’ll reflect on current and emerging concepts and models, and their usefulness in addressing community health and wellbeing.","Code":"","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"ef9544e4-22c3-4dd5-8ed3-49a2a1c2ade3"},{"Title":"Grand Challenge","Description":"In this module, you'll use creative art as a structured, process-led and ethically rigorous approach to address local and global challenges at different scales. You will engage with social, environmental and economic issues affecting health and wellbeing, moving beyond traditional problem–solution thinking to respond to the needs of place, environment and community. Through themes such as ageing societies, sustainable growth, health and safety, future mobility and resilience, you will investigate, develop and test methods, systems and interventions that can create meaningful impact. You'll work collaboratively in groups, often with an industry or government partner, to address a pressing real-world challenge. You will develop ideas into a multidisciplinary creative project, drawing on perspectives from Art, Health and Wellbeing and creative health framework principles and practices, while critically examining the relationships between creative interventions and wider systems such as economics, politics, ethics, environment, culture, resources and human behaviour. In doing so, you will build networks, develop partnerships and strengthen your capacity to contribute to society specific solutions. The module is delivered in a multidisciplinary, industry- and partner-led environment through interactive lectures, case studies, seminars, workshops, and demonstrations and role-play, supported by online learning. You will actively participate in discussion, critique and applied learning throughout, using these opportunities to refine your ideas, develop your skills and build confidence. Alongside your creative practice, you will also be supported to explore enterprise and business development, enabling you to generate new opportunities and use creative innovation to contribute to more sustainable, cultural welfare, healthy and equitable futures. ","Code":"MOD008702","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"87888a2d-e1e4-4d15-99f5-23d14980203a"},{"Title":"Care Practices: Creative Future Health","Description":"In this module you’ll examine how communities can be active participants in the problem-finding and -solving process by identifying and mobilising capabilities and relationships in different social, political, and institutional environments. You’ll develop skills necessary to deliver specialist creative approaches relating to participatory creative art projects for diverse communities with non-linear and emergent behaviour. In this context, and when delivered effectively, your output can be used as effective therapeutic and advocacy tools by participants and the health sector. Recognising that health and wellbeing interventions take place in complex adaptive systems, you’ll undertake systematic learning processes that bring together key agents involved in the creation and service delivery, and understand how iterative, evidence-informed approaches can impact people of different ages and cultures.","Code":"","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"130fe7c0-277c-46fc-9ca3-3ebf2e55b2a1"},{"Title":"Art for Health and Wellbeing","Description":"On this module, you’ll integrate your values, beliefs, and passions with research and experimentation to define, develop and deliver a project that demonstrates mastery in Art, Health, and Wellbeing, applying your personal approach to issues surrounding current and future health. Postgraduate MBA Professional Experience option available Banking and Finance Become an all-rounder with skills and knowledge in both management and finance. Study for an internationally recognised qualification at ARU. Our course pages need JavaScript enabled to work correctly. Previous Section Course Overview Next Section Jump to a section Course overview Careers Teaching and modules Facilities Entry requirements Fees and funding Apply Apply now Book on a postgraduate open event MBA Professional Experience MBA Start date September 2027 January 2027 Location Chelmsford Award MBA Duration 1 year full-time Course durations vary slightly: 12 months (September starts), or 16 months (January starts). The Professional Experience option takes 24 months (September starts), or 28 months (January starts). Professional Experience Start date September 2027 January 2027 Location Chelmsford Award MBA Duration 2 years with professional experience Course durations vary slightly: 12 months (September starts), or 16 months (January starts). The Professional Experience option takes 24 months (September starts), or 28 months (January starts). £4,000 You may be eligible for our MBA Scholarship, which offers a fee reduction of up to £4,000. See if you're eligible for our MBA Scholarship If you’re looking for a rigorous grounding in management, strategy and leadership, as well as international finance and investment, this is the course for you. You’ll gain skills and experience by closely analysing real numbers and business plans alongside your classmates, and learn to trade in the safe, supportive environment of our Bloomberg Financial Market Lab. You’ll graduate with a valuable, career-boosting qualification that’s recognised around the world. Why ARU? Prepare for an exciting career in international finance and investment Gain knowledge and experience of management, strategy and leadership Develop your analytical and trading skills in our Bloomberg Financial Market Lab Enhance your employability with our optional Professional Experience year Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers An MBA signals to employers that you’re well-prepared for the fast-moving world of business. You’ll graduate with a solid understanding of the principles of business management and finance and advanced level skills across a range of financial areas. Graduation doesn’t have to be the end of your time with us. You could choose to continue your academic career with a PhD programme at ARU. Take advantage of our Alumni Scholarship and save £400 on your fees. What can you do with a Banking and Finance degree? Our MBA course prepares you for careers in more advanced areas of finance, such as working with complex data and using sophisticated mathematical and simulation modelling techniques. You'll also be able to manipulate data to aid decision- and policy-making. You may ultimately work at managerial and directorial levels in a wide range of financial environments. ARU Business students are European Champions A team of ARU students came first in Europe and sixth in the world in the prestigious Bloomberg Global Trading Challenge. How can ARU help with my employability and career development? We want you to be a step ahead when you graduate, so we offer: courses designed with employers tutors with professional industry knowledge hands-on learning which may include industry-led projects, placements or Professional Experience modules . Alongside your course, there are lots of other opportunities to build your skills and experience: add value to your CV with an ARU Certificate of Professional Development get involved in a thriving volunteering programme develop your brilliant business ideas work with businesses to make a social impact . We’re here to help you develop your CV and find that all-important role after graduation. Our Employability Service offers tailored career appointments, advice on writing your CV, help to complete job applications, and much more. You’ll have 24/7 access to an online Careers Centre too, which is packed with useful resources. The support continues after you graduate, with lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . Find out more about careers support at ARU . Teaching and modules A degree in banking and finance teaches you how to navigate complex financial systems, manage risk, and create opportunities that can shape industries and communities. Laura Muncey, Deputy Head of School Take a closer look at key subjects in business management and finance. You’ll study corporate finance and strategy, considering how financial information is relevant to decision-making and planning. You’ll also explore international financial markets, focussing on investment analysis and portfolio management. You’ll go on to learn about business strategy, approaches to leadership, and principles of marketing management that can be applied across different types of business. You’ll complete your MBA with your Postgraduate Major Project – a substantial research project focussed on a topic of particular interest and relevance to you. What will I study? MBA Professional Experience MBA Modules are subject to change and availability, and may vary by location. If you have the choice of optional modules, these are indicated with a *. Year 1 Applied Corporate Finance and Financial Strategy Principles of Marketing Management (30 credits) International Financial Markets and Investment Leadership and Change (15 credits) Management and Strategy (15 credits) Postgraduate Major Project Into ARU Module details Professional Experience You can choose to study with us over two years (full-time), and take Professional Experience modules in Year 2, with a Preparation for Professional Experience module in Year 1. Professional Experience modules are a great way to learn more about an industry. They take place in Year 2 of your course, with each module lasting approximately 12 weeks (or one trimester). Postgraduate MSc Biomedical Science If you’re already a working scientist, take a step towards Chartered Scientist status with this distance learning course. Our course pages need JavaScript enabled to work correctly. Previous Section Course Overview Next Section Jump to a section Course overview Careers Teaching and modules Facilities Entry requirements Fees and funding Apply Apply now Book on a postgraduate open event Start date September 2027 January 2027 Location Distance learning Award MSc Duration 3 years part-time You can choose to start this course in September or January. Course durations may vary slightly and you can contact us for more information. Course content and modules remain the same. 1st in the region for postgraduates progressing into senior roles. Source: Graduate Outcomes Survey 2026 Offered by distance learning and designed to fit in with your working life, our part-time degree is guided by an employers’ panel that includes the NHS. You can tailor your studies by choosing a specialist pathology area to either enhance your knowledge of your current field or open up a new career path in a different specialism or an area such as management. A number of activities will be carried out in your workplace and are aimed at evidence-gathering as well as improving employability skills appropriate to your work environment. Accredited by IBMS Our MSc Biomedical Science degree is accredited by the Institute of Biomedical Science and can help you take a step towards Chartered Scientist status. Why ARU? Study by distance learning while you work Enhance your existing knowledge or explore new areas Tailor your studies by choosing a specialist pathology area Join a course that’s accredited by the Institute of Biomedical Science Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers Enhance your career prospects and take a major step towards Chartered Scientist status. You’ll be able to personalise your studies to reflect your career goals as a biomedical scientist. Graduation doesn’t have to be the end of your time with us. You could choose to continue your academic career with a research programme at ARU, such as our MPhil/PhD Biomedical Science . How can ARU help with my employability and career development? We want you to be a step ahead when you graduate, so we offer: courses designed with employers tutors with professional industry knowledge hands-on learning which may include industry-led projects, placements or Professional Experience modules . Alongside your course, there are lots of other opportunities to build your skills and experience: add value to your CV with an ARU Certificate of Professional Development get involved in a thriving volunteering programme develop your brilliant business ideas work with businesses to make a social impact . We’re here to help you develop your CV and find that all-important role after graduation. Our Employability Service offers tailored career appointments, advice on writing your CV, help to complete job applications, and much more. You’ll have 24/7 access to an online Careers Centre too, which is packed with useful resources. The support continues after you graduate, with lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . Find out more about careers support at ARU . Teaching and modules You’ll develop an understanding of disciplinary methodologies, both theoretical and research-based, with a full understanding of the principles of pathology, and illustrate this through a series of learning activities. We’ll support you to develop your skills in biomedical research as you make your research proposal for your final year project. You’ll also have the opportunity to develop a range of management skills that can be applied to your own workplace in any of the pathology specialisms. We’ll encourage you to make full use of the facilities and staff in your work environment. What will I study? Modules are subject to change and availability, and may vary by location. If you have the choice of optional modules, these are indicated with a *. Year 1 Moving towards Mastery General Pathology Research Methods in Biomedical Science An Introduction to Management in Biomedical Science Year 2 Biomedical Specialisms 1 - Epidemiology and Pathogenesis Biomedical Specialisms 2 - Diagnostics and Treatment Year 3 Masters Project Module details How is Biomedical Science assessed? At the end of each module, you’ll present a portfolio of evidence for assessment. There are no examinations. Self-evaluation is an important part of your learning throughout this course and for all modules (except the Masters Project) you’ll produce a critical reflective commentary justifying your approach. You’ll be able to demonstrate the required depth and systematic understanding of knowledge in applied areas and across areas, and the ability to work with theoretical and research-based knowledge at the forefront of your academic discipline. Who teaches Biomedical Science at ARU? Your tutors include ARU lecturers and Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC)-registered hospital practitioners: Senior Biomedical and Clinical Scientists. Dr Richard Jones Senior Lecturer in Biomedical Science Dr Grisha Pirianov Senior Lecturer Facilities Enjoy a range of facilities designed to support your studies and career development. These include extensive library and IT resources, and careers support through our Employability Service . After you graduate, you’ll have lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre .
