Fees and Paying for University Facilities Outstanding student support Join our postgraduate student community and: benefit from award-winning learning facilities, including extensive library and IT resources learn from expert staff who will guide your research interests and career development receive full support from our Employability Service , while you're studying with us and after you graduate access support, should you need it, with study skills, health and wellbeing, and more. Links with industry and professional recognition With strong links to Local Authorities and schools, we’re experienced providers of in-house training for schools and academies locally, nationally and internationally. Our Education courses are practice-focused and relevant to today’s classroom. Take a guided tour and meet our students . Lecturers Previous. Next. Gill Thomas Senior Lecturer Gill Thomas's profile page [email protected] Phil Kirkman Associate Professor Phil Kirkman's profile page [email protected] Follow Phil on Twitter Simon Pratt-Adams Associate Professor in Academic Development Simon Pratt-Adams's profile page [email protected] 01245 683 520 Follow Simon on Twitter Careers Whether you’re a teacher or lecturer with some management responsibilities, a leader in an educational institution, or an education leader in a different sector, you can enhance your impact and improve your career opportunities with our MBA course. An MBA in Educational Leadership and Management can help your career progression and will open up new opportunities in senior management, strategic leadership, directorships and consultancy. If you’ve completed an undergraduate degree, this higher-level award will help you to develop a deeper knowledge of your subject. Masters study will also enhance your transferable skills such as independent and team working, verbal and written communication, critical and creative thinking, presentation skills, research and project management, and increased self-confidence. This course can also be your first step towards working in research or university lecturing. When you graduate, you might choose to progress to doctoral studies, such as our School of Education PhD . var configOptions = {"HeroIntroduction":"","HeroImage":null,"CourseInfoDisclosureTitle":"Combining course options","CourseInfoDisclosure":"","StartDateDisclaimer":"","AdditionalInfoSectionTitle":"","AdditionalInfoSectionText":"","AdditionalInfoTitle":"","AdditionalInfo":"","StaffHeader":"","StaffRichText":[],"CourseOptions":[{"Duration":{"Name":"2 years part-time","Id":"25c0270c-414a-4f1a-9051-74ede4591875"},"StartDate":[{"Name":"September 2027","Id":"12ba467c-68e1-4784-9b56-3b8ccb7cca9f"}],"Location":[{"ShortName":"Distance learning","AstraLocationCode":"NON","DisplayOrder":0,"Id":"ac93c34f-43de-40d2-8b8c-f30ce534db91"}],"Modules":[{"Title":"Year 1","CoreModuleSectionHeading":"Core modules","OptionModuleSectionHeading":"","Summary":"

During Year 1, you'll develop a deep understanding of factors which shape ways of thinking, working, and learning in educational environments.

As an education leader, it is essential that you can identify, understand and develop a coherent strategic approach to management. You’ll focus on developing your understanding of effective planning and change management to achieve strategic organisational aims.

You’ll critically analyse research to develop your understanding of your organisation and its wider context through the lens of several key leadership and development models. This will help you evaluate and review existing practices and organisational structures, as well as plan and deliver sustained improvements that match your vision and values.

You’ll also have the opportunity to develop specialist knowledge and expertise by engaging in work or literature-based professional enquiry into an area of interest, relating to education.

You'll show your progress though a variety of methods that draw on ‘live’ opportunities for learning from your current role. You'll also be supported to develop and refine your writing and presentation skills for different audiences, helping you develop a range of approaches to presenting evidence and action planning.

Modules are subject to change and availability.

","CoreModules":[{"Title":"Leading Educational Change and Improvement","Description":"Within this module students will engage in theory and wider research in relation to performance evaluation, leading change, and improvement planning and change management. Students are required to use metrics and their knowledge and understanding of benchmarking performance in order to identify an area of practice that would benefit from improvement they will produce a critically reflective commentary that will provide the underpinning rationale for the action plan, linked to models of good practice. The commentary will be required to evidence a deep level of understanding of change management and include proposed strategies for mitigating against any perceived barriers to change. ","Code":"MOD003361","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"89a7f60d-6e2a-47a2-8535-0c08b4b33adc"},{"Title":"Strategic Management in Education","Description":"This module will focus on developing a deeper understanding of effective strategic planning in order to achieve organisational aims. Students will need to be able to make clear links between the strategic planning and the strategic vision of their institutions. They will engage with theoretical models that will encourage them to evaluate and review existing provision and to consider planning for improved management within their institutions. They will combine independent reading and wider research with focused work based learning to draw from real context experience and practice. They will develop an implementation plan in the form of a presentation complete with rationale and reflective commentary. ","Code":"MOD003360","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"d0747ee9-b003-42e5-a131-27c3c7e267ba"},{"Title":"Professional Enquiry for Education","Description":"This module offers students the opportunity to develop specialist knowledge and expertise in an area of personal and professional interest, relating to education. The notion of enquiry used in this module is broad and is intended to reflect the contributions which students bring to advanced study of education from both their academic and professional contexts. Students may pursue individual or small group enquiries or a larger group of students may work, with a specialist tutor, to enquire into an agreed subject area together.","Code":"MOD003706","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"b9376920-f1e1-420d-ad19-93ecd2a6ccf1"}],"OptionalModules":[],"Id":"5d35d7df-447d-430b-a4ae-1b86ab83775d","SelectedModule":false},{"Title":"Year 2","CoreModuleSectionHeading":"Core modules","OptionModuleSectionHeading":"","Summary":"

Across Year 2 of your MBA, you’ll engage in critical evaluations of systems for managing information, relationships, communication, and reporting. We consider wider research and compare and contrast practices across other organisations to learn from successful models.

You’ll develop your ability to ask and answer meaningful questions in relation to professional practice. You’ll also demonstrate your critical understanding of research designs to draw careful and evidence-based conclusions from complex qualitative and quantitative data.

You’ll be assessed in a variety of ways, with assessments drawing on learning opportunities arising from your current role. The assessments will help you to develop critical, reflective, evidence-based and systematic approaches to leadership and management.

Modules are subject to change and availability.

","CoreModules":[{"Title":"Research Methodology (30 credits)","Description":"With the increased emphasis on research in contemporary healthcare, it’s essential that you are familiar with research methodology. The ability to critically analyse and synthesise research is a necessary skill for all students, to be able to apply research in all areas of specialist interest in the delivery of effective patient care. You’ll revisit existing knowledge of the research process and we’ll assist you in further developing skills of critical analysis and synthesis. You’ll also have the opportunity to critically appraise the ethical dimensions of research studies that seek to develop, improve and advance healthcare services.","Code":"MOD006793","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"9465ae1e-e3af-409b-b6c2-bb155e799867"},{"Title":"Developing Effective Management Systems","Description":"This module will enable students to engage in a process of critical evaluation and analysis to focus upon systems for managing information, relationships including staff and stakeholders, communication and reporting. Ensuring knowledge is managed effectively in order to provide comprehensive information that will facilitate efficient leadership and management in relation to staff, stakeholders, finance, facilities and measures for dealing with wider policy issues. This module encourages students to focus on internal and external systems in order to engage in a meaning review of their own organisation whilst drilling down to evaluate procedural systems and the effectiveness of information management. The module will concentrate on programme rather than project management and students will not only review and evaluate their own systems and processes, but also engage in wider research by comparing and contrasting management systems across other organisations; either from education, associated disciplines such as health or social care or from industry. ","Code":"MOD003453","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"8e93d336-6aad-415d-a1eb-907b69dc2d2d"},{"Title":"Postgraduate Major Project","Description":"This project enables you to demonstrate the ability to raise significant and meaningful questions in relation to your professional practice, which may involve working at the current limits of theoretical and/or research understanding. You'll be expected to demonstrate critical understanding of research methodologies and methods with particular reference to Reflective Practice and Action Research and apply fitness for purpose criteria for the purposes of undertaking research and/or investigating professional practice. You should be able to draw meaningful and justifiable conclusions from information which may be complex or contradictory, expand or redefine existing knowledge and develop new approaches to changing situations. You'll be expected to communicate in an articulate and appropriately clear and elegant fashion and will be capable of evaluating your work from the perspective of an autonomous reflective learner. Postgraduate MSc Engineering Management Develop the skills to lead complex projects, teams and organisations while driving sustainable change. Our course pages need JavaScript enabled to work correctly. Previous Section Course Overview Next Section Jump to a section Course overview Careers Teaching and modules Facilities Entry requirements Fees and funding Apply Apply now Book on a postgraduate open event MSc 2 years part-time MSc Start date September 2027 January 2027 Location Chelmsford Award MSc Duration 1 year full-time Course durations vary slightly: 12 months (September starts), or 16 months (January and May starts). The part-time option takes 28 months (September starts), or 33 months (January starts). 2 years part-time You can choose to study this course part-time, and start in September or January. The course durations vary slightly: 28 months (September starts) or 33 months (January starts). Course content and modules remain the same. 1st in the region for postgraduates progressing into senior roles. Source: Graduate Outcomes Survey 2026 Designed for engineers and recent graduates, this Master's degree prepares you to progress into senior management roles. Combining engineering, management and practical decision-making, you’ll tackle real-world challenges across project management, operations, quality, finance, supply chains and sustainability. Study with us, and become a confident, future-focused engineering leader. Why ARU? Develop your leadership skills, with a focus on engineering projects and organisations Build practical expertise across finance, operations, supply chains and contract management Apply your learning to real engineering management challenges Choose full- or part-time study to fit your career and lifestyle Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers This course marked my first academic experience in England and played an important role in shaping my career. Amanda Del Rio Suzart, PhD student Gain the confidence, knowledge and leadership skills to progress your engineering career. When you graduate, you’ll be ready to apply your engineering expertise to management and leadership roles. You’ll have the skills to lead with confidence, manage people, projects and technical organisations, solve complex problems, make informed decisions and drive sustainable change. This MSc can support progression into roles in engineering, manufacturing, technology, operations and project management. What can you do with an MSc Engineering Management? As a graduate, you can progress into roles across the engineering and technology sectors. Previous graduates have moved into positions such as Operations Manager and Planning Manager, using their engineering expertise alongside advanced management and leadership skills. You’re also in the perfect position to continue your academic career, with our Engineering and the Built Environment PhD . Take advantage of our Alumni Scholarship and save £400 on your fees. Where have previous graduates worked? Our graduates have gone on to roles with organisations including: Anglia Water Services Unipart Tesla Engineering Ltd Ipsos How can ARU help with my employability and career development? We want you to be a step ahead when you graduate, so we offer: courses designed with employers tutors with professional industry knowledge hands-on learning which may include industry-led projects, placements or Professional Experience modules . Alongside your course, there are lots of other opportunities to build your skills and experience: add value to your CV with an ARU Certificate of Professional Development get involved in a thriving volunteering programme develop your brilliant business ideas work with businesses to make a social impact . We’re here to help you develop your CV and find that all-important role after graduation. Our Employability Service offers tailored career appointments, advice on writing your CV, help to complete job applications, and much more. You’ll have 24/7 access to an online Careers Centre too, which is packed with useful resources. The support continues after you graduate, with lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . Find out more about careers support at ARU . Teaching and modules This MSc prepares you for a career in the management of engineering projects, in an increasingly dynamic environment. Dr Olalekan Oshodi, Lecturer Develop your management skills and discover your leadership style. You’ll build a broad understanding of approaches to managing engineering projects, people and organisations. Through practical learning, you'll explore project and engineering management systems, quality assurance, and finance and cost management. You'll also develop your own approach to leadership and decision making. You’ll consider the economic, legal, political, sustainability and environmental factors that shape engineering management. Finally, you’ll complete a substantial research project on a relevant topic of your choice. What will I study? MSc 2 years part-time MSc Modules are subject to change and availability, and may vary by location. If you have the choice of optional modules, these are indicated with a *. Year 1 Management Theory (15 credits) Project Management Systems (15 credits) Engineering Management Systems (15 credits) Engineering Quality Management (15 credits) Research Design and Methods (15 credits) Economic, Political and Legal Framework (15 credits) Sustainability and Environmental Management (15 credits) Cost and Financial Management (15 credits) Dissertation (60 credits) Into ARU Module details 2 years part-time It's possible to study this course part-time. You'll take the same modules as MSc/MA students, but sometimes in a different order or in different years. As a part-time student you'll typically study for twice as long as full-time students. For example if the MSc/MA course takes one year, you can expect to study over two years, though for some courses this may vary. Who teaches Engineering Management at ARU? Read profiles of teaching and research staff on this course. Dr Olalekan Oshodi Lecturer Dr Samuel J. McMaster Senior Lecturer Negar Ahmadpoor Lecturer Dr Mohamed Yehia Senior Lecturer Facilities Enjoy a range of facilities designed to support your studies and career development. These include extensive library and IT resources, and careers support through our Employability Service . After you graduate, you’ll have lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . You can also access support, should you need it, with study skills, health and wellbeing, and more. Take a guided tour and meet our students . Please enable JavaScript for "Fees Information" section to function. Other equivalent qualifications may be accepted for entry to this course; please email [email protected] for further information. Applicants to undergraduate courses can also check our information about undergraduate entry qualifications . You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your course. 2 years part-time Important additional notes Our published entry requirements are a guide only and our decision will be based on your overall suitability for the course as well as whether you meet the minimum entry requirements. Other equivalent qualifications may be accepted for entry to this course; please email [email protected] for further information. Applicants to undergraduate courses can also check our information about undergraduate entry qualifications . You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your course. International students We welcome applications from international and EU students, and accept a range of international qualifications. See international and EU entry requirements See information about application deadlines You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your course. English language requirements If English is not your first language, you'll need to make sure you meet our English language requirements for postgraduate courses . Check the section ' English language requirements ' for IELTS requirements. Please enable JavaScript for "Fees Information" section to function. Fees and funding UK students MSc 2 years part-time MSc £12,275 UK students starting 2027/28 (full-time, per year) Fees are payable upfront, in full or in instalments, but there's no need to pay until you've accepted an offer to study with us. Find out more about paying your fees and about postgraduate loans and funding . 2 years part-time £6,137 UK students starting 2027/28 (part-time, per year) Fees are payable upfront, in full or in instalments, but there's no need to pay until you've accepted an offer to study with us. Find out more about paying your fees and about postgraduate loans and funding . International students MSc 2 years part-time MSc £20,925 International students starting 2027/28 (full-time, per year) You can pay your fees upfront, in full or in two instalments. We will ask for a deposit of £4,000 or a sponsorship letter Find out about paying your fees . 2 years part-time £9,412 International students starting 2027/28 (part-time, per year) You can pay your fees upfront, in full or in two instalments. We will ask for a deposit of £4,000 or a sponsorship letter Find out about paying your fees . Part-time fees Part-time course fees assume that you’re studying at half the rate of a full-time student (50% intensity). Course fees will be different if you study over a longer period. All fees are for guidance purposes only. Your offer letter will contain full details of credits and fees, or you can contact us if you'd like more information. Paying for university There are several ways to fund postgraduate study, and we recommend finding out more before you apply. Explore: postgraduate loans and other funding scholarships and bursaries for UK and international students our Alumni Scholarship , worth 20% off fees for ARU graduates. Postgraduate English Language and Intercultural Communication MPhil, PhD Research ( full-time, part-time) Cambridge January 2027, April, September 2027 Distance-learning supervision available on this course. Apply online For application deadlines visit our how to apply page . Overview Our PhD research programmes will allow you to join one of our research projects or explore your own interests in English Language and Intercultural Communication, supported by the expertise of our staff. Full description You’ll be allocated two supervisors, with additional staff members available if necessary. Our supervisors are experienced in most areas of English language and intercultural communication, with a strong focus on contemporary European/migrant cinema and literature, second-language acquisition, urban multilingualism, socio-linguistic theory. You’ll conduct your research in a collaborative environment with strong links to a number of other centres in our University and the wider community. We host and take part in many research oriented events for staff and postgraduate students, including our regular Faculty and departmental research seminars and international conferences. Our seminars will give you the chance to present papers in a supportive setting. We’re also key contributors to our Faculty's Anglia Ruskin Research Centre for Intercultural and Multilingual Studies (ARRCIMS) who organise many talks you’ll be welcome to attend, or even contribute to. These events, along with our online environment, will help you connect with other research students from a range of disciplines. You could also benefit from financial support – we allocate a substantial sum every year towards postgraduate travel and conference expenses, as well as some bursaries. All your subject-specific studies will be enhanced and supported by our University-wide training sessions, where you’ll gain important research expertise in areas like ethics, presentations, intellectual property and digital scholarship. Completion times MPhil: full-time 1-3 years, part-time 2-4 years. PhD via progression from MPhil, including that period: full-time 2.5-5 years, part-time 3.5-6 years. PhD: full-time 2-4 years, part-time 3-6 years. For further guidance on the duration of research degrees please refer to the Research Degrees Regulations . PhD project opportunities in the Faculty of Arts, Humanities, Education and Social Sciences World-leading research at ARU Anglia Ruskin Research Centre for Intercultural and Multilingual Studies (ARRCIMS) Centre for Media, Arts & Creative Technologies School of Humanities and Social Sciences research Supervision and support Our permanent supervisory staff are recognised experts in their field, and have produced a number of influential books, journal articles and edited collections. Our research expertise includes: Professor Guido Rings , PD, PhD: migrant cinema and literature, questions of identity in postcolonial European narrative or film, contemporary Latin American cinema and literature, intercultural communication. Dr Sebastian Rasinger , PhD: second language acquisition and urban multilingualism, with a particular focus on language use and its impact on linguistic development and the emergence of ethnic and cultural identity. Dr Bettina Beinhoff , Dr Bettina Beinhoff, MPhil (Cantab), PhD (Cantab): acquisition of second/foreign language phonology, linguistic and cultural identities (especially attitudes, stereotypes and identity construction in multilingual contexts and dialect contact situations) and sociolinguistic aspects of constructed languages. Where you'll research Your department and faculty At the School of Humanities and Social Sciences, we believe in thinking critically about the past, present and future to challenge perceptions and better understand communities and people. With expertise from gender issues to literary analysis to exploring how the past has shaped our modern world, all our staff members are active researchers. This is reflected in our teaching, allowing us to support our students with the latest theories and practices, as well as essential employability advice. Visit your department Where can I study? Cambridge Our campus is close to the centre of Cambridge, often described as the perfect student city. Explore our Cambridge campus Specialist facilities You’ll have access to our fully-equipped language centre, the British Film Institute, the University of Cambridge Library, and our own campus library. You’ll also be able to use our Faculty’s PhD room, where all our doctoral students can meet up to work and take an active part in our postgraduate student community. Fees & funding Course fees UK students, 2026/27 (per year) £5,238 UK students, 2026/27 (part-time, per year) £2,619 International students, 2026/27 (per year) £17,500 International students, 2026/27 (part-time, per year) £8,750 Bench fees In some cases extra costs known as bench fees will be charged for a postgraduate research degree. These are to cover additional/exceptional costs directly related to a specific research project. Some examples of these costs are (the list is not exhaustive): equipment hire, access costs to specialist equipment/workshops, volunteer expenses, specialist tissue/cell culture, specialist reagents or materials, specialist software, access to specialist databases, data collection costs, specialist media, recording or digital storage needs. We charge bench fees in bands. They may apply for every year of your course. These bands are the same for full- and part-time students. If you have to pay bench fees this will be made clear at your interview, and stated in your offer letter. For 2026/27 the bench fee bands are: £500 £1,400 £2,400 £4,900 £9,800 PhD by Published Work Initial registration: £1,700 Full registration: £4,900 Writing up fees 2026/27 £1,400 How do I pay my fees? You can pay your fees upfront, in full or in instalments – though you won't need to pay until you've accepted an offer to study with us. Find out more about paying your fees . Funding For advice on the Doctoral Loan and other sources of funding, including ARU scholarships, visit our finance guide for postgraduate researchers . You might also find The Alternative Guide to Postgraduate Funding helpful. ARU research ARU's academic excellence was recognised in 2021, as part of the Research Excellence Framework (REF), an exercise which assesses the quality of academic research. Sixteen areas of our work were classed as generating world-leading research . The results showed that we're making a significant impact on the societies we live in. Careers We’ll provide you with many opportunities for career development and training, in areas like writing up a paper for publication; placing an academic article; giving a conference paper; the doctoral writing style; updates on research methods and literature searches; internet training; editing skills for doctoral research; subsequent monograph publication; and dealing with festivals, agents, and publishers. You might also be able to take on teaching responsibilities in the department, or organise research events like seminars and conferences. In conjunction with the University’s research support, you can request specific support for writing-up, conference papers, general research methods and other research skills if you need it. Contact details If you're interested in finding out more about research study opportunities in this area, please email [email protected] . Entry requirements MPhil or PhD with progression from MPhil: You’ll need a Bachelors degree or equivalent with first or upper second class honours, in a related subject area. PhD: You’ll need a Masters degree or equivalent in a related subject area. Please note we consider candidates for PhD with progression from MPhil in the first instance. If you want to be considered for direct entry to the PhD route then this can be discussed at interview if you are shortlisted. Please note you’ll also need to provide academic justification for this request. If English is not your first language, you'll require a minimum IELTS score of 6.5, with a minimum of 5.5 in each component (or equivalent test). If you don't meet our English language requirements, we offer a range of courses which could help you achieve the level required for entry. Loading... Entry requirements are not currently available, please try again later. Important additional notes Our published entry requirements are a guide only and our decision will be based on your overall suitability for the programme as well as whether you meet the minimum entry requirements. Contact our postgraduate research degree team for more information about studying a PhD, MPhil or Professional Doctorate at ARU. You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your research programme. Jump to a section Introduction Course options Key facts Student experience Teaching and assessment Entry requirements Fees and paying for university Facilities and showcase Lecturers Careers Introduction Take your passion for reading to the next level explore important topics such as global citizenship, human and animal rights, equality, and truth with our Master's in English Literature. Hear from Maisie Studying English Literature at ARU Hear student Maisie talk about how our MA English Literature helped further her passions. Already have an ARU degree? You may be eligible for our Alumni Scholarship for students starting postgraduate courses. If you love reading and want to advance and gain research skills that will provide new directions for future employment and form the basis for further study, this is the postgraduate course for you. The core modules focus on three key areas: Literature and Landscape; Utopias and Dystopias; and a special topic, such as life writing or children’s literature. You'll study texts – both fiction and non-fiction – from different periods and a range of genres and consider the relationship between each text and the political, social, historical, scientific and/or religious contexts of its production. You'll gain skills in research, critical thinking, fluent expression, and enterprise, and can add further strings to your bow with optional modules including novel writing, publishing, and history. Read more Teaching times 2025-26 (subject to change for 2026-27) Trimester 2: Monday 6-8pm, Thursday 11am-1pm All English Literature and History modules are daytime delivery, while Creative Writing and Publishing options run on Monday and Thursday evenings. You’ll develop skills and knowledge through a range of teaching and learning methods and by producing essays, presentations, annotated bibliographies and a major research project in the form of a dissertation. You can attend events organised by our Cambridge Writing Centre , including guest talks and live lit jams, where you can showcase your own creative writing and make new contacts in the industry. The impact of our English Language and Literature research was judged as "world-leading" in the Research Excellence Framework 2021 (REF2021) . Read Cassie's Spotlight interview ARU Spotlight Podcast Dr Cassie Gorman Hear Course Leader Cassie talk about her project to unearth manuscripts by 17th-century women writers, and how studying English Literature helped her gain confidence to voice new ideas. Take a guided tour and meet our students. Take a closer look Our Creative Showcase shines a spotlight on what makes ARU creative and cultural – our spaces, places and people. Find out more about our community, the difference we make, the stories we tell, and the things that inspire us. You can also explore the work of our graduating students in our digital graduate showcase. Lecturers Previous. Next. If you are a teacher, you could study with us to update your knowledge and further your existing career, or even move into another discipline. Or, if you are looking to move on to an academic post, this course will give you the research skills you will need for your future career. Graduation doesn’t have to be the end of your time with us. You could choose to continue your academic career with a research programme at ARU, such as our PhD English Literature or PhD English Language and Linguistics . Take advantage of our Alumni Scholarship and save £400 on your fees. Apply now for MA English Literature Our course pages need JavaScript enabled for you to apply. Want to talk to someone? ","CoreModules":[{"Title":"Into ARU","Description":"Entering higher education is exciting; but it can also be a daunting experience. At ARU, we want all our students to make the most of the opportunities higher education provides, reach your potential, become lifelong learners and find fulfilling careers. However, we appreciate that the shift from secondary education, or a return to formal education is, in itself, quite a journey. This module is designed to ease that transition. You'll be enrolled on it as soon as you receive an offer from ARU so you can begin to learn about university life before your course starts. Through Into ARU, you'll explore a virtual land modelled around ARU values: Courage, Innovation, Community, Integrity, Responsibility, and Ambition. This innovative module is designed as a game, where you collect knowledge and complete mini tasks. You'll proceed at your own pace, though we you to have completed your Into ARU exploration by week 6. If for any reason you're unable to complete by that date, we'll signpost to existing services so that we can be confident that you are supported.","Code":"MOD999910","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"4f3c4a41-2e3f-49aa-8860-037c9fba5c37"},{"Title":"Research Methods in Practice","Description":"In this module you'll learn advanced research methods through a hands-on approach. Each week, we’ll introduce you to various methods of study, such as language analysis (written and/or spoken) and archival research, and take you through the processes of how to undertake each type of research step by step. This will allow you to become a confident independent researcher and give you the skills to undergo a research project from the ground up. This module will equip you with a structure and the skills and methodologies that you'll need for your dissertation, develop your confidence in identifying and engaging with primary and secondary sources, and teach you vital research skills that will be important in your professional career.","Code":"MOD010703","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"fa1d5ece-70ab-448c-9a98-f9ba081ed30e"},{"Title":"Major Project in English Literature","Description":"This project enables you to demonstrate: the ability to raise significant and meaningful questions in relation to your specialism; depth of knowledge which may involve working at the current limits of theoretical and / or research understanding; critical understanding of method and its relationship to knowledge awareness of and ability to develop solutions to ethical dilemmas likely to arise in your research; the ability to draw meaningful and justifiable conclusions from information which may be complex or contradictory; the capability to expand or redefine existing knowledge; to develop new approaches to changing situations / and contribute to the development of best practice; the ability to communicate these processes in a clear and elegant fashion; the capability to evaluate your work from the perspective of an autonomous reflective learner. This module involves secondary research only and does not require primary data generation. You will be required to carry out a literature review using publicly available documents. Any use of the internet is limited to searching for publicly available documents only.","Code":"MOD010709","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"711be868-2db7-4459-8049-591f3c036529"}],"OptionalModules":[{"Title":"Utopias and Dystopias","Description":"In this interdisciplinary module you will explore a varied selection of texts which reflect the development of both utopian visions and dystopian fears in literature throughout history. You will analyse texts – including political, historical and religious writings – from different periods and a range of genres and consider the relationship between each text and the contexts within which it was produced. You will evaluate relevant critical and theoretical debates and reflect on ambiguities and uncertainties in the way the words ‘dystopia’ and ‘utopia’ have been used and understood. The term ‘utopian’, in particular, with its uncertain etymology (‘no place’ or ‘pleasant place’) is fraught with contradiction. Indicative topics for study include: Thomas More’s Utopia and other Early Modern utopias; utopian and dystopian thought in the writings of the English Civil Wars; Swift, Johnson and anti-Utopianism; the late nineteenth-century utopian visions of William Morris and Edward Bellamy; Huxley, Orwell and their influences; Katharine Burdekin, Rex Warner and the twentieth-century antifascist dystopia; Feminist dystopias and utopias; Octavia Butler and environmental dystopias; Prayaag Akbar and global dystopian writing.","Code":"MOD010704","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"da453ea3-5be0-4add-97c1-5ff7a1de5cd5"},{"Title":"Special Topic in English Literature","Description":"This Special Topic module gives you the opportunity to study a topic that will be taught by a member of staff whose particular academic interests and/or research is reflected in the area. A topic may be the study of a single author, a group of cognate authors, an aspect of literary theory. Topics may also cover a literary genre such as Life Writing or Children’s Literature. As the designated topics vary from-year-to-year you will consult with tutors to check which topics are being offered. This information is always made public in good time for informed student choices to be made. In this module, you'll investigate issues of changing landscapes, climate crises, and ecology through a range of texts and through arguments from environmental literary criticism. While the period focus in each delivery may differ (eg a focus on the nineteenth-century might be specified), you'll develop a working knowledge of conceptual issues involved in analysing the literary and cultural representation of landscapes, from the mountainous and wild to the flat and urban. Indicative topics for study include poetry, fiction, essays, and life-writing by William Wordsworth, George Eliot, Thomas Hardy, Mary Shelley, Jane Austen, John Ruskin, Mary Seacole, and Mary Prince. Contemporary fiction and poetry by Ali Smith, Margaret Atwood, Alice Oswald, Sarah Perry and others may also be included in some deliveries and topics.","Code":"MOD010705","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"a6798b78-8c79-4bfb-856c-82e3c190b36e"},{"Title":"Literature and Landscape","Description":"In this module, you'll investigate issues of changing landscapes, climate crises, and ecology through a range of texts and through arguments from environmental literary criticism. While the period focus in each delivery may differ (eg a focus on the nineteenth-century might be specified), you will develop a working knowledge of conceptual issues involved in analysing the literary and cultural representation of landscapes, from the mountainous and wild to the flat and urban. Indicative topics for study include poetry, fiction, essays, and life-writing by William Wordsworth, George Eliot, Thomas Hardy, Mary Shelley, Jane Austen, John Ruskin, Mary Seacole, and Mary Prince. Contemporary fiction and poetry by Ali Smith, Margaret Atwood, Alice Oswald, Sarah Perry and others may also be included in some deliveries and topics such as Shakespeare and Ecocriticism and Early Modern pastoral in others.","Code":"MOD010706","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"c88dab47-bda8-42d3-be16-4b32c004bebb"},{"Title":"Workshop: the Novel","Description":"In this module you'll study and practice the techniques of novel writing. It is designed in a workshop format. To maximise the use of group feedback and feedback from the tutor, we'll undertake many exercises in workshop time, but you'll be given longer writing exercises to consolidate your classroom learning, and you'll be expected to complete these each week in preparation for class. You'll undertake a series of structured exercises designed to develop your techniques in, for instance, characterisation, dialogue, plot structure, the selection and effectiveness of different points of view, setting, time frames and time sequencing. You'll read extracts from a number of well-known novels and the writing of other students to underpin our discussions of technique. As the module progresses, you'll be expected to reflect critically both on your own writing and that of your peers, as well as developing your critical judgement. This module will also incorporate practical advice on agents, the marketplace, and how to get work published.","Code":"MOD000520","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"8ee2fd61-dff7-422a-a300-5e9c16cb1bea"},{"Title":"Independent Research Project ","Description":"In this module, you'll have the opportunity to plan, develop and execute an independent research project of your own choice, such as an extended piece of academic research or a project in partnership with an outside organisation. This is an exciting opportunity for you to pursue your passions and work in an area that fascinates you. The project will be based on original research and extensive secondary source analysis to make a novel and exciting contribution to the literature or public sector. You'll work closely with a supervisor who will offer advice and guide you through the project’s completion. The project will need to be negotiated and decided prior to the beginning of trimester 2, so we can ensure it is viable and staff expertise is available.","Code":"MOD010702","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"ac319383-900e-4265-a597-4288e7138eb5"},{"Title":"Special Topic in Creative Writing/English Literature","Description":"This Special Topic module gives you the opportunity to study a particular genre or topic that will be taught by a practising writer whose current or recent writing has been in this area. This module enables you to extend the specific writing techniques you've learned in other modules to a particular genre, or to work on a particular set of ideas or challenges. A topic may be the study of a particular genre such as writing for children, creative non-fiction, historical fiction, or crime writing, or may be the study of a particular topic such as adaptation (for instance, exploring the challenges and techniques used by writers working on adapting one text into another: novel to film, film to play, poem to short story). As the designated topics vary from year to year, you'll consult with tutors to check which topics are being offered.","Code":"MOD000522","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"97b25074-815b-4669-8d6d-171fab0d0e58"},{"Title":"Patterns of Story: Fiction and its Forms","Description":"This module is a literary history course for writers. It examines the history of the novel from its formation in the eighteenth century through to some of its more modern forms, examining along the way some of the cultural and social contexts that have helped to shape these changing patterns of story. It will include some narrative theory. Although the course is chronological it is not a history of form that is teleological - different patterns of story emerge and re-emerge at particular cultural moments and eighteenth-century forms such as the picaresque are, for instance, re-invented by postmodernist writers such as Angela Carter, who famously said 'I like to put new wine into old bottles in such a way as to make the old bottles explode'. Through the reading and discussion of recent and classic books on the history and structure of the novel by writers such as Jane Smiley, Christopher Booker, John Mullen and Dorothea Brande, you'll consider what it means to write novels and what it means to be a writer, as well as considering the ways in which some contemporary writers use and reuse much older forms of storytelling and patterns of story.","Code":"MOD003085","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"1b2d25ee-346b-44b6-b7fc-5d7857eaefee"},{"Title":"Creativity and Content in Publishing","Description":"This module introduces you to the world of contemporary publishing in all its variety, and to the processes by which publishers work with authors and designers to shape text and image for specific audiences. You'll cover issues, principles and practices related to the commissioning, concept development and packaging of a wide range of publications across digital and print platforms: from academic to children’s books, illustrated nonfiction to social media content marketing. The module stresses the importance of determining the strategic direction of a publisher's list, the publisher's relationship with content creators, an understanding of the zeitgeist or cultural context, and the need for quality control in managing editorial projects. Workshops enable you to experiment and develop the practical skills that you'll need when working in a publishing environment, such as copywriting, blurb writing, digital marketing, proposal development and project management, communicating with different audiences and pitching. Visiting industry specialists will contribute specialist insights and case studies.","Code":"MOD000527","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"80ed46c2-eed0-43e6-87e9-3f922b228960"},{"Title":"Every Object Tells a Story: Material Culture and Heritage in History","Description":"Objects are vital to study, both for the public and the academic historian. They allow us to understand past societies in exciting and original ways and to communicate history to diverse audiences. After all, we all make sense of the world through the objects around us, such as the chair, computer, desk or glasses through which you might be reading this very description. People of the past were no different. Their everyday lives were dictated by what they had, what they could make, what they used and what they worked hard to acquire. No matter what period or type of history you are most interested in, objects will allow you to study the topic in new and interesting ways. In this module, you'll learn about the role of objects in heritage and academic studies. ","CoreModules":[{"Title":"Into ARU","Description":"Entering higher education is exciting; but it can also be a daunting experience. At ARU, we want all our students to make the most of the opportunities higher education provides, reach your potential, become lifelong learners and find fulfilling careers. However, we appreciate that the shift from secondary education, or a return to formal education is, in itself, quite a journey. This module is designed to ease that transition. You'll be enrolled on it as soon as you receive an offer from ARU so you can begin to learn about university life before your course starts. Through Into ARU, you'll explore a virtual land modelled around ARU values: Courage, Innovation, Community, Integrity, Responsibility, and Ambition. This innovative module is designed as a game, where you collect knowledge and complete mini tasks. You'll proceed at your own pace, though we you to have completed your Into ARU exploration by week 6. If for any reason you're unable to complete by that date, we'll signpost to existing services so that we can be confident that you are supported.","Code":"MOD999910","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"4f3c4a41-2e3f-49aa-8860-037c9fba5c37"},{"Title":"Research Methods in Practice","Description":"In this module you'll learn advanced research methods through a hands-on approach. Each week, we’ll introduce you to various methods of study, such as language analysis (written and/or spoken) and archival research, and take you through the processes of how to undertake each type of research step by step. This will allow you to become a confident independent researcher and give you the skills to undergo a research project from the ground up. This module will equip you with a structure and the skills and methodologies that you'll need for your dissertation, develop your confidence in identifying and engaging with primary and secondary sources, and teach you vital research skills that will be important in your professional career.","Code":"MOD010703","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"fa1d5ece-70ab-448c-9a98-f9ba081ed30e"},{"Title":"Major Project in English Literature","Description":"This project enables you to demonstrate: the ability to raise significant and meaningful questions in relation to your specialism; depth of knowledge which may involve working at the current limits of theoretical and / or research understanding; critical understanding of method and its relationship to knowledge awareness of and ability to develop solutions to ethical dilemmas likely to arise in your research; the ability to draw meaningful and justifiable conclusions from information which may be complex or contradictory; the capability to expand or redefine existing knowledge; to develop new approaches to changing situations / and contribute to the development of best practice; the ability to communicate these processes in a clear and elegant fashion; the capability to evaluate your work from the perspective of an autonomous reflective learner. This module involves secondary research only and does not require primary data generation. You will be required to carry out a literature review using publicly available documents. Any use of the internet is limited to searching for publicly available documents only.","Code":"MOD010709","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"711be868-2db7-4459-8049-591f3c036529"}],"OptionalModules":[{"Title":"Utopias and Dystopias","Description":"In this interdisciplinary module you will explore a varied selection of texts which reflect the development of both utopian visions and dystopian fears in literature throughout history. You will analyse texts – including political, historical and religious writings – from different periods and a range of genres and consider the relationship between each text and the contexts within which it was produced. You will evaluate relevant critical and theoretical debates and reflect on ambiguities and uncertainties in the way the words ‘dystopia’ and ‘utopia’ have been used and understood. The term ‘utopian’, in particular, with its uncertain etymology (‘no place’ or ‘pleasant place’) is fraught with contradiction. Indicative topics for study include: Thomas More’s Utopia and other Early Modern utopias; utopian and dystopian thought in the writings of the English Civil Wars; Swift, Johnson and anti-Utopianism; the late nineteenth-century utopian visions of William Morris and Edward Bellamy; Huxley, Orwell and their influences; Katharine Burdekin, Rex Warner and the twentieth-century antifascist dystopia; Feminist dystopias and utopias; Octavia Butler and environmental dystopias; Prayaag Akbar and global dystopian writing.","Code":"MOD010704","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"da453ea3-5be0-4add-97c1-5ff7a1de5cd5"},{"Title":"Special Topic in English Literature","Description":"This Special Topic module gives you the opportunity to study a topic that will be taught by a member of staff whose particular academic interests and/or research is reflected in the area. A topic may be the study of a single author, a group of cognate authors, an aspect of literary theory. Topics may also cover a literary genre such as Life Writing or Children’s Literature. As the designated topics vary from-year-to-year you will consult with tutors to check which topics are being offered. This information is always made public in good time for informed student choices to be made. In this module, you'll investigate issues of changing landscapes, climate crises, and ecology through a range of texts and through arguments from environmental literary criticism. While the period focus in each delivery may differ (eg a focus on the nineteenth-century might be specified), you'll develop a working knowledge of conceptual issues involved in analysing the literary and cultural representation of landscapes, from the mountainous and wild to the flat and urban. Indicative topics for study include poetry, fiction, essays, and life-writing by William Wordsworth, George Eliot, Thomas Hardy, Mary Shelley, Jane Austen, John Ruskin, Mary Seacole, and Mary Prince. Contemporary fiction and poetry by Ali Smith, Margaret Atwood, Alice Oswald, Sarah Perry and others may also be included in some deliveries and topics.","Code":"MOD010705","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"a6798b78-8c79-4bfb-856c-82e3c190b36e"},{"Title":"Literature and Landscape","Description":"In this module, you'll investigate issues of changing landscapes, climate crises, and ecology through a range of texts and through arguments from environmental literary criticism. While the period focus in each delivery may differ (eg a focus on the nineteenth-century might be specified), you will develop a working knowledge of conceptual issues involved in analysing the literary and cultural representation of landscapes, from the mountainous and wild to the flat and urban. Indicative topics for study include poetry, fiction, essays, and life-writing by William Wordsworth, George Eliot, Thomas Hardy, Mary Shelley, Jane Austen, John Ruskin, Mary Seacole, and Mary Prince. Contemporary fiction and poetry by Ali Smith, Margaret Atwood, Alice Oswald, Sarah Perry and others may also be included in some deliveries and topics such as Shakespeare and Ecocriticism and Early Modern pastoral in others.","Code":"MOD010706","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"c88dab47-bda8-42d3-be16-4b32c004bebb"},{"Title":"Workshop: the Novel","Description":"In this module you'll study and practice the techniques of novel writing. It is designed in a workshop format. To maximise the use of group feedback and feedback from the tutor, we'll undertake many exercises in workshop time, but you'll be given longer writing exercises to consolidate your classroom learning, and you'll be expected to complete these each week in preparation for class. You'll undertake a series of structured exercises designed to develop your techniques in, for instance, characterisation, dialogue, plot structure, the selection and effectiveness of different points of view, setting, time frames and time sequencing. You'll read extracts from a number of well-known novels and the writing of other students to underpin our discussions of technique. As the module progresses, you'll be expected to reflect critically both on your own writing and that of your peers, as well as developing your critical judgement. This module will also incorporate practical advice on agents, the marketplace, and how to get work published.","Code":"MOD000520","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"8ee2fd61-dff7-422a-a300-5e9c16cb1bea"},{"Title":"Independent Research Project ","Description":"In this module, you'll have the opportunity to plan, develop and execute an independent research project of your own choice, such as an extended piece of academic research or a project in partnership with an outside organisation. This is an exciting opportunity for you to pursue your passions and work in an area that fascinates you. The project will be based on original research and extensive secondary source analysis to make a novel and exciting contribution to the literature or public sector. You'll work closely with a supervisor who will offer advice and guide you through the project’s completion. The project will need to be negotiated and decided prior to the beginning of trimester 2, so we can ensure it is viable and staff expertise is available.","Code":"MOD010702","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"ac319383-900e-4265-a597-4288e7138eb5"},{"Title":"Special Topic in Creative Writing/English Literature","Description":"This Special Topic module gives you the opportunity to study a particular genre or topic that will be taught by a practising writer whose current or recent writing has been in this area. This module enables you to extend the specific writing techniques you've learned in other modules to a particular genre, or to work on a particular set of ideas or challenges. A topic may be the study of a particular genre such as writing for children, creative non-fiction, historical fiction, or crime writing, or may be the study of a particular topic such as adaptation (for instance, exploring the challenges and techniques used by writers working on adapting one text into another: novel to film, film to play, poem to short story). As the designated topics vary from year to year, you'll consult with tutors to check which topics are being offered.","Code":"MOD000522","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"97b25074-815b-4669-8d6d-171fab0d0e58"},{"Title":"Patterns of Story: Fiction and its Forms","Description":"This module is a literary history course for writers. It examines the history of the novel from its formation in the eighteenth century through to some of its more modern forms, examining along the way some of the cultural and social contexts that have helped to shape these changing patterns of story. It will include some narrative theory. Although the course is chronological it is not a history of form that is teleological - different patterns of story emerge and re-emerge at particular cultural moments and eighteenth-century forms such as the picaresque are, for instance, re-invented by postmodernist writers such as Angela Carter, who famously said 'I like to put new wine into old bottles in such a way as to make the old bottles explode'. Through the reading and discussion of recent and classic books on the history and structure of the novel by writers such as Jane Smiley, Christopher Booker, John Mullen and Dorothea Brande, you'll consider what it means to write novels and what it means to be a writer, as well as considering the ways in which some contemporary writers use and reuse much older forms of storytelling and patterns of story.","Code":"MOD003085","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"1b2d25ee-346b-44b6-b7fc-5d7857eaefee"},{"Title":"Workshop: the Short Story","Description":"On this workshop-based module you will study and practice the techniques of short story writing. To maximise the use of group feedback and feedback from the tutor you will undertake many exercises in workshop time, but also longer writing exercises to consolidate what you have done in class. You will undertake a series of structured exercises designed to develop your techniques in, for instance, characterisation, dialogue, plot structure, time frames and time sequencing with a particular emphasis placed on how these techniques differ from those used in novel writing. You will read short stories from a range of classic and contemporary short story writers such as Chekhov, Henry James and Alice Munro and the work of other writers featured on the East of the Web short story website. As the module progresses you will be expected to reflect critically both on your own writing and that of your peers. This module will also incorporate practical advice on agents, the marketplace, writing competitions and how to get writing published.","Code":"MOD000521","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"1bbf9b09-83cb-4a2d-91cc-9a4f4c92ebfb"},{"Title":"Creativity and Content in Publishing","Description":"This module introduces you to the world of contemporary publishing in all its variety, and to the processes by which publishers work with authors and designers to shape text and image for specific audiences. You'll cover issues, principles and practices related to the commissioning, concept development and packaging of a wide range of publications across digital and print platforms: from academic to children’s books, illustrated nonfiction to social media content marketing. The module stresses the importance of determining the strategic direction of a publisher's list, the publisher's relationship with content creators, an understanding of the zeitgeist or cultural context, and the need for quality control in managing editorial projects. Workshops enable you to experiment and develop the practical skills that you'll need when working in a publishing environment, such as copywriting, blurb writing, digital marketing, proposal development and project management, communicating with different audiences and pitching. Visiting industry specialists will contribute specialist insights and case studies.","Code":"MOD000527","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"80ed46c2-eed0-43e6-87e9-3f922b228960"},{"Title":"Every Object Tells a Story: Material Culture and Heritage in History","Description":"Objects are vital to study, both for the public and the academic historian. They allow us to understand past societies in exciting and original ways and to communicate history to diverse audiences. After all, we all make sense of the world through the objects around us, such as the chair, computer, desk or glasses through which you might be reading this very description. People of the past were no different. Their everyday lives were dictated by what they had, what they could make, what they used and what they worked hard to acquire. No matter what period or type of history you are most interested in, objects will allow you to study the topic in new and interesting ways. In this module, you'll learn about the role of objects in heritage and academic studies. You will learn about the importance of objects in museums, such as how they can be researched and put to use in public displays, as well as how objects can be used to study literature as well as social, cultural, political and many other forms of history. From learning these skills, you will then curate a project relating to objects with an academic partner, develop vital skills for employment in the heritage sector, and obtain new ways of researching the topics you love.","Code":"MOD010707","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"586f9f70-0748-43ad-94e8-6f6a762eaa76"}],"Id":"000bec4d-a297-41e3-8e53-4f5e979adc4e","SelectedModule":false}],"UcasCode":"","SITSCode":"","AstraCode":"P1264","ModeOfStudy":{"KisCode":"FullTime","ModeOfStudyCode":"FT","ExcludeFromCourseSummary":false,"Name":"Full-time","Id":"3188d331-b419-4c02-bf25-30c84b6fff3d"},"CoreOption":false,"FoundationOption":false,"PlacementOption":false,"ProfessionalExperienceOption":false,"PartTimeOption":false,"Extra1":false,"Extra2":false,"Status":null,"StartDateDisclaimer":null,"DegreeApprenticeship":false,"Award":null,"Qualification":null,"LocationOverride":null,"EntryRequirementYears":[{"Name":"2026","Id":"b0de6795-6e13-4745-98d9-c1515ee46eae"}],"EntryRequirementsInformation":[{"HeadingTitle":"Standard entry requirements","RichTextContent":[{"RichTextTitle":"","RichTextContent":"
