Each week, we’ll introduce you to various methods of study, such as language analysis (written and/or spoken) and archival research, and take you through the processes of how to undertake each type of research step by step. This will allow you to become a confident independent researcher and give you the skills to undergo a research project from the ground up. This module will equip you with a structure and the skills and methodologies that you'll need for your dissertation, develop your confidence in identifying and engaging with primary and secondary sources, and teach you vital research skills that will be important in your professional career.","Code":"MOD010703","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"fa1d5ece-70ab-448c-9a98-f9ba081ed30e"},{"Title":"Major Project in English Literature","Description":"This project enables you to demonstrate: the ability to raise significant and meaningful questions in relation to your specialism; depth of knowledge which may involve working at the current limits of theoretical and / or research understanding; critical understanding of method and its relationship to knowledge awareness of and ability to develop solutions to ethical dilemmas likely to arise in your research; the ability to draw meaningful and justifiable conclusions from information which may be complex or contradictory; the capability to expand or redefine existing knowledge; to develop new approaches to changing situations / and contribute to the development of best practice; the ability to communicate these processes in a clear and elegant fashion; the capability to evaluate your work from the perspective of an autonomous reflective learner. This module involves secondary research only and does not require primary data generation. You will be required to carry out a literature review using publicly available documents. Any use of the internet is limited to searching for publicly available documents only.","Code":"MOD010709","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"711be868-2db7-4459-8049-591f3c036529"}],"OptionalModules":[{"Title":"Utopias and Dystopias","Description":"In this interdisciplinary module you will explore a varied selection of texts which reflect the development of both utopian visions and dystopian fears in literature throughout history. You will analyse texts – including political, historical and religious writings – from different periods and a range of genres and consider the relationship between each text and the contexts within which it was produced. You will evaluate relevant critical and theoretical debates and reflect on ambiguities and uncertainties in the way the words ‘dystopia’ and ‘utopia’ have been used and understood. The term ‘utopian’, in particular, with its uncertain etymology (‘no place’ or ‘pleasant place’) is fraught with contradiction. Indicative topics for study include: Thomas More’s Utopia and other Early Modern utopias; utopian and dystopian thought in the writings of the English Civil Wars; Swift, Johnson and anti-Utopianism; the late nineteenth-century utopian visions of William Morris and Edward Bellamy; Huxley, Orwell and their influences; Katharine Burdekin, Rex Warner and the twentieth-century antifascist dystopia; Feminist dystopias and utopias; Octavia Butler and environmental dystopias; Prayaag Akbar and global dystopian writing.","Code":"MOD010704","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"da453ea3-5be0-4add-97c1-5ff7a1de5cd5"},{"Title":"Special Topic in English Literature","Description":"This Special Topic module gives you the opportunity to study a topic that will be taught by a member of staff whose particular academic interests and/or research is reflected in the area. A topic may be the study of a single author, a group of cognate authors, an aspect of literary theory. Topics may also cover a literary genre such as Life Writing or Children’s Literature. As the designated topics vary from-year-to-year you will consult with tutors to check which topics are being offered. This information is always made public in good time for informed student choices to be made. In this module, you'll investigate issues of changing landscapes, climate crises, and ecology through a range of texts and through arguments from environmental literary criticism. While the period focus in each delivery may differ (eg a focus on the nineteenth-century might be specified), you'll develop a working knowledge of conceptual issues involved in analysing the literary and cultural representation of landscapes, from the mountainous and wild to the flat and urban. Indicative topics for study include poetry, fiction, essays, and life-writing by William Wordsworth, George Eliot, Thomas Hardy, Mary Shelley, Jane Austen, John Ruskin, Mary Seacole, and Mary Prince. Contemporary fiction and poetry by Ali Smith, Margaret Atwood, Alice Oswald, Sarah Perry and others may also be included in some deliveries and topics.","Code":"MOD010705","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"a6798b78-8c79-4bfb-856c-82e3c190b36e"},{"Title":"Literature and Landscape","Description":"In this module, you'll investigate issues of changing landscapes, climate crises, and ecology through a range of texts and through arguments from environmental literary criticism. While the period focus in each delivery may differ (eg a focus on the nineteenth-century might be specified), you will develop a working knowledge of conceptual issues involved in analysing the literary and cultural representation of landscapes, from the mountainous and wild to the flat and urban. Indicative topics for study include poetry, fiction, essays, and life-writing by William Wordsworth, George Eliot, Thomas Hardy, Mary Shelley, Jane Austen, John Ruskin, Mary Seacole, and Mary Prince. Contemporary fiction and poetry by Ali Smith, Margaret Atwood, Alice Oswald, Sarah Perry and others may also be included in some deliveries and topics such as Shakespeare and Ecocriticism and Early Modern pastoral in others.","Code":"MOD010706","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"c88dab47-bda8-42d3-be16-4b32c004bebb"},{"Title":"Workshop: the Novel","Description":"In this module you'll study and practice the techniques of novel writing. It is designed in a workshop format. To maximise the use of group feedback and feedback from the tutor, we'll undertake many exercises in workshop time, but you'll be given longer writing exercises to consolidate your classroom learning, and you'll be expected to complete these each week in preparation for class. You'll undertake a series of structured exercises designed to develop your techniques in, for instance, characterisation, dialogue, plot structure, the selection and effectiveness of different points of view, setting, time frames and time sequencing. You'll read extracts from a number of well-known novels and the writing of other students to underpin our discussions of technique. As the module progresses, you'll be expected to reflect critically both on your own writing and that of your peers, as well as developing your critical judgement. This module will also incorporate practical advice on agents, the marketplace, and how to get work published.","Code":"MOD000520","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"8ee2fd61-dff7-422a-a300-5e9c16cb1bea"},{"Title":"Independent Research Project ","Description":"In this module, you'll have the opportunity to plan, develop and execute an independent research project of your own choice, such as an extended piece of academic research or a project in partnership with an outside organisation. This is an exciting opportunity for you to pursue your passions and work in an area that fascinates you. The project will be based on original research and extensive secondary source analysis to make a novel and exciting contribution to the literature or public sector. You'll work closely with a supervisor who will offer advice and guide you through the project’s completion. The project will need to be negotiated and decided prior to the beginning of trimester 2, so we can ensure it is viable and staff expertise is available.","Code":"MOD010702","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"ac319383-900e-4265-a597-4288e7138eb5"},{"Title":"Special Topic in Creative Writing/English Literature","Description":"This Special Topic module gives you the opportunity to study a particular genre or topic that will be taught by a practising writer whose current or recent writing has been in this area. This module enables you to extend the specific writing techniques you've learned in other modules to a particular genre, or to work on a particular set of ideas or challenges. A topic may be the study of a particular genre such as writing for children, creative non-fiction, historical fiction, or crime writing, or may be the study of a particular topic such as adaptation (for instance, exploring the challenges and techniques used by writers working on adapting one text into another: novel to film, film to play, poem to short story). As the designated topics vary from year to year, you'll consult with tutors to check which topics are being offered.","Code":"MOD000522","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"97b25074-815b-4669-8d6d-171fab0d0e58"},{"Title":"Patterns of Story: Fiction and its Forms","Description":"This module is a literary history course for writers. It examines the history of the novel from its formation in the eighteenth century through to some of its more modern forms, examining along the way some of the cultural and social contexts that have helped to shape these changing patterns of story. It will include some narrative theory. Although the course is chronological it is not a history of form that is teleological - different patterns of story emerge and re-emerge at particular cultural moments and eighteenth-century forms such as the picaresque are, for instance, re-invented by postmodernist writers such as Angela Carter, who famously said 'I like to put new wine into old bottles in such a way as to make the old bottles explode'. Through the reading and discussion of recent and classic books on the history and structure of the novel by writers such as Jane Smiley, Christopher Booker, John Mullen and Dorothea Brande, you'll consider what it means to write novels and what it means to be a writer, as well as considering the ways in which some contemporary writers use and reuse much older forms of storytelling and patterns of story.","Code":"MOD003085","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"1b2d25ee-346b-44b6-b7fc-5d7857eaefee"},{"Title":"Workshop: the Short Story","Description":"On this workshop-based module you will study and practice the techniques of short story writing. To maximise the use of group feedback and feedback from the tutor you will undertake many exercises in workshop time, but also longer writing exercises to consolidate what you have done in class. You will undertake a series of structured exercises designed to develop your techniques in, for instance, characterisation, dialogue, plot structure, time frames and time sequencing with a particular emphasis placed on how these techniques differ from those used in novel writing. You will read short stories from a range of classic and contemporary short story writers such as Chekhov, Henry James and Alice Munro and the work of other writers featured on the East of the Web short story website. As the module progresses you will be expected to reflect critically both on your own writing and that of your peers. This module will also incorporate practical advice on agents, the marketplace, writing competitions and how to get writing published.","Code":"MOD000521","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"1bbf9b09-83cb-4a2d-91cc-9a4f4c92ebfb"},{"Title":"Creativity and Content in Publishing","Description":"This module introduces you to the world of contemporary publishing in all its variety, and to the processes by which publishers work with authors and designers to shape text and image for specific audiences. You'll cover issues, principles and practices related to the commissioning, concept development and packaging of a wide range of publications across digital and print platforms: from academic to children’s books, illustrated nonfiction to social media content marketing. The module stresses the importance of determining the strategic direction of a publisher's list, the publisher's relationship with content creators, an understanding of the zeitgeist or cultural context, and the need for quality control in managing editorial projects. Workshops enable you to experiment and develop the practical skills that you'll need when working in a publishing environment, such as copywriting, blurb writing, digital marketing, proposal development and project management, communicating with different audiences and pitching. Visiting industry specialists will contribute specialist insights and case studies.","Code":"MOD000527","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"80ed46c2-eed0-43e6-87e9-3f922b228960"},{"Title":"Every Object Tells a Story: Material Culture and Heritage in History","Description":"Objects are vital to study, both for the public and the academic historian. They allow us to understand past societies in exciting and original ways and to communicate history to diverse audiences. After all, we all make sense of the world through the objects around us, such as the chair, computer, desk or glasses through which you might be reading this very description. People of the past were no different. Their everyday lives were dictated by what they had, what they could make, what they used and what they worked hard to acquire. No matter what period or type of history you are most interested in, objects will allow you to study the topic in new and interesting ways. In this module, you'll learn about the role of objects in heritage and academic studies. You will learn about the importance of objects in museums, such as how they can be researched and put to use in public displays, as well as how objects can be used to study literature as well as social, cultural, political and many other forms of history. From learning these skills, you will then curate a project relating to objects with an academic partner, develop vital skills for employment in the heritage sector, and obtain new ways of researching the topics you love.","Code":"MOD010707","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"586f9f70-0748-43ad-94e8-6f6a762eaa76"}],"Id":"fb3f224e-7d9d-404d-b8f5-e7a0afdcbd08","SelectedModule":false}],"UcasCode":"","SITSCode":"","AstraCode":"P1264","ModeOfStudy":{"KisCode":"PartTime","ModeOfStudyCode":"PT","ExcludeFromCourseSummary":false,"Name":"Part-time","Id":"77ee6eb5-cef9-4099-87c0-3c2819c645cd"},"CoreOption":false,"FoundationOption":false,"PlacementOption":false,"ProfessionalExperienceOption":false,"PartTimeOption":false,"Extra1":false,"Extra2":false,"Status":null,"StartDateDisclaimer":null,"DegreeApprenticeship":false,"Award":null,"Qualification":null,"LocationOverride":null,"EntryRequirementYears":[{"Name":"2026","Id":"b0de6795-6e13-4745-98d9-c1515ee46eae"}],"EntryRequirementsInformation":[{"HeadingTitle":"Standard entry requirements","RichTextContent":[{"RichTextTitle":"","RichTextContent":"

As the designated topics vary from year to year, you'll consult with tutors to check which topics are being offered.","Code":"MOD000522","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"97b25074-815b-4669-8d6d-171fab0d0e58"},{"Title":"Patterns of Story: Fiction and its Forms","Description":"This module is a literary history course for writers. It examines the history of the novel from its formation in the eighteenth century through to some of its more modern forms, examining along the way some of the cultural and social contexts that have helped to shape these changing patterns of story. It will include some narrative theory. Although the course is chronological it is not a history of form that is teleological - different patterns of story emerge and re-emerge at particular cultural moments and eighteenth-century forms such as the picaresque are, for instance, re-invented by postmodernist writers such as Angela Carter, who famously said 'I like to put new wine into old bottles in such a way as to make the old bottles explode'. Through the reading and discussion of recent and classic books on the history and structure of the novel by writers such as Jane Smiley, Christopher Booker, John Mullen and Dorothea Brande, you'll consider what it means to write novels and what it means to be a writer, as well as considering the ways in which some contemporary writers use and reuse much older forms of storytelling and patterns of story.","Code":"MOD003085","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"1b2d25ee-346b-44b6-b7fc-5d7857eaefee"},{"Title":"Workshop: the Short Story","Description":"On this workshop-based module you will study and practice the techniques of short story writing. To maximise the use of group feedback and feedback from the tutor you will undertake many exercises in workshop time, but also longer writing exercises to consolidate what you have done in class. You will undertake a series of structured exercises designed to develop your techniques in, for instance, characterisation, dialogue, plot structure, time frames and time sequencing with a particular emphasis placed on how these techniques differ from those used in novel writing. You will read short stories from a range of classic and contemporary short story writers such as Chekhov, Henry James and Alice Munro and the work of other writers featured on the East of the Web short story website. As the module progresses you will be expected to reflect critically both on your own writing and that of your peers. This module will also incorporate practical advice on agents, the marketplace, writing competitions and how to get writing published.","Code":"MOD000521","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"1bbf9b09-83cb-4a2d-91cc-9a4f4c92ebfb"},{"Title":"Creativity and Content in Publishing","Description":"This module introduces you to the world of contemporary publishing in all its variety, and to the processes by which publishers work with authors and designers to shape text and image for specific audiences. You'll cover issues, principles and practices related to the commissioning, concept development and packaging of a wide range of publications across digital and print platforms: from academic to children’s books, illustrated nonfiction to social media content marketing. The module stresses the importance of determining the strategic direction of a publisher's list, the publisher's relationship with content creators, an understanding of the zeitgeist or cultural context, and the need for quality control in managing editorial projects. Workshops enable you to experiment and develop the practical skills that you'll need when working in a publishing environment, such as copywriting, blurb writing, digital marketing, proposal development and project management, communicating with different audiences and pitching. Visiting industry specialists will contribute specialist insights and case studies.","Code":"MOD000527","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"80ed46c2-eed0-43e6-87e9-3f922b228960"},{"Title":"Every Object Tells a Story: Material Culture and Heritage in History","Description":"Objects are vital to study, both for the public and the academic historian. They allow us to understand past societies in exciting and original ways and to communicate history to diverse audiences. After all, we all make sense of the world through the objects around us, such as the chair, computer, desk or glasses through which you might be reading this very description. People of the past were no different. Their everyday lives were dictated by what they had, what they could make, what they used and what they worked hard to acquire. No matter what period or type of history you are most interested in, objects will allow you to study the topic in new and interesting ways. In this module, you'll learn about the role of objects in heritage and academic studies. You will learn about the importance of objects in museums, such as how they can be researched and put to use in public displays, as well as how objects can be used to study literature as well as social, cultural, political and many other forms of history. From learning these skills, you will then curate a project relating to objects with an academic partner, develop vital skills for employment in the heritage sector, and obtain new ways of researching the topics you love.","Code":"MOD010707","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"586f9f70-0748-43ad-94e8-6f6a762eaa76"}],"Id":"d3a33184-e5d6-4d60-93ec-55153ac4ee8f","SelectedModule":false}],"UcasCode":"","SITSCode":"","AstraCode":"P1264","ModeOfStudy":{"KisCode":"PartTime","ModeOfStudyCode":"PT","ExcludeFromCourseSummary":false,"Name":"Part-time","Id":"77ee6eb5-cef9-4099-87c0-3c2819c645cd"},"CoreOption":false,"FoundationOption":false,"PlacementOption":false,"ProfessionalExperienceOption":false,"PartTimeOption":false,"Extra1":false,"Extra2":false,"Status":null,"StartDateDisclaimer":null,"DegreeApprenticeship":false,"Award":null,"Qualification":null,"LocationOverride":null,"EntryRequirementYears":[{"Name":"2026","Id":"b0de6795-6e13-4745-98d9-c1515ee46eae"}],"EntryRequirementsInformation":[{"HeadingTitle":"Standard entry requirements","RichTextContent":[{"RichTextTitle":"","RichTextContent":"

Postgraduate English Literature MPhil, PhD Research ( full-time, part-time) Cambridge January 2027, April, September 2027 Distance-learning supervision available on this course. This course is located in the School of Humanities and Social Sciences. Find out more about our research. Apply online For application deadlines visit our how to apply page . Overview Our PhD research programmes will allow you to join one of our research projects or explore your own interests in English Literature, supported by the expertise of our staff. Full description You’ll be allocated two supervisors, with additional staff members available if necessary. Our supervisors are experienced in most areas of English literature, with a strong focus on Renaissance literature, Shakespeare, Romantic and Victorian studies; modernism; women's writing; science and the creative imagination; classical reception; film and theatre; and popular culture. You’ll conduct your research in a collaborative environment with strong links to research networks in our University and the wider community. We host and take part in many research oriented events for staff and postgraduate students, including our regular Faculty and departmental research seminars, international conferences and the bi-annual Skinner Young lecture on Shakespeare and Renaissance literature. Our seminars will give you the chance to present papers in a supportive setting, and you’ll have the chance to attend graduate research seminars at the University of Cambridge’s Faculty of English. These events, along with our online environment, will help you connect with other research students from a range of disciplines. You could also benefit from financial support – we allocate a substantial sum every year towards postgraduate travel and conference expenses, as well as some bursaries. All your subject-specific studies will be enhanced and supported by our University-wide training sessions, where you’ll gain important research expertise in areas like ethics, presentations, intellectual property and digital scholarship. Completion times MPhil: full-time 1-3 years, part-time 2-4 years. PhD via progression from MPhil, including that period: full-time 2.5-5 years, part-time 3.5-6 years. PhD: full-time 2-4 years, part-time 3-6 years. For further guidance on the duration of research degrees please refer to the Research Degrees Regulations . PhD project opportunities in the Faculty of Arts, Humanities, Education and Social Sciences World-leading research at ARU 19th Century Studies Research Unit Supervision and support Our permanent supervisory staff are recognised experts in their field, and have produced a number of influential books, journal articles and edited collections. Our research expertise includes: Dr Jeannette Baxter , BA, MA, PhD: twentieth-century literature; contemporary fiction; post-1945 novel; Surrealism and the avant-garde; Holocaust writing. Professor Sarah Brown , BA, MA, PhD: adaptations of classical texts and myths; Renaissance literature, especially Shakespeare; science fiction. Dr John Gardner , BA, MA, PhD: poetry and politics in the eighteenth century or nineteenth century; the novel in the eighteenth/nineteenth century; the relationship between text and illustration; engineering and culture. Professor Eugene Giddens , BA, PhD: Shakespeare and Renaissance drama; early print culture; children's literature. Dr Elizabeth Ludlow , BA, MA, PhD: nineteenth-century literature and culture; literature and theology; Victorian print cultures and periodical publication; Victorian illustration. Dr Tory Young , BA, MA, PhD: modernism; contemporary fiction, especially the influence of modernism on contemporary fiction since 2000; narratology; queer and feminist theories of narrative. Staff from our Creative Writing programme may also be available for supervision, where appropriate. Where you'll research Your department and faculty At the School of Humanities and Social Sciences, we believe in thinking critically about the past, present and future to challenge perceptions and better understand communities and people. With expertise from gender issues to literary analysis to exploring how the past has shaped our modern world, all our staff members are active researchers. This is reflected in our teaching, allowing us to support our students with the latest theories and practices, as well as essential employability advice. Visit your department Where can I study? Cambridge Our campus is close to the centre of Cambridge, often described as the perfect student city. Explore our Cambridge campus Specialist facilities You’ll have access to the University of Cambridge Library, our own campus library and many multimedia, video and radio production facilities. You’ll also be able to use our Faculty’s PhD room, where all our doctoral students can meet up to work and take an active part in our postgraduate student community. Fees & funding Course fees UK students, 2026/27 (per year) £5,238 UK students, 2026/27 (part-time, per year) £2,619 International students, 2026/27 (per year) £17,500 International students, 2026/27 (part-time, per year) £8,750 Bench fees In some cases extra costs known as bench fees will be charged for a postgraduate research degree. These are to cover additional/exceptional costs directly related to a specific research project. Some examples of these costs are (the list is not exhaustive): equipment hire, access costs to specialist equipment/workshops, volunteer expenses, specialist tissue/cell culture, specialist reagents or materials, specialist software, access to specialist databases, data collection costs, specialist media, recording or digital storage needs. We charge bench fees in bands. They may apply for every year of your course. These bands are the same for full- and part-time students. If you have to pay bench fees this will be made clear at your interview, and stated in your offer letter. For 2026/27 the bench fee bands are: £500 £1,400 £2,400 £4,900 £9,800 PhD by Published Work Initial registration: £1,700 Full registration: £4,900 Writing up fees 2026/27 £1,400 How do I pay my fees? You can pay your fees upfront, in full or in instalments – though you won't need to pay until you've accepted an offer to study with us. Find out more about paying your fees . Funding For advice on the Doctoral Loan and other sources of funding, including ARU scholarships, visit our finance guide for postgraduate researchers . You might also find The Alternative Guide to Postgraduate Funding helpful. ARU research ARU's academic excellence was recognised in 2021, as part of the Research Excellence Framework (REF), an exercise which assesses the quality of academic research. Sixteen areas of our work were classed as generating world-leading research . The results showed that we're making a significant impact on the societies we live in. Careers We’ll provide you with many opportunities for career development and training, in areas like writing up a paper for publication; placing an academic article; giving a conference paper; the doctoral writing style; updates on research methods and literature searches; internet training; editing skills for doctoral research; subsequent monograph publication; and dealing with festivals, agents, and publishers. You might also be able to take on teaching responsibilities in the department, or organise research events like seminars and conferences. In conjunction with the University’s research support, you can request specific support for writing-up, conference papers, general research methods and other research skills if you need it. Contact details If you're interested in finding out more about research study opportunities in this area, please email [email protected] Entry requirements MPhil or PhD with progression from MPhil: You’ll need a Bachelors degree or equivalent with first or upper second class honours, in a related subject area. PhD: You’ll need a Masters degree or equivalent in a related subject area. Please note we consider candidates for PhD with progression from MPhil in the first instance. If you want to be considered for direct entry to the PhD route then this can be discussed at interview if you are shortlisted. Please note you’ll also need to provide academic justification for this request. If English is not your first language, you'll require a minimum IELTS score of 6.5, with a minimum of 5.5 in each component (or equivalent test). If you don't meet our English language requirements, we offer a range of courses which could help you achieve the level required for entry. Loading... Entry requirements are not currently available, please try again later. Important additional notes Our published entry requirements are a guide only and our decision will be based on your overall suitability for the programme as well as whether you meet the minimum entry requirements. Contact our postgraduate research degree team for more information about studying a PhD, MPhil or Professional Doctorate at ARU. You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your research programme. Postgraduate MSc Equine Performance Science Take your equine knowledge, academic skills and research practice to the next level. Study for a Master’s with residential weeks at ARU in Writtle. Our course pages need JavaScript enabled to work correctly. You'll take the same modules as MSc/MA students, but sometimes in a different order or in different years. As a part-time student you'll typically study for twice as long as full-time students. For example if the MSc/MA course takes one year, you can expect to study over two years, though for some courses this may vary. 1st in the region for postgraduates progressing into senior roles. Source: Graduate Outcomes Survey 2026 If you’re passionate about the science behind advancing equine athletic performance, this is the course for you. Blending online and campus study, you’ll explore topics including gait evaluation, injury pathophysiology and rehabilitation, advanced nutrition, and equitation science and human influences on performance. You’ll learn how to assess, monitor and enhance both performance and welfare in real-world contexts. You’ll graduate ready to drive innovation and deliver better outcomes for horses and riders alike. Why ARU? Learn how you can deliver better outcomes for horses and riders Study through a combination of online learning and residential weeks at ARU in Writtle Use dedicated equine facilities and industry-standard equipment on campus Learn from experienced tutors and industry professionals Develop scientific, analytical and communication skills tailored to careers in performance management, therapy, nutrition or research Fit your studies into your life, with options to study full- or part-time Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers Prepare for a career in the competitive and evolving equine sector. Whether your future lies in performance, therapy, research or consultancy, this MSc prepares you to drive innovation and deliver better outcomes for horses and riders alike. As well as gaining scientific and therapeutic knowledge and skills, you’ll develop as a leader, communicator, and problem-solver. Graduation doesn't have to be the end of your time with us. You might decide to continue your academic career and join a research programme at ARU. Take advantage of our Alumni Scholarship and save £400 on your fees. What can you do with an Equine Performance Science degree? This degree will equip you for specialist roles that combine scientific knowledge with practical application in the equine industry. You might pursue a career in elite equine sports performance management, rehabilitation and therapy, equine nutrition consultancy, equine science research or welfare assessment. Opportunities also exist in academia, rider and coach support roles, and within governing bodies or commercial sectors focused on performance enhancement and innovation. Where have previous Equine Performance Science graduates worked? Graduates of the MSc Equine Performance Science have progressed into a variety of roles across the equine, veterinary and animal performance sectors. Alumni have gone on to work in equine performance and rehabilitation, veterinary practice support, equine welfare organisations, consultancy, education, and research. Others have used the qualification to enhance their professional practice within the equine industry or as a stepping stone to doctoral study. The course's emphasis on evidence-based practice, applied research and professional skills prepares graduates to contribute to the advancement of equine performance, health and welfare in both industry and academic settings. Examples of career pathways include: Equine Performance and Rehabilitation Specialist Equine Consultant Research Assistant or Researcher Equine Welfare Officer Lecturer or educator Veterinary support and allied animal health roles PhD and doctoral research programmes How can ARU help with my employability and career development? We want you to be a step ahead when you graduate, so we offer: courses designed with employers tutors with professional industry knowledge hands-on learning which may include industry-led projects, placements or Professional Experience modules . Alongside your course, there are lots of other opportunities to build your skills and experience: add value to your CV with an ARU Certificate of Professional Development get involved in a thriving volunteering programme develop your brilliant business ideas work with businesses to make a social impact . We’re here to help you develop your CV and find that all-important role after graduation. Our Employability Service offers tailored career appointments, advice on writing your CV, help to complete job applications, and much more. You’ll have 24/7 access to an online Careers Centre too, which is packed with useful resources. The support continues after you graduate, with lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . Find out more about careers support at ARU . Teaching and modules Our course blends academic excellence with real-world application, developing the knowledge, skills and connections needed to succeed in the equine industry, consultancy or research. Prof Roberta Blake, Professor of Animal Performance Science and Course Director Develop the knowledge and skills to keep equine athletes on top form. Using our dynamic online platform, you’ll learn the theory behind equine evaluation, welfare, biomechanics and sports medicine, and nutrition, as well as the horse-human dyad. You’ll also explore potential careers and develop professional skills. You’ll spend two weeks in June on campus, putting your new skills into practice with our horses. You have the option to spend an additional two weeks carrying out data collection, which may inform your Major Project – a substantial research project on a relevant topic of your choice. What will I study? MSc 2 years part-time MSc Modules are subject to change and availability, and may vary by location. If you have the choice of optional modules, these are indicated with a *. Year 1 Welfare of the Performance Horse (15 credits) Professional Practice in Equine Science (15 credits) Advanced Equine Biomechanics and Sports Medicine (30 credits) Optimising Nutrition for the Equine Athlete (15 credits) Applied Research for Equine Graduates (15 credits) Human Influence on Equine Performance (15 credits) Performance Evaluation and Enhancement (15 credits) Major Project (60 credits) Equine Performance in Practice (two residential weeks in June) (0 credits) Data collection (two residential weeks in June or July) (0 credits) * Module details 2 years part-time It's possible for UK students to study this course part-time. You'll take the same modules as MSc/MA students, but sometimes in a different order or in different years. As a part-time student you'll typically study for twice as long as full-time students. For example if the MSc/MA course takes one year, you can expect to study over two years, though for some courses this may vary. How is Equine Performance Science assessed? You'll be assessed through a variety of coursework-based assessments, including case studies, scientific reports, presentations, practical evaluations and research projects. The course concludes with a Major Project, enabling you to apply your knowledge to a real-world equine performance science question. Who teaches Equine Performance Science at ARU? Our course team includes industry-experienced staff and practitioners in equine performance science, as well as industry professionals such as nutritionists, veterinarians, behaviourists, therapists and researchers. Professor Roberta Blake Professor Rosa Verwijs Senior Lecturer in Equine Behaviour and Nutrition Jane Hart Lecturer in Equine Performance Briony Witherow Senior Lecturer Dr Amy R. Holtby Senior lecturer Facilities Study equine courses with ARU in Writtle and benefit from our Equine Training and Development Centre . On our 150-hectare campus, we have around 70 horses, a working stable yard, indoor and outdoor riding arenas, an oval horse walker, and a therapy barn. We also have a DIY Livery Yard for your horse. You’ll also be able to make full use of facilities including extensive library and IT resources and access support, should you need it, with study skills, careers advice, health and wellbeing, and more. We will ask for a deposit of £4,000 or a sponsorship letter Find out about paying your fees . Part-time fees Part-time course fees assume that you’re studying at half the rate of a full-time student (50% intensity). Course fees will be different if you study over a longer period. All fees are for guidance purposes only. Your offer letter will contain full details of credits and fees, or you can contact us if you'd like more information. Additional course costs For this course, you'll need access to a laptop and a reliable internet connection. To take part in practical activities safely and comfortably, you’ll need a riding hat or skull cap that meets current BETA safety standards, riding gloves and sturdy yard boots, long or short. Clothing should be smart and practical, such as dark trousers, waterproofs, or plain jeans (no rips or embellishments). A warm, waterproof outdoor coat is also important, plus a digital camera or phone can come in handy for recording your practical work. (estimated cost: £100-£150) A lab coat will also be needed for practical sessions in the laboratory. (estimated cost: £15) You’ll be responsible for arranging and covering the cost of travel, accommodation and subsistence costs for residential weeks, as these are not included in the course fee. Paying for university There are several ways to fund postgraduate study, and we recommend finding out more before you apply. You’ll learn how to formulate data-informed trading strategies, financial models and business forecasts. You’ll create your own applications and analyse big data using R and Python, and make extensive use of our Bloomberg Financial Markets Lab. At the same time, you’ll develop strategic, marketing and leadership skills to help you climb the career ladder. Why ARU? Learn how to create data-informed trading strategies, financial models and business forecasts Gain skills and experience in strategy and leadership Build your network with our industry contacts and guest speakers Enhance your employability with our optional Professional Experience year Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers This course prepares you for an exciting career in an innovative, fast-moving area. We teach leadership, management, strategy and marketing skills alongside technical skills, so you’ll graduate as a well-rounded candidate ready to ascend the career ladder. Graduation doesn’t have to be the end of your time with us. You could choose to continue your academic career with our Business PhD – School of Management or Business PhD – School of Economics, Finance and Law . Take advantage of our Alumni Scholarship and save £400 on your fees. What can you do with a FinTech and Data Analytics degree? Depending on your interests, as a FinTech and Data Analysis MBA graduate you could find yourself working for an online payment system, peer-to-peer lending or crowdfunding platform, online stockbroker, or robo-advisory service for individual investors, to name just a few examples. You could also work in banking, insurance, or other financial services, or start up your own business. With our start-up hub and annual business competition, if you’ve got a great idea, you don’t even need to wait for graduation to make it happen. ARU Business students are European Champions A team of ARU students came first in Europe and sixth in the world in the prestigious Bloomberg Global Trading Challenge. Postgraduate MPH Global Public Health Prepare to take on global public health challenges. Gain specialised skills to make a valuable contribution to communities’ health and wellbeing. Our course pages need JavaScript enabled to work correctly. Previous Section Course Overview Next Section Jump to a section Course overview Careers Teaching and modules Facilities Entry requirements Fees and funding Apply Apply now Book on a postgraduate open event MPH Part-time option(s) MPH Start date January 2027 Location Cambridge Award MPH Duration 1 year full-time Part-time option(s) Start date January 2027 Location Cambridge Award MPH Duration 2 years part-time 1st in the region for postgraduates progressing into senior roles. Source: Graduate Outcomes Survey 2026 Covid-19, Ebola, health inequality, conflict, vaccine hesitancy, the role of the state in health. Public health is constantly in the news – and our Master’s degree will equip you to meet contemporary challenges. You’ll take a modern approach, exploring the social, economic and political factors that influence population health. Modules cover the field of public health globally and are applicable to any country or health system. This course will suit you if you’re working in a health-related role and want to take the next step in your career. Faculty of Public Health This Master’s degree is mapped against the Faculty of Public Health training curriculum, supporting professional recognition. Why ARU? Prepare for a career in public health in the UK or internationally Learn about the factors that influence population health Explore public health issues, policies and communication Achieve professional recognition, with a course that maps to the Public Health Training Curriculum Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers Gain the knowledge and skills for a public health career worldwide. Across the globe, increasing demand for healthcare services alongside reduction in funding means there’s a real need for public health professionals. On this course, you’ll cover key concepts including epidemiological research, disease, addiction policy-making and migration, and mental health. As a graduate, you could consider roles in sectors such as health, government, voluntary and community organisations. Graduation doesn’t have to be the end of your time with us. You could choose to continue your academic career with a PhD programme at ARU. Take advantage of our Alumni Scholarship and save £400 on your fees. How can ARU help with my employability and career development? We want you to be a step ahead when you graduate, so we offer: courses designed with employers tutors with professional industry knowledge hands-on learning which may include industry-led projects, placements or Professional Experience modules . Alongside your course, there are lots of other opportunities to build your skills and experience: add value to your CV with an ARU Certificate of Professional Development get involved in a thriving volunteering programme develop your brilliant business ideas work with businesses to make a social impact . We’re here to help you develop your CV and find that all-important role after graduation. Our Employability Service offers tailored career appointments, advice on writing your CV, help to complete job applications, and much more. You’ll have 24/7 access to an online Careers Centre too, which is packed with useful resources. The support continues after you graduate, with lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . Find out more about careers support at ARU . Teaching and modules Develop your understanding of public health and learn to apply your knowledge to real-world situations. You’ll explore contemporary issues such as infectious disease control, vaccine hesitancy, mental health and migration. Alongside this, you’ll look at local and national policy, health inequalities, and health communication and behaviour change strategies. We’ll prepare you to take on global challenges, as you learn to use demographic statistics and epidemiological data to improve public health. Finally, you’ll plan, design and conduct a major piece of research work with your Postgraduate Research Project. This can be either research- or work-based. What will I study? MPH Part-time option(s) MPH Modules are subject to change and availability, and may vary by location. If you have the choice of optional modules, these are indicated with a *. Year 1 Essential Issues in Public Health and Practice Statistics and Epidemiology Public Health Ethics: Mental Health, Bioethics, and Society Postgraduate Research Project - Public Health Globalisation and Public Health Module details Part-time option(s) It's possible to study this course part-time. You'll take the same modules as MPH students, but sometimes in a different order or in different years. As a part-time student you'll typically study for twice as long as full-time students. For example, if the MPH course takes one year, you can expect to study over two years, though for some courses this may vary. Year 1 Essential Issues in Public Health and Practice Public Health Ethics: Mental Health, Bioethics, and Society Globalisation and Public Health Year 2 Statistics and Epidemiology Postgraduate Research Project - Public Health Module details How is MPH Global Public Health assessed? We'll assess both your theoretical knowledge and practical skills. Assessments have been developed to include skills you'll need in your career such as policy briefs, persuasive arguments, intervention development and written evaluations, debates, and outbreak management plans. Who teaches MPH Global Public Health at ARU? Read profiles of teaching and research staff on this course. Dr Russell Kabir Associate Professor & Course Leader Dr Ali Davod Parsa Associate Professor Clare Jacobs Deputy Head of School Dr Richard Hayhoe Senior Lecturer Dr Lyndsay S. Baines Senior Lecturer in Global Public Health Facilities Enjoy a range of facilities designed to support your studies and career development. These include extensive library and IT resources, and careers support through our Employability Service . After you graduate, you’ll have lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . You can also access support, should you need it, with study skills, health and wellbeing, and more. Please enable JavaScript for "Fees Information" section to function. Entry requirements Standard entry requirements MPH Part-time option(s) MPH A UK Honours Degree or equivalent International students Applicants will be required to demonstrate the University standard of English language (IELTS) at Level 6.5 prior to commencement on a course. Students who do not meet this criterion will be advised to seek support from ALS English language programme prior to commencement of the course. Selection Process Candidates should normally have a good first degree or equivalent and be working, or hope to work, within any area of the public health arena. They do not necessarily need a professional qualification for access to the course but do need to demonstrate a strong interest in public health and local health improvement. Candidates with a third class honours, or ordinary (pass) degree plus a minimum of one year of relevant post-graduate work experience, will be considered on an individual basis. Candidates who do not have a first degree, but have relevant work experience, may be able to gain access to the course by completing a Non Graduate Entry Profile demonstrating, and reflecting on, achievement of generic undergraduate learning outcomes through experiential learning. Admission to the Course with Non-Traditional entry Non graduates may gain entry to the course by clearly demonstrating on their application that their qualifications and experience are equivalent to an Honours degree. Admission with Credit Applicants seeking admission with credit (either APCL or APEL) are referred initially to the AP(E)L Advisor for the Faculty of Health, Education, Medicine and Social Care. Important additional notes Our published entry requirements are a guide only and our decision will be based on your overall suitability for the course as well as whether you meet the minimum entry requirements. Other equivalent qualifications may be accepted for entry to this course; please email [email protected] for further information. Applicants to undergraduate courses can also check our information about undergraduate entry qualifications . You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your course. Part-time option(s) See entry requirements for the MA or MSc International students We welcome applications from international and EU students, and accept a range of international qualifications. See international and EU entry requirements See information about application deadlines You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your course. English language requirements If English is not your first language, you'll need to make sure you meet our English language requirements for postgraduate courses . Check the section ' English language requirements ' for IELTS requirements. Please enable JavaScript for "Fees Information" section to function. Find out more about paying your fees and about postgraduate loans and funding . Part-time option(s) £6,137 UK students starting 2027/28 (part-time, per year) Fees are payable upfront, in full or in instalments, but there's no need to pay until you've accepted an offer to study with us. Find out more about paying your fees and about postgraduate loans and funding . International students MPH Part-time option(s) MPH £18,825 International students starting 2027/28 (full-time, per year) You can pay your fees upfront, in full or in two instalments. We will ask for a deposit of £4,000 or a sponsorship letter Find out about paying your fees . Part-time option(s) £9,412 International students starting 2027/28 (part-time, per year) You can pay your fees upfront, in full or in two instalments. We will ask for a deposit of £4,000 or a sponsorship letter Find out about paying your fees . Part-time fees Part-time course fees assume that you’re studying at half the rate of a full-time student (50% intensity). Course fees will be different if you study over a longer period. All fees are for guidance purposes only. Your offer letter will contain full details of credits and fees, or you can contact us if you'd like more information. Whether you're new to the field or already have some experience, our course will give you the skills and knowledge to pursue a career in management. With a strong focus on compassion and social justice in the global healthcare community, you'll learn to evolve your practice to make the most of new opportunities and tackle challenges – while maintaining a healthy culture within which service users, carers, families and colleagues can thrive. Through self-reflection, you'll develop your own management style and consider your personal effectiveness. Take your clinical career to the next level by moving into management. Assistant Principal Dr Esther Norton introduces our Masters degree at ARU Peterborough. Close full-screen gallery. Take your clinical career to the next level by moving into management. Focus on compassion and social justice in the global healthcare community Engage in an innovative research-based consultancy project Enjoy a multi-disciplinary approach that can help you build a strong professional network Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers As a graduate you could enter a variety of management posts in healthcare and associated fields. This course will equip you with a wide range of transferable skills, including critical analysis, report writing, presentation and group/teamwork. There's a real emphasis on working with others and understanding your role within diverse teams. By studying at ARU Peterborough, you'll be able to increase your employability and make strong professional connections. There are opportunities to build your business management experience by regularly working with sector professionals in the Peterborough area. You'll be able to focus on specific organisations and brands – thereby developing your understanding of key organisations and potential employers. We also invite guest speakers to share their experiences of working in different organisations and industries. Graduation doesn’t have to be the end of your time with us. You could choose to continue your academic career with a PhD programme at ARU. Take advantage of our Alumni Scholarship and save £400 on your fees. We’re here to help you develop your CV and find that all-important role after graduation. Our Employability Service offers tailored career appointments, advice on writing your CV, help to complete job applications, and much more. You’ll have 24/7 access to an online Careers Centre too, which is packed with useful resources. The support continues after you graduate, with lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . Find out more about careers support at ARU . Teaching and modules Our MSc Healthcare Leadership and Management features six core modules. You’ll understand the complex challenges that health systems globally are facing and how they meet them, what you can do to address them in your workplace, and learn how to develop a supportive workplace culture. You’ll learn how to manage complex operations across national borders and respond to global challenges in international strategic management. In your consultancy project you’ll review a significant problem for a real client organisation and develop managerial recommendations. If you study the PG Cert option, you'll complete two modules: Compassionate Leadership, and Emerging Approaches to Health Systems. What will I study? MSc 2 years part-time MSc Modules are subject to change and availability, and may vary by location. If you have the choice of optional modules, these are indicated with a *. Year 1 Compassionate Leadership Emerging Approaches to Health Systems Into ARU Global Operations Management International Business Strategy Consultancy Major Project Module details 2 years part-time It's possible to study this course part-time. You'll take the same modules as MSc/MA students, but sometimes in a different order or in different years. As a part-time student you'll typically study for twice as long as full-time students. For example if the MSc/MA course takes one year, you can expect to study over two years, though for some courses this may vary. How is Healthcare Leadership and Management assessed? All assessment is designed to allow you to demonstrate what you’ve learned, and to make sure you’re developing the knowledge and skills you need to complete the course. You can expect an interesting mix of coursework, reports, presentations, real-life assessments, case studies, problem-solving activities, group work and a consultancy project. Facilities Enjoy a range of facilities designed to support your studies and career development. These include extensive library and IT resources, and careers support through our Employability Service . After you graduate, you’ll have lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . You can also access support, should you need it, with study skills, health and wellbeing, and more. Please enable JavaScript for "Fees Information" section to function. Other equivalent qualifications may be accepted for entry to this course; please email [email protected] for further information. Applicants to undergraduate courses can also check our information about undergraduate entry qualifications . You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your course. 2 years part-time See entry requirements for the MA or MSc International students We welcome applications from international and EU students, and accept a range of international qualifications. See international and EU entry requirements See information about application deadlines You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your course. Part-time fees Part-time course fees assume that you’re studying at half the rate of a full-time student (50% intensity). Course fees will be different if you study over a longer period. Jump to a section Introduction Student work Course options Key facts Teaching and assessment Entry requirements Fees and paying for university Facilities and showcase Lecturers Careers Introduction Study MA Illustration and discover how illustration can change the world for the better. Develop crucial skills such as observation and creative thinking, and learn to apply them to the issues that society faces today. Student experience Previous. Next. Student work Yetta Xu A sketchbook page made in part for the module Image and Impact. See more work by our MA Illustration students ARU Spotlight Dr Nanette Hoogslag Nanette is Senior Lecturer for our MA Illustration, a practising illustrator and Principal Editor of the Journal of Illustration. Discover her inspirations and thoughts on the future of illustration. Read Nanette's Spotlight interview Fruszina Menihei Study Response to the Design Methods and Context module - a Victorian cemetery as a space for the living as well the passed. Live project Wordsworth Museum Visiting the Lake District as part of a live project for the Wordsworth Museum. Ran Ding Isolation Museum - Intrapersonal Isolation As part of her Master’s Project, Ding used mirrored paper and print to create a book exploring introspection. Orit Bergman Lecture and workshop Enjoying a creative moment in the workshop “Illustration Beyond the Page” with award-winning Visiting Lecturer Orit Bergman. Shunan Ma The favour of emotions Experiments with augmented reality, to make the emotion of flavours come alive. Jewel Chang Control Collaboration and Compromise One of five collages for the Master’s Project, exploring the power dynamics within an intimate relationship. Team project Graphic Notetaking Students acted as as live scribes at a one-day conference for the NHS and research partners, resulting in illustrations of a published report. Jinpu Zhou Line A Master’s Project exploring the narrative and interactive potential of a VR environment. Jiatong Dai Invisible Woe Cover of practice-based research for Master’s Project exploring how adults with visual impairment experience illustration. Student work Observational drawing Observational drawing as part of the module Image and Impact. Jianing Wang Room Echoes One of 50 image-and-sound illustrations for her Master’s Project, exploring how to capture everyday moments of solitude. Already have an ARU degree? You may be eligible for our Alumni Scholarship for students starting postgraduate courses. Illustration is a broad visual narrative practice that has many applications in publishing and the wider creative industry. On our MA Illustration degree you'll focus on illustration for social change, an innovative and growing area that addresses the complex social and environmental problems faced by society today. Illustration skills such as visual storytelling, visual mediation, observation, creative thinking and of course image making are much sought-after, and more and more illustrators take part in change-making processes in organisations, institutes, and government. Our Masters in Illustration is unique in its focus on building your illustration practice and exploring and developing your role in addressing issues including integration and diversity, behavioural change, community cohesion, and environmental challenges. Whatever your background, you will develop your visual practice in important areas for illustrators, such as image creation; visual sequencing; concept development; and textuality. You’ll also extend your knowledge of the complexities of socio-environmental problems; institutional and government structures; creative project development and management; design methods; and collaboration processes. As a graduate, you'll have the confidence to start out in a career as an illustrator and play an active creative role in social and environmental change-making processes. Read more Teaching times 2025-26 (subject to change for 2026-27) Full-time: Mondays and Wednesdays 10am–4pm Part-time: Year 1: Wednesdays 10am–4pm, Year 2: Mondays 10am–4pm As a postgraduate student at ARU, you'll have access to a dedicated base studio, as well as specialist facilities such as animation suites, film and photography studios, a printmaking workshop, and our Futures Lab. In our printmaking workshop and Futures Lab you’ll be able to access both traditional and emerging processes, including relief and intaglio printing, screen-printing, plate lithography, and photo-based, digital media and 3D printing. You'll receive training in creative software such as Adobe Cloud, – and you can also get training in all our other art and creative industries facilities, too. Studying in our dedicated studios at Cambridge School of Art and project locations, much of your work will be practice-based. You’ll take part in live projects, working with an external partner and students from related Masters degrees, as well as proposing and undertaking your own self-directed projects. At the end of the course, you will use all the skills you have developed to research and complete a final visual project relating to your own specialisms. Throughout your studies, you'll collaborate and discuss your work with staff, external partners, visiting professionals and fellow students, giving you an invaluable opportunity to see how others respond to it. All our teaching team are practising designers, design researchers and artists, so you'll hear about the latest news and issues in the industry and have access to sound careers advice. Course Director: Karin Eklund Course options Please enable JavaScript for "Course options" section to function. Course options Key facts Please enable JavaScript for "Key Facts" section to function. Looking for different course options? Please enable JavaScript for "Entry Requirements" section to function. Entry Requirements Loading... Entry requirements are not currently available, please try again later. Please enable JavaScript for "Fees Information" section to function. Fees and Paying for University Facilities and showcase Studios and workshops As well as our dedicated illustration studio, where you’ll have your own desk, you’ll have use of the following facilities : a printmaking workshop a 3D workshop a digital photography lab photography studios and darkrooms Mac and PC suites. Take a guided tour and meet our students . Industry-standard equipment All our Illustration students have access to facilities including: the full Adobe Creative suite Apple iMacs wide-format printers and scanners vintage printmaking presses letterpress machine photography equipment, including digital cameras and lighting kits. Our team of technical officers will be on hand to offer training and support. Take a closer look Our Creative Showcase shines a spotlight on what makes ARU creative and cultural – our spaces, places and people. Find out more about our community, the difference we make, the stories we tell, and the things that inspire us. You can also explore the work of our graduating students in our digital graduate showcase. Lecturers Previous. Next. Nurbanu Asena Senior Lecturer Nurbanu Asena's profile page Visit Nurbanu's website Follow Nurbanu on Instagram Connect with Nurbanu on LinkedIn [email protected] Nanette Hoogslag Senior Lecturer Nanette Hoogslag's profile page Visit Nanette's website Visit the Journal of Illustration website [email protected] Nicholas Jeeves Lecturer Nicholas Jeeves's profile page [email protected] Visit Nick's website View Nick's profile on our Creative Showcase Inbal Leitner Lecturer Practitioner Inbal Leitner's profile page [email protected] Karin Eklund Associate Lecturer Karin Eklund's profile page Visit Karin's website Follow Karin on Instagram [email protected] Careers Our MA Illustration course will prepare you for a career as a freelance illustrator and creative consultant. In recent years, roles in illustration - either on a freelance basis or as creative team members - have been increasing. This is due to the understanding of the important role of visual storytelling and the need for distinct visual identity and connection. Depending on your own interests, your career might take you into self-publishing and artistic production; book and magazine illustration; in-house media and creative teams in publishing, advertising, games and animation and communication agencies; as well as freelance or in-house creative consultancy and institutional and organisational change-making teams. As an MA Illustration student you’ll also gain skills that will be useful in many other fields, such as teaching and creative management. You might even find a way to combine it with your current career, as did ARU graduate Dr Katy Shorttle, whose artwork on health issues was featured in The Guardian . Or you might decide to move on to a research degree, like our PhD Art and Design , PhD Graphic Design and Typography , or PhD Fine Art . Take advantage of our Alumni Scholarship and save £400 on your fees, and take a look at some of our current PhD project opportunities . Kelley Donner "My kids and I began talking about what life would be like at the North Pole and how Santa would respond to COVID-19. There is so much uncertainty and anxiety right now, so I thought it would be helpful to talk about COVID-19 in a way that’s both engaging and reassuring for children." Kelley Donner MA Illustration student and author of A Very Corona Christmas Read more Apply now for MA Illustration Our course pages need JavaScript enabled for you to apply. Want to talk to someone? Do you have a question that we haven't answered so far? Talk to our application experts. You can also ask our Student Ambassadors about life at ARU. [email protected] Call 01245 686868 We're here Monday-Thursday 9am-5pm (please note we close at 3.30pm on the first and third Thursday of the month for staff training), and Friday 9am-4.30pm. Come to an Open Day Use our enquiry form Talk to one of our students Benefits of postgraduate study Improve your employability, progress in your career, and take on an intellectual challenge with our flexible postgraduate degrees. Through a structured curriculum with lectures, seminars, workshops, teamwork and independent studio practice, you'll explore different aspects of illustration such as its role and impact in social and changemaking projects; material expression; image and text relationships; and semiotics and narratology, as well as audience engagement; illustration, design and social research methods; critical analysis; and creative project management, which you will put to immediate use on the course as well as in your future career.

Modules are subject to change and availability. Some modules are shared to encourage cross-disciplinary exchange.

Assessment
You’ll show your progress through your self-directed visual projects, which will include extended written project proposals, developmental and final visual work, a reflective commentary, and an academic report of 3000 words. The Masters Project will allow you to build on all previous modules to design a visual project which shows mastery of your subject. We offer the guidance and structure to self-organise a degree show, which will show your work, but also evidence your project management abilities.

","CoreModules":[{"Title":"Design Methods and Contexts","Description":"In this cross-disciplinary module, you'll explore how design and creative methods and structures inherent to graphic design and illustration and those used in other design approaches, such as in social design, systems design, design narratives and speculative design can play an important role in enabling and driving innovation processes. You'll investigate these methods and approaches in practice and theory and contextualise your findings with discussions around issues of modern-day societal connectivity, audience participation and environmental impact. You'll explore how existing and created tools can be effective in addressing a wide range of issues, particularly within the context of complex social and environmental issues, typical within public-facing institutes, organisations and social enterprises. Alongside theoretical, ethical, and structural understanding, you'll engage with professional strategies such as creative project management, cocreation, feasibility studies, and presentation. This wide-ranging enquiry is designed to equip you with background knowledge and a ‘tool-kit’ of methods and strategies which will enable you to embark on a multi-disciplinary and collaborative projects within social settings. This is a research-led but equally practice-based module, where reading and lectures are developed through critical reading, assignments, seminars and workshops in which you test your finding and developments.","Code":"MOD009035","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"210505fc-2d1e-47f3-bd9f-6a42b5451dec"},{"Title":"Image and Impact","Description":"In this investigative module you are asked to explore the key principles of the illustrated image, namely aesthetics, narration, semantics and rhetoric and how these shape the role of illustration as well as your personal visual language and approach. This is a practice-led research module. Supported by lectures and seminars where you will reflect on contemporary theory and practice in relation to visual language, narratology, material expression and visual rhetoric in single and serial visual work. You are expected to propose and resolve a self-contained project or projects. A large proportion of the teaching and learning activities will be focused around the development and resolution of individual student research projects, with group critiques and tutorials centred on developing visual practice. Self-directed study and the ongoing development of visual work on weekly basis outside of taught sessions is a necessary part of the module.","Code":"MOD009037","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"a533961a-fe9f-4e1a-abbe-6dc101b3fa2b"},{"Title":"Visual Text","Description":"In this studio-based module, relationships between text and image, words, authorship, and the artist's voice are explored through a series of set and self-directed visual projects. Lectures and seminars will examine the role of text and typographic identity in the generation of meaning, and explore more complex and ambiguous text-image relationships. A large proportion of the teaching and learning activities will be focused around the development and resolution of individual student research projects, with group critiques and tutorials centred on developing visual practice. As with all our modules, self-directed study, and the ongoing development of visual work on a weekly basis outside of taught sessions, is a necessary part of this module.","Code":"MOD000228","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"9cca733d-a3e4-4946-85d6-998ab3747d21"},{"Title":"Practice Through Partnership","Description":"In this module you will build on the knowledge and skills you have obtained in Design Methods and Contexts, and apply them to a live project in a real-world setting. In partnership with a mentor from an institutional, research, or governmental body, you will develop a creative proposal that seeks to make a social or environmental change. Working as a member of a cross-disciplinary team, you will test your ability to respond creatively and effectively to complex, change making briefs, as well as developing your organisational, team-working, and networking skills. As part of the team your tasks could include visual research, mapping, analysis, stakeholder interaction, socio-environmental and technical research, event organisation, and client negotiations - each a necessary aspect of developing real-world creative solutions and communications. Giving you first-hand experience of the diversity of issues around socio-environmental projects, this module will show how design methods can play a considerable, even essential role in the development of research, analysis, communication, and problem solving.","Code":"MOD009036","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"c7fd371e-bc33-4cf5-b2cc-851c23374f95"},{"Title":"Master's Project: Illustration","Description":"The Masters Project represents the culmination of your learning on the programme, giving you the opportunity to develop and resolve a major area of enquiry. This is a self-directed visual project negotiated with the staff team and peers. You'll need to negotiate, manage, co-ordinate and bring to successful conclusion a complex, practice-based project within your field of art, media or design. You'll start by formally presenting your research proposal to staff and peers, and will be expected to build on your previous modules to identify a complex area for investigation and enquiry, as well as research methods appropriate to the project. Following negotiation with staff, peers and, where appropriate, outside agencies, you'll then submit a written research proposal. Your project may involve external engagement alongside a personal exploration of themes and concepts in your specialist field. You'll need to show your ability to innovate, think strategically and be sensitive to changing cultural and social climates.
