","CoreModules":[{"Title":"Theoretical Foundations: Critiques, Debates and Contexts","Description":"You will examine the theory and key concepts of international relations and the development of the state, ground them in their historical context, and explore their policy implications. You will begin by examining where the boundaries of the discipline might lie, before looking at debates over the role of theory in explaining International Relations. You will receive detailed explanations of the key competing theories within the discipline, and their development and evolution. Key themes you will explore include the development of Classical Realism from its roots in doctrines of war, Liberalism and the dream of global order, through the tussles between Neorealism and neoliberalism throughout the decades of the Cold War. You will also look at Constructivism and the English School, radical Marxist and Neo-Marxist perspectives, through to Feminism, Post-Colonialism, Postmodernism and cosmopolitanism. You will learn to place the theory firmly in the context of 20th century events, exploring the way in which political and academic ideas are shaped by and in turn influence international affairs. You will also explore other directions in which the study of International Relations might travel in the future. Your assessment will comprise a report of 1,000 words, a presentation, a literature search equivalent to 1,000 words and a longer essay of 3,500 words.","Code":"MOD003643","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"78fa93a7-a13b-4a8d-b48f-44a2610bae4a"},{"Title":"Global Governance","Description":"In this module we'll critically analyse the origins, evolution and role of international institutions in the global order over the course of the 20th and 21st century. You'll gain an understanding of why these institutions have developed, and why states choose, or do not choose, to use these institutions as a means to achieve their objectives. We'll examine the still evolving structures of global governance, and the role of these organisations and institutions in contemporary politics and diplomacy. You'll consider the work of specific organisations, including the UN, the EU, the IMF and World Bank etc. We'll pay particular attention to the challenges inherent in attempting to foster international co-operation and consensus between sovereign nation states, including the limitations of international law, and examines potential future developments.","Code":"MOD003642","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"afe592d2-583d-48d4-af07-a14847f38e01"},{"Title":"Postgraduate Major Project","Description":"In this module you’ll explore a topic of your choice in greater depth (on the condition that we have the expertise to supervise it). This format of this project is also flexible; you may choose the standard dissertation format to present your work. You may also, under the guidance of your supervisor, opt to undertake a project that, for example, involves the production of an artefact, staging of an exhibition or publishing on-line content that has a public education or community enrichment brief. You may also consider, again under the guidance of your supervisor, designing a project that tests an hypothesis you ultimately write up as a report but which you test through the production of material for public consumption. You can undertake some of this work in collaboration with other members of the course, conditional on a clear agreement is reached about the division of labour across this team. This project gives you the opportunity to use material and research methods from the rest of the course. It is an opportunity for you to demonstrate that you have the detailed knowledge and understanding of your chosen research area, a critical appreciation of the appropriate methodologies and theories, and the ability to locate, to critically engage with and evaluate an appropriate range of sources. You will also be expected to recognise and manage appropriately any ethical issues that arise in the completion of this project. Finally, you should be able to present your findings so that tin they can be clearly understood across a range of audiences.","Code":"MOD000835","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"efbf015a-bc9d-41a5-bcfb-681a829bd76d"},{"Title":"Into ARU","Description":"Entering higher education is exciting; but it can also be a daunting experience. At ARU, we want all our students to make the most of the opportunities higher education provides, reach your potential, become lifelong learners and find fulfilling careers. However, we appreciate that the shift from secondary education, or a return to formal education is, in itself, quite a journey. This module is designed to ease that transition. You'll be enrolled on it as soon as you receive an offer from ARU so you can begin to learn about university life before your course starts. Through Into ARU, you'll explore a virtual land modelled around ARU values: Courage, Innovation, Community, Integrity, Responsibility, and Ambition. This innovative module is designed as a game, where you collect knowledge and complete mini tasks. You'll proceed at your own pace, though we you to have completed your Into ARU exploration by week 6. If for any reason you're unable to complete by that date, we'll signpost to existing services so that we can be confident that you are supported.","Code":"MOD999910","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"4f3c4a41-2e3f-49aa-8860-037c9fba5c37"}],"OptionalModules":[{"Title":"War, Peacekeeping and Military Intervention","Description":"In this module, you'll study the history and the contemporary status of peacekeeping, military humanitarian intervention, and the ‘responsibility to protect’. The role of international institutions in multilateral intervention will also be probed, as will the challenges involved in post-conflict security, and peacebuilding. The module will underline the significance of unilateral and multilateral military intervention in contemporary international relations and global politics, as well as its limitations. It will use a variety of real-world case studies of war, peacekeeping and military intervention and will use a range of teaching methods to engage you and develop your understanding of intervention from a pragmatic, empirical, strategic and policy-oriented perspective. The assessment for this module will contribute to the development of skills in writing, comparative analysis of data and new insights or perspectives on existing data and/or materials, helping to develop postgraduate research skills.","Code":"MOD003646","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"709e35da-dfe1-4810-bb2b-56a5536a2ef8"},{"Title":"Globalisation Organised Crime and Crime Control","Description":"The globalisation of contemporary societies has meant that criminal activity that was once primarily a national concern is increasingly becoming global in nature. In this module, you'll learn all about criminal activities that cross state boundaries, regardless of whether those are physical borders or the virtual boundaries of cyberspace. You'll also develop an understanding of the relevant policing bodies and how they are required to manage risk and security on a much wider scale. On Globalisation, Organised Crime, and Crime Control, you'll have the opportunity to explore the important social changes that have contributed to the emergence of ‘global’ cities and new patterns of crime and control. There are several questions you'll be able to consider in-depth over the course of the module. One issue is the notion of 'organised crime' itself. How organised is it? For example, how organised is illegal drug trafficking in Europe? What external threats to the 'licit' political economies are there? What is the relationship between the different research strategies and the formulation of international policies to tackle organised illicit trade? This module offers you the opportunity to explore the structure and nature of organised crime and examine other crimes of globalisation. You'll engage in discussions and debates on the concept of criminal networks, including criminal opportunity and routine activities, which will allow you to then analyse different case studies. In addition, you will measure and evaluate the scale of illicit trade to analyse the regulatory issues involved and potential preventative strategies. In this module, you'll be able to examine the local roots of transnational patterns of crime before widening the lens to evaluate a wide range of transnational crimes and how they have been policed. Together we'll explore organised illicit activities such as financial crime, environmental crime, human trafficking, and state crime, before examining newer and emergent transnational crimes such as cybercrime. Successful completion of this module will entail significant contributions on your part to the weekly seminars by researching and discussing different cases.","Code":"MOD009757","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"77c3e56f-0a6b-489f-81a7-e2e461110eb2"},{"Title":"Race, Racism and Resistance in Modern Britain since the Eighteenth Century","Description":"This module will present a history of race, racism and the resistances to racism in modern Britain. It will open with a consideration of early definitions of ‘race’ and the rise of ‘scientific racism’ in the late eighteenth century. It will then move to an examination of slavery in the British West Indies, the slave resistances and the British abolitionist movement. This history is less known than that of the US. This will be followed by one session on the role of the British Empire and its impact on Britain in terms of racialised ideology. The subsequent sessions will address race as constructed, contested and lived in Britain: the Black and Asian presence pre-World War I, interwar and Second World War, as well as the influence of ideas about race, sexuality, eugenics and anti-Semitism; the Windrush generation, Black politics and anti-racism of the 1920s to 1980s, including Black feminism, rock against racism, and anti-fascism. The history of the presence of mixed-race relationships in Britain will also be considered as well as ‘mixed-race’ as a 21st century identity. Finally ‘whiteness’ as a racial and privileged identity will be scrutinised.","Code":"MOD006395","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"db7d6f07-f541-4bd7-ae7e-051820efdd2f"},{"Title":"Beyond Borders Intercultural Communication Welfare and Policy","Description":"This module takes an interdisciplinary approach to introducing key topics and ways of working in the social sciences. You'll look at the development of relations, communicative styles and values between individuals and groups of different cultural backgrounds and delve into comparative issues concerning social policy and social welfare in the international and intercultural context. You'll do this by exploring areas such as gender equality, social housing, education and immigration and wider social concepts such as identity, intersectionality and inequality. You'll work with case studies to exemplify these concepts. In this way, you'll develop the foundation for a deeper understanding and appreciation of fundamental topics in the social sciences. You'll also receive guidance on study at Master’s level and the module will guide you towards the academic research and writing skills needed to work independently at this level.","Code":"MOD010759","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"bbb89968-3e72-43f6-86a5-634020d297e9"},{"Title":"Intercultural Consultancy Project","Description":"Working with an external collaborative partner, you will negotiate a 12 week consultancy project that demonstrates and builds upon theoretical and practical skills you have acquired on your course. The module will enable you to work contextually within the framework of work-based learning by facilitating knowledge exchange between the student and their external partner. The project will respond to the opportunities and needs of the external partner as applied to the field of intercultural communications. You will critically engage with how this professional sector operates in context of the wider business environments and how this can be applied to your career development. This module supports you in the development of key skills required in contemporary intercultural work environments, such as face-to-face and asynchronous communications, collaborative and cooperative decision making or intra-team conflict resolution.","Code":"MOD008998","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"828f471c-8924-483e-b522-4be3447c71d2"},{"Title":"Communication and Conflict","Description":"On this module you'll explore historical and thematic approaches to reporting on conflict and also how communication functions in a crisis. You'll examine the reciprocal relationships between the military, governments and the media, including how the media can be used to legitimise conflict, and the changing role of social media in building consensus and protest, including the use of Twitter and Facebook to organise demonstrations and undermine the power of state-dominated discourses. You’ll also consider more traditional forms of communication, including censorship and propaganda, and whether the state is ever able to retain control of the narrative, as well as the role of the war reporter, and the way in which governments can utilise the independent media and how independent it really is. Other areas of exploration include consent, public interest, ethics and the representation of suffering, looking at whether the dominance of media in the debate in the West means that public interest in conflict is limited by the limitations of the media, and what this means for winning hearts and minds during insurgencies, military interventions and peacekeeping operations. Finally, you'll look at the way war and conflict is portrayed in fictional accounts and the underlying assumptions of such portrayals, and will examine conflicting discourses about war in post-conflict environments and the way the media can contribute to or hamper the process of post-conflict reconstruction. Themes throughout the module will include the question of who owns, defines and propagates the truth, and the implications of this in the context of conflict and war.","Code":"MOD003644","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"a956aeb6-6c48-423b-b081-fb889035e622"},{"Title":"Terrorism: Crime, Justice and Historical Continuities","Description":"Terrorism is often presented as a uniquely modern threat shaped by globalisation, digital radicalisation and the so-called war on terror. This module challenges that assumption by situating contemporary terrorism within broader historical continuities of political violence, state response and criminal justice intervention. You'll examine terrorism through a criminological lens, gaining insight into how acts of political violence are defined, constructed and governed as crime. By interrogating contested concepts such as radicalisation and extremism, you will sharpen your analytical skills and learn to question taken-for-granted assumptions. You'll assess how media narratives, public fear and political rhetoric influence public understandings of threat and legitimacy, equipping you to engage more confidently in academic, professional and public debates. Through diverse case studies, you'll explore connections between terrorism and organised crime, the growth of emergency powers, suspect communities, punishment and prison management. You'll evaluate whether criminal justice responses reduce violence or risk prolonging conflict. By the end of the module, you'll have enhanced your research, evaluation and critical reasoning skills while gaining a nuanced understanding of prevention, legitimacy and how justice can be reimagined in response to political violence.","Code":"MOD000829","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"27d13061-b77c-4866-a0e8-2beb247f3cec"},{"Title":"Going Global: Making the Modern World, 1979-1999","Description":"This module examines the main themes in contemporary world history, focusing specifically on the 1980s and 1990s as the foundations of the modern, globalising, world were being laid down. You'll critically assess the breakdown of the state-led economic model adopted after the Second World War and consider the development of the more globalised system which replaced it. You'll examine what globalisation meant in reality as changes in technology drove the new consumerism but also contributed to deindustrialisation. In addition, you'll consider how the changes in capitalism influenced the political left as socialist and communist parties across the world turned to market-based ideas and policies. The module also focuses on the ‘third wave of democracy’ which saw apparently stable regimes such as Pinochet’s Chile and Botha’s South Africa fall, and it considers how these factors fed into and influenced the late Cold War years. You'll uncover the ways in which the 1980s was a transformative but incomplete decade as the new ideas introduced by New Right politicians were not completely established until the 1990s with the development of the ‘Third Way’ politics and the victory of neoliberalism at home and abroad. This module is taught through weekly sessions and the emphasis will be on building individual understanding of the key themes of the period as well as encouraging teamwork and oral skills through group discussion and group work. You will develop analytical skills through the investigation of documentary material (identified in the ‘accessible archives’ seminar) from the Thatcher, Kinnock, Reagan or Clinton papers (for example) and you will be expected to bring a relevant document to each class to discuss each week.","Code":"MOD006397","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"1839fd5b-1815-4e4d-b975-e5eae0b1035e"},{"Title":"Postgraduate Research Methods","Description":"In this module you'll gain the research skills and techniques needed both to critically evaluate the literature you'll be using in your course and to put into practice in your own dissertation. We'll explore the methodologies and methods applied in contemporary social science research to enable you to select an appropriate range for your own needs. You'll have the opportunity to experiment with a variety of methods so that you'll fully understood them and be able to adapt them creatively for your own projects. The module will place research methods in a wider framework of social research strategies at a postgraduate level. We'll examine the research design options available to you at Masters level and explore thoroughly the issues involved in planning a research project and formulating research questions. With the aid of library expertise, you'll have access to and understand current tools for reviewing and researching existing literature. Particular attention will be paid to ethical principles and the politics of social research. A central part of the module will address the practicalities of employing both qualitative and quantitative methodologies. Computer-assisted analysis methods will be introduced.","Code":"MOD000825","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"5b02c3ba-c947-4e80-93fc-9a64099bcba0"},{"Title":"Global Development: Policy and Practice","Description":"This module aims to critically examine the key policies, politics and practices in the field of international development. It explores the key policies undertaken by various actors in the development field, including international organisations, national governments, the private sector, non-governmental organisations, and grassroots movements. You'll learn about the politics of ‘doing’ development and the challenges encountered at each level of policy: global, national, and local levels. You'll also critically examine the key debates in the literature on ‘best practise’ and ‘what works’ drawing on a variety of case studies and examples. You'll cover a range of related topics such as social protection programmes, grassroots movements, advocacy and public action. You'll also gain several practical skills related to project design, project monitoring and evaluation and other themes related to development management especially in the NGO sector. Key development challenges from climate change, poverty, inequality, migration, conflict and human rights will be critically examined in vibrant class discussions, debates and presentations drawing on historical and current events and case studies. You are encouraged to critically examine these challenges in light of relevant theoretical and empirical literature as well as to think about practical solutions to address these challenges. You'll be also critically analysing the difficulties encountered during the implementation of these policies and collectively discuss ways to overcome these difficulties.","Code":"MOD009232","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"0831cea3-1be3-4c1b-928f-166d81bde741"}],"Id":"5a53645a-22f1-4a82-b4c6-1fd3a6e67771","SelectedModule":false}],"UcasCode":"","SITSCode":"AGTTINRL","AstraCode":"P0185","ModeOfStudy":{"KisCode":"FullTime","ModeOfStudyCode":"FT","ExcludeFromCourseSummary":false,"Name":"Full-time","Id":"3188d331-b419-4c02-bf25-30c84b6fff3d"},"CoreOption":false,"FoundationOption":false,"PlacementOption":false,"ProfessionalExperienceOption":false,"PartTimeOption":false,"Extra1":false,"Extra2":false,"Status":null,"StartDateDisclaimer":null,"DegreeApprenticeship":false,"Award":null,"Qualification":null,"LocationOverride":null,"EntryRequirementYears":[{"Name":"2026","Id":"b0de6795-6e13-4745-98d9-c1515ee46eae"}],"EntryRequirementsInformation":[{"HeadingTitle":"Standard entry requirements","RichTextContent":[{"RichTextTitle":"","RichTextContent":"

","CoreModules":[{"Title":"Global Governance","Description":"In this module we'll critically analyse the origins, evolution and role of international institutions in the global order over the course of the 20th and 21st century. You'll gain an understanding of why these institutions have developed, and why states choose, or do not choose, to use these institutions as a means to achieve their objectives. We'll examine the still evolving structures of global governance, and the role of these organisations and institutions in contemporary politics and diplomacy. You'll consider the work of specific organisations, including the UN, the EU, the IMF and World Bank etc. We'll pay particular attention to the challenges inherent in attempting to foster international co-operation and consensus between sovereign nation states, including the limitations of international law, and examines potential future developments.","Code":"MOD003642","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"afe592d2-583d-48d4-af07-a14847f38e01"},{"Title":"Theoretical Foundations: Critiques, Debates and Contexts","Description":"You will examine the theory and key concepts of international relations and the development of the state, ground them in their historical context, and explore their policy implications. You will begin by examining where the boundaries of the discipline might lie, before looking at debates over the role of theory in explaining International Relations. You will receive detailed explanations of the key competing theories within the discipline, and their development and evolution. Key themes you will explore include the development of Classical Realism from its roots in doctrines of war, Liberalism and the dream of global order, through the tussles between Neorealism and neoliberalism throughout the decades of the Cold War. You will also look at Constructivism and the English School, radical Marxist and Neo-Marxist perspectives, through to Feminism, Post-Colonialism, Postmodernism and cosmopolitanism. You will learn to place the theory firmly in the context of 20th century events, exploring the way in which political and academic ideas are shaped by and in turn influence international affairs. You will also explore other directions in which the study of International Relations might travel in the future. Your assessment will comprise a report of 1,000 words, a presentation, a literature search equivalent to 1,000 words and a longer essay of 3,500 words.","Code":"MOD003643","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"78fa93a7-a13b-4a8d-b48f-44a2610bae4a"},{"Title":"Postgraduate Major Project","Description":"In this module you’ll explore a topic of your choice in greater depth (on the condition that we have the expertise to supervise it). This format of this project is also flexible; you may choose the standard dissertation format to present your work. You may also, under the guidance of your supervisor, opt to undertake a project that, for example, involves the production of an artefact, staging of an exhibition or publishing on-line content that has a public education or community enrichment brief. You may also consider, again under the guidance of your supervisor, designing a project that tests an hypothesis you ultimately write up as a report but which you test through the production of material for public consumption. You can undertake some of this work in collaboration with other members of the course, conditional on a clear agreement is reached about the division of labour across this team. This project gives you the opportunity to use material and research methods from the rest of the course. It is an opportunity for you to demonstrate that you have the detailed knowledge and understanding of your chosen research area, a critical appreciation of the appropriate methodologies and theories, and the ability to locate, to critically engage with and evaluate an appropriate range of sources. You will also be expected to recognise and manage appropriately any ethical issues that arise in the completion of this project. Finally, you should be able to present your findings so that tin they can be clearly understood across a range of audiences.","Code":"MOD000835","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"efbf015a-bc9d-41a5-bcfb-681a829bd76d"},{"Title":"Into ARU","Description":"Entering higher education is exciting; but it can also be a daunting experience. At ARU, we want all our students to make the most of the opportunities higher education provides, reach your potential, become lifelong learners and find fulfilling careers. However, we appreciate that the shift from secondary education, or a return to formal education is, in itself, quite a journey. This module is designed to ease that transition. You'll be enrolled on it as soon as you receive an offer from ARU so you can begin to learn about university life before your course starts. Through Into ARU, you'll explore a virtual land modelled around ARU values: Courage, Innovation, Community, Integrity, Responsibility, and Ambition. This innovative module is designed as a game, where you collect knowledge and complete mini tasks. You'll proceed at your own pace, though we you to have completed your Into ARU exploration by week 6. You’ll also consider more traditional forms of communication, including censorship and propaganda, and whether the state is ever able to retain control of the narrative, as well as the role of the war reporter, and the way in which governments can utilise the independent media and how independent it really is. Other areas of exploration include consent, public interest, ethics and the representation of suffering, looking at whether the dominance of media in the debate in the West means that public interest in conflict is limited by the limitations of the media, and what this means for winning hearts and minds during insurgencies, military interventions and peacekeeping operations. Finally, you'll look at the way war and conflict is portrayed in fictional accounts and the underlying assumptions of such portrayals, and will examine conflicting discourses about war in post-conflict environments and the way the media can contribute to or hamper the process of post-conflict reconstruction. Themes throughout the module will include the question of who owns, defines and propagates the truth, and the implications of this in the context of conflict and war.","Code":"MOD003644","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"a956aeb6-6c48-423b-b081-fb889035e622"},{"Title":"Terrorism: Crime, Justice and Historical Continuities","Description":"Terrorism is often presented as a uniquely modern threat shaped by globalisation, digital radicalisation and the so-called war on terror. This module challenges that assumption by situating contemporary terrorism within broader historical continuities of political violence, state response and criminal justice intervention. You'll examine terrorism through a criminological lens, gaining insight into how acts of political violence are defined, constructed and governed as crime. By interrogating contested concepts such as radicalisation and extremism, you will sharpen your analytical skills and learn to question taken-for-granted assumptions. You'll assess how media narratives, public fear and political rhetoric influence public understandings of threat and legitimacy, equipping you to engage more confidently in academic, professional and public debates. Through diverse case studies, you'll explore connections between terrorism and organised crime, the growth of emergency powers, suspect communities, punishment and prison management. You'll evaluate whether criminal justice responses reduce violence or risk prolonging conflict. By the end of the module, you'll have enhanced your research, evaluation and critical reasoning skills while gaining a nuanced understanding of prevention, legitimacy and how justice can be reimagined in response to political violence.","Code":"MOD000829","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"27d13061-b77c-4866-a0e8-2beb247f3cec"},{"Title":"Going Global: Making the Modern World, 1979-1999","Description":"This module examines the main themes in contemporary world history, focusing specifically on the 1980s and 1990s as the foundations of the modern, globalising, world were being laid down. You'll critically assess the breakdown of the state-led economic model adopted after the Second World War and consider the development of the more globalised system which replaced it. You'll examine what globalisation meant in reality as changes in technology drove the new consumerism but also contributed to deindustrialisation. In addition, you'll consider how the changes in capitalism influenced the political left as socialist and communist parties across the world turned to market-based ideas and policies. The module also focuses on the ‘third wave of democracy’ which saw apparently stable regimes such as Pinochet’s Chile and Botha’s South Africa fall, and it considers how these factors fed into and influenced the late Cold War years. You'll uncover the ways in which the 1980s was a transformative but incomplete decade as the new ideas introduced by New Right politicians were not completely established until the 1990s with the development of the ‘Third Way’ politics and the victory of neoliberalism at home and abroad. This module is taught through weekly sessions and the emphasis will be on building individual understanding of the key themes of the period as well as encouraging teamwork and oral skills through group discussion and group work. You will develop analytical skills through the investigation of documentary material (identified in the ‘accessible archives’ seminar) from the Thatcher, Kinnock, Reagan or Clinton papers (for example) and you will be expected to bring a relevant document to each class to discuss each week.","Code":"MOD006397","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"1839fd5b-1815-4e4d-b975-e5eae0b1035e"},{"Title":"Postgraduate Research Methods","Description":"In this module you'll gain the research skills and techniques needed both to critically evaluate the literature you'll be using in your course and to put into practice in your own dissertation. We'll explore the methodologies and methods applied in contemporary social science research to enable you to select an appropriate range for your own needs. You'll have the opportunity to experiment with a variety of methods so that you'll fully understood them and be able to adapt them creatively for your own projects. The module will place research methods in a wider framework of social research strategies at a postgraduate level. We'll examine the research design options available to you at Masters level and explore thoroughly the issues involved in planning a research project and formulating research questions. With the aid of library expertise, you'll have access to and understand current tools for reviewing and researching existing literature. Particular attention will be paid to ethical principles and the politics of social research. A central part of the module will address the practicalities of employing both qualitative and quantitative methodologies. Computer-assisted analysis methods will be introduced.","Code":"MOD000825","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"5b02c3ba-c947-4e80-93fc-9a64099bcba0"},{"Title":"Global Development: Policy and Practice","Description":"This module aims to critically examine the key policies, politics and practices in the field of international development. It explores the key policies undertaken by various actors in the development field, including international organisations, national governments, the private sector, non-governmental organisations, and grassroots movements. You'll learn about the politics of ‘doing’ development and the challenges encountered at each level of policy: global, national, and local levels. You'll also critically examine the key debates in the literature on ‘best practise’ and ‘what works’ drawing on a variety of case studies and examples. You'll cover a range of related topics such as social protection programmes, grassroots movements, advocacy and public action. You'll also gain several practical skills related to project design, project monitoring and evaluation and other themes related to development management especially in the NGO sector. Key development challenges from climate change, poverty, inequality, migration, conflict and human rights will be critically examined in vibrant class discussions, debates and presentations drawing on historical and current events and case studies. You are encouraged to critically examine these challenges in light of relevant theoretical and empirical literature as well as to think about practical solutions to address these challenges. You'll be also critically analysing the difficulties encountered during the implementation of these policies and collectively discuss ways to overcome these difficulties.","Code":"MOD009232","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"0831cea3-1be3-4c1b-928f-166d81bde741"}],"Id":"e2866f1c-c1f2-4174-bd72-f04121723126","SelectedModule":false}],"UcasCode":"","SITSCode":"AGTTINRL","AstraCode":"P0185","ModeOfStudy":{"KisCode":"FullTime","ModeOfStudyCode":"FT","ExcludeFromCourseSummary":false,"Name":"Full-time","Id":"3188d331-b419-4c02-bf25-30c84b6fff3d"},"CoreOption":false,"FoundationOption":false,"PlacementOption":false,"ProfessionalExperienceOption":false,"PartTimeOption":false,"Extra1":false,"Extra2":false,"Status":null,"StartDateDisclaimer":null,"DegreeApprenticeship":false,"Award":null,"Qualification":null,"LocationOverride":null,"EntryRequirementYears":[{"Name":"2026","Id":"b0de6795-6e13-4745-98d9-c1515ee46eae"}],"EntryRequirementsInformation":[{"HeadingTitle":"Standard entry requirements","RichTextContent":[{"RichTextTitle":"","RichTextContent":"

We offer a range of core and optional modules, with optional modules sometimes changing depending on staff availability.

You’ll demonstrate your progress through a combination of role-play scenarios, briefs, written reports, poster presentations, group projects, dissertation, longer essays, case studies, research proposal, short analyses of global events, short review papers, practical data gathering exercises, and short abstracts of core course readings.

","CoreModules":[{"Title":"Theoretical Foundations: Critiques, Debates and Contexts","Description":"You will examine the theory and key concepts of international relations and the development of the state, ground them in their historical context, and explore their policy implications. You will begin by examining where the boundaries of the discipline might lie, before looking at debates over the role of theory in explaining International Relations. You will receive detailed explanations of the key competing theories within the discipline, and their development and evolution. Key themes you will explore include the development of Classical Realism from its roots in doctrines of war, Liberalism and the dream of global order, through the tussles between Neorealism and neoliberalism throughout the decades of the Cold War. You will also look at Constructivism and the English School, radical Marxist and Neo-Marxist perspectives, through to Feminism, Post-Colonialism, Postmodernism and cosmopolitanism. You will learn to place the theory firmly in the context of 20th century events, exploring the way in which political and academic ideas are shaped by and in turn influence international affairs. You will also explore other directions in which the study of International Relations might travel in the future. Your assessment will comprise a report of 1,000 words, a presentation, a literature search equivalent to 1,000 words and a longer essay of 3,500 words.","Code":"MOD003643","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"78fa93a7-a13b-4a8d-b48f-44a2610bae4a"},{"Title":"Global Governance","Description":"In this module we'll critically analyse the origins, evolution and role of international institutions in the global order over the course of the 20th and 21st century. You'll gain an understanding of why these institutions have developed, and why states choose, or do not choose, to use these institutions as a means to achieve their objectives. We'll examine the still evolving structures of global governance, and the role of these organisations and institutions in contemporary politics and diplomacy. You'll consider the work of specific organisations, including the UN, the EU, the IMF and World Bank etc. We'll pay particular attention to the challenges inherent in attempting to foster international co-operation and consensus between sovereign nation states, including the limitations of international law, and examines potential future developments.","Code":"MOD003642","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"afe592d2-583d-48d4-af07-a14847f38e01"},{"Title":"Postgraduate Major Project","Description":"In this module you’ll explore a topic of your choice in greater depth (on the condition that we have the expertise to supervise it). This format of this project is also flexible; you may choose the standard dissertation format to present your work. You may also, under the guidance of your supervisor, opt to undertake a project that, for example, involves the production of an artefact, staging of an exhibition or publishing on-line content that has a public education or community enrichment brief. You may also consider, again under the guidance of your supervisor, designing a project that tests an hypothesis you ultimately write up as a report but which you test through the production of material for public consumption. You can undertake some of this work in collaboration with other members of the course, conditional on a clear agreement is reached about the division of labour across this team. This project gives you the opportunity to use material and research methods from the rest of the course. It is an opportunity for you to demonstrate that you have the detailed knowledge and understanding of your chosen research area, a critical appreciation of the appropriate methodologies and theories, and the ability to locate, to critically engage with and evaluate an appropriate range of sources. You will also be expected to recognise and manage appropriately any ethical issues that arise in the completion of this project. Finally, you should be able to present your findings so that tin they can be clearly understood across a range of audiences.","Code":"MOD000835","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"efbf015a-bc9d-41a5-bcfb-681a829bd76d"},{"Title":"Into ARU","Description":"Entering higher education is exciting; but it can also be a daunting experience. At ARU, we want all our students to make the most of the opportunities higher education provides, reach your potential, become lifelong learners and find fulfilling careers. However, we appreciate that the shift from secondary education, or a return to formal education is, in itself, quite a journey. This module is designed to ease that transition. You'll be enrolled on it as soon as you receive an offer from ARU so you can begin to learn about university life before your course starts. Through Into ARU, you'll explore a virtual land modelled around ARU values: Courage, Innovation, Community, Integrity, Responsibility, and Ambition. This innovative module is designed as a game, where you collect knowledge and complete mini tasks. You'll proceed at your own pace, though we you to have completed your Into ARU exploration by week 6. If for any reason you're unable to complete by that date, we'll signpost to existing services so that we can be confident that you are supported.","Code":"MOD999910","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"4f3c4a41-2e3f-49aa-8860-037c9fba5c37"}],"OptionalModules":[{"Title":"War, Peacekeeping and Military Intervention","Description":"In this module, you'll study the history and the contemporary status of peacekeeping, military humanitarian intervention, and the ‘responsibility to protect’. The role of international institutions in multilateral intervention will also be probed, as will the challenges involved in post-conflict security, and peacebuilding. The module will underline the significance of unilateral and multilateral military intervention in contemporary international relations and global politics, as well as its limitations. It will use a variety of real-world case studies of war, peacekeeping and military intervention and will use a range of teaching methods to engage you and develop your understanding of intervention from a pragmatic, empirical, strategic and policy-oriented perspective. The assessment for this module will contribute to the development of skills in writing, comparative analysis of data and new insights or perspectives on existing data and/or materials, helping to develop postgraduate research skills.","Code":"MOD003646","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"709e35da-dfe1-4810-bb2b-56a5536a2ef8"},{"Title":"Globalisation Organised Crime and Crime Control","Description":"The globalisation of contemporary societies has meant that criminal activity that was once primarily a national concern is increasingly becoming global in nature. In this module, you'll learn all about criminal activities that cross state boundaries, regardless of whether those are physical borders or the virtual boundaries of cyberspace. You'll also develop an understanding of the relevant policing bodies and how they are required to manage risk and security on a much wider scale. On Globalisation, Organised Crime, and Crime Control, you'll have the opportunity to explore the important social changes that have contributed to the emergence of ‘global’ cities and new patterns of crime and control. There are several questions you'll be able to consider in-depth over the course of the module. One issue is the notion of 'organised crime' itself. How organised is it? For example, how organised is illegal drug trafficking in Europe? What external threats to the 'licit' political economies are there? What is the relationship between the different research strategies and the formulation of international policies to tackle organised illicit trade? This module offers you the opportunity to explore the structure and nature of organised crime and examine other crimes of globalisation. You'll engage in discussions and debates on the concept of criminal networks, including criminal opportunity and routine activities, which will allow you to then analyse different case studies. In addition, you will measure and evaluate the scale of illicit trade to analyse the regulatory issues involved and potential preventative strategies. In this module, you'll be able to examine the local roots of transnational patterns of crime before widening the lens to evaluate a wide range of transnational crimes and how they have been policed. Together we'll explore organised illicit activities such as financial crime, environmental crime, human trafficking, and state crime, before examining newer and emergent transnational crimes such as cybercrime. Successful completion of this module will entail significant contributions on your part to the weekly seminars by researching and discussing different cases.","Code":"MOD009757","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"77c3e56f-0a6b-489f-81a7-e2e461110eb2"},{"Title":"Race, Racism and Resistance in Modern Britain since the Eighteenth Century","Description":"This module will present a history of race, racism and the resistances to racism in modern Britain. It will open with a consideration of early definitions of ‘race’ and the rise of ‘scientific racism’ in the late eighteenth century. It will then move to an examination of slavery in the British West Indies, the slave resistances and the British abolitionist movement. This history is less known than that of the US. This will be followed by one session on the role of the British Empire and its impact on Britain in terms of racialised ideology. The subsequent sessions will address race as constructed, contested and lived in Britain: the Black and Asian presence pre-World War I, interwar and Second World War, as well as the influence of ideas about race, sexuality, eugenics and anti-Semitism; the Windrush generation, Black politics and anti-racism of the 1920s to 1980s, including Black feminism, rock against racism, and anti-fascism. The history of the presence of mixed-race relationships in Britain will also be considered as well as ‘mixed-race’ as a 21st century identity. Finally ‘whiteness’ as a racial and privileged identity will be scrutinised.","Code":"MOD006395","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"db7d6f07-f541-4bd7-ae7e-051820efdd2f"},{"Title":"Beyond Borders Intercultural Communication Welfare and Policy","Description":"This module takes an interdisciplinary approach to introducing key topics and ways of working in the social sciences. You'll look at the development of relations, communicative styles and values between individuals and groups of different cultural backgrounds and delve into comparative issues concerning social policy and social welfare in the international and intercultural context. You'll do this by exploring areas such as gender equality, social housing, education and immigration and wider social concepts such as identity, intersectionality and inequality. You'll work with case studies to exemplify these concepts. In this way, you'll develop the foundation for a deeper understanding and appreciation of fundamental topics in the social sciences. You'll also receive guidance on study at Master’s level and the module will guide you towards the academic research and writing skills needed to work independently at this level.","Code":"MOD010759","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"bbb89968-3e72-43f6-86a5-634020d297e9"},{"Title":"Intercultural Consultancy Project","Description":"Working with an external collaborative partner, you will negotiate a 12 week consultancy project that demonstrates and builds upon theoretical and practical skills you have acquired on your course. The module will enable you to work contextually within the framework of work-based learning by facilitating knowledge exchange between the student and their external partner. The project will respond to the opportunities and needs of the external partner as applied to the field of intercultural communications. You will critically engage with how this professional sector operates in context of the wider business environments and how this can be applied to your career development. This module supports you in the development of key skills required in contemporary intercultural work environments, such as face-to-face and asynchronous communications, collaborative and cooperative decision making or intra-team conflict resolution.","Code":"MOD008998","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"828f471c-8924-483e-b522-4be3447c71d2"},{"Title":"Communication and Conflict","Description":"On this module you'll explore historical and thematic approaches to reporting on conflict and also how communication functions in a crisis. You'll be also critically analysing the difficulties encountered during the implementation of these policies and collectively discuss ways to overcome these difficulties.","Code":"MOD009232","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"0831cea3-1be3-4c1b-928f-166d81bde741"}],"Id":"17db3d29-479c-4b79-92ab-b1a6b5c4dd9e","SelectedModule":false}],"UcasCode":"","SITSCode":"AGTTINRL","AstraCode":"P0185","ModeOfStudy":{"KisCode":"PartTime","ModeOfStudyCode":"PT","ExcludeFromCourseSummary":false,"Name":"Part-time","Id":"77ee6eb5-cef9-4099-87c0-3c2819c645cd"},"CoreOption":false,"FoundationOption":false,"PlacementOption":false,"ProfessionalExperienceOption":false,"PartTimeOption":false,"Extra1":false,"Extra2":false,"Status":null,"StartDateDisclaimer":null,"DegreeApprenticeship":false,"Award":null,"Qualification":null,"LocationOverride":null,"EntryRequirementYears":[{"Name":"2026","Id":"b0de6795-6e13-4745-98d9-c1515ee46eae"}],"EntryRequirementsInformation":[{"HeadingTitle":"Standard entry requirements","RichTextContent":[{"RichTextTitle":"","RichTextContent":"

We offer a range of core and optional modules, with optional modules sometimes changing depending on staff availability.

You’ll demonstrate your progress through a combination of role-play scenarios, briefs, written reports, poster presentations, group projects, dissertation, longer essays, case studies, research proposal, short analyses of global events, short review papers, practical data gathering exercises, and short abstracts of core course readings.

Modules are subject to change and availability.

","CoreModules":[{"Title":"Theoretical Foundations: Critiques, Debates and Contexts","Description":"You will examine the theory and key concepts of international relations and the development of the state, ground them in their historical context, and explore their policy implications. You will begin by examining where the boundaries of the discipline might lie, before looking at debates over the role of theory in explaining International Relations. You will receive detailed explanations of the key competing theories within the discipline, and their development and evolution. Key themes you will explore include the development of Classical Realism from its roots in doctrines of war, Liberalism and the dream of global order, through the tussles between Neorealism and neoliberalism throughout the decades of the Cold War. You will also look at Constructivism and the English School, radical Marxist and Neo-Marxist perspectives, through to Feminism, Post-Colonialism, Postmodernism and cosmopolitanism. You will learn to place the theory firmly in the context of 20th century events, exploring the way in which political and academic ideas are shaped by and in turn influence international affairs. You will also explore other directions in which the study of International Relations might travel in the future. Your assessment will comprise a report of 1,000 words, a presentation, a literature search equivalent to 1,000 words and a longer essay of 3,500 words.","Code":"MOD003643","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"78fa93a7-a13b-4a8d-b48f-44a2610bae4a"},{"Title":"Global Governance","Description":"In this module we'll critically analyse the origins, evolution and role of international institutions in the global order over the course of the 20th and 21st century. You'll gain an understanding of why these institutions have developed, and why states choose, or do not choose, to use these institutions as a means to achieve their objectives. We'll examine the still evolving structures of global governance, and the role of these organisations and institutions in contemporary politics and diplomacy. You'll consider the work of specific organisations, including the UN, the EU, the IMF and World Bank etc. We'll pay particular attention to the challenges inherent in attempting to foster international co-operation and consensus between sovereign nation states, including the limitations of international law, and examines potential future developments.","Code":"MOD003642","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"afe592d2-583d-48d4-af07-a14847f38e01"},{"Title":"Postgraduate Major Project","Description":"In this module you’ll explore a topic of your choice in greater depth (on the condition that we have the expertise to supervise it). This format of this project is also flexible; you may choose the standard dissertation format to present your work. You may also, under the guidance of your supervisor, opt to undertake a project that, for example, involves the production of an artefact, staging of an exhibition or publishing on-line content that has a public education or community enrichment brief. You may also consider, again under the guidance of your supervisor, designing a project that tests an hypothesis you ultimately write up as a report but which you test through the production of material for public consumption. You can undertake some of this work in collaboration with other members of the course, conditional on a clear agreement is reached about the division of labour across this team. This project gives you the opportunity to use material and research methods from the rest of the course. It is an opportunity for you to demonstrate that you have the detailed knowledge and understanding of your chosen research area, a critical appreciation of the appropriate methodologies and theories, and the ability to locate, to critically engage with and evaluate an appropriate range of sources. You will also be expected to recognise and manage appropriately any ethical issues that arise in the completion of this project. Finally, you should be able to present your findings so that tin they can be clearly understood across a range of audiences.","Code":"MOD000835","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"efbf015a-bc9d-41a5-bcfb-681a829bd76d"},{"Title":"Into ARU","Description":"Entering higher education is exciting; but it can also be a daunting experience. At ARU, we want all our students to make the most of the opportunities higher education provides, reach your potential, become lifelong learners and find fulfilling careers. However, we appreciate that the shift from secondary education, or a return to formal education is, in itself, quite a journey. This module is designed to ease that transition. You'll be enrolled on it as soon as you receive an offer from ARU so you can begin to learn about university life before your course starts. Through Into ARU, you'll explore a virtual land modelled around ARU values: Courage, Innovation, Community, Integrity, Responsibility, and Ambition. This innovative module is designed as a game, where you collect knowledge and complete mini tasks. You'll proceed at your own pace, though we you to have completed your Into ARU exploration by week 6. If for any reason you're unable to complete by that date, we'll signpost to existing services so that we can be confident that you are supported.","Code":"MOD999910","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"4f3c4a41-2e3f-49aa-8860-037c9fba5c37"}],"OptionalModules":[{"Title":"War, Peacekeeping and Military Intervention","Description":"In this module, you'll study the history and the contemporary status of peacekeeping, military humanitarian intervention, and the ‘responsibility to protect’. The role of international institutions in multilateral intervention will also be probed, as will the challenges involved in post-conflict security, and peacebuilding. The module will underline the significance of unilateral and multilateral military intervention in contemporary international relations and global politics, as well as its limitations. It will use a variety of real-world case studies of war, peacekeeping and military intervention and will use a range of teaching methods to engage you and develop your understanding of intervention from a pragmatic, empirical, strategic and policy-oriented perspective. The assessment for this module will contribute to the development of skills in writing, comparative analysis of data and new insights or perspectives on existing data and/or materials, helping to develop postgraduate research skills.","Code":"MOD003646","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"709e35da-dfe1-4810-bb2b-56a5536a2ef8"},{"Title":"Globalisation Organised Crime and Crime Control","Description":"The globalisation of contemporary societies has meant that criminal activity that was once primarily a national concern is increasingly becoming global in nature. In this module, you'll learn all about criminal activities that cross state boundaries, regardless of whether those are physical borders or the virtual boundaries of cyberspace. You'll also develop an understanding of the relevant policing bodies and how they are required to manage risk and security on a much wider scale. On Globalisation, Organised Crime, and Crime Control, you'll have the opportunity to explore the important social changes that have contributed to the emergence of ‘global’ cities and new patterns of crime and control. There are several questions you'll be able to consider in-depth over the course of the module. One issue is the notion of 'organised crime' itself. How organised is it? For example, how organised is illegal drug trafficking in Europe? What external threats to the 'licit' political economies are there? What is the relationship between the different research strategies and the formulation of international policies to tackle organised illicit trade? This module offers you the opportunity to explore the structure and nature of organised crime and examine other crimes of globalisation. You'll engage in discussions and debates on the concept of criminal networks, including criminal opportunity and routine activities, which will allow you to then analyse different case studies. In addition, you will measure and evaluate the scale of illicit trade to analyse the regulatory issues involved and potential preventative strategies. In this module, you'll be able to examine the local roots of transnational patterns of crime before widening the lens to evaluate a wide range of transnational crimes and how they have been policed. Together we'll explore organised illicit activities such as financial crime, environmental crime, human trafficking, and state crime, before examining newer and emergent transnational crimes such as cybercrime. Successful completion of this module will entail significant contributions on your part to the weekly seminars by researching and discussing different cases.","Code":"MOD009757","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"77c3e56f-0a6b-489f-81a7-e2e461110eb2"},{"Title":"Race, Racism and Resistance in Modern Britain since the Eighteenth Century","Description":"This module will present a history of race, racism and the resistances to racism in modern Britain. It will open with a consideration of early definitions of ‘race’ and the rise of ‘scientific racism’ in the late eighteenth century. It will then move to an examination of slavery in the British West Indies, the slave resistances and the British abolitionist movement. This history is less known than that of the US. This will be followed by one session on the role of the British Empire and its impact on Britain in terms of racialised ideology. The subsequent sessions will address race as constructed, contested and lived in Britain: the Black and Asian presence pre-World War I, interwar and Second World War, as well as the influence of ideas about race, sexuality, eugenics and anti-Semitism; the Windrush generation, Black politics and anti-racism of the 1920s to 1980s, including Black feminism, rock against racism, and anti-fascism. The history of the presence of mixed-race relationships in Britain will also be considered as well as ‘mixed-race’ as a 21st century identity. Finally ‘whiteness’ as a racial and privileged identity will be scrutinised.","Code":"MOD006395","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"db7d6f07-f541-4bd7-ae7e-051820efdd2f"},{"Title":"Beyond Borders Intercultural Communication Welfare and Policy","Description":"This module takes an interdisciplinary approach to introducing key topics and ways of working in the social sciences. You'll look at the development of relations, communicative styles and values between individuals and groups of different cultural backgrounds and delve into comparative issues concerning social policy and social welfare in the international and intercultural context. You'll do this by exploring areas such as gender equality, social housing, education and immigration and wider social concepts such as identity, intersectionality and inequality. You'll work with case studies to exemplify these concepts. In this way, you'll develop the foundation for a deeper understanding and appreciation of fundamental topics in the social sciences. You'll also receive guidance on study at Master’s level and the module will guide you towards the academic research and writing skills needed to work independently at this level.","Code":"MOD010759","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"bbb89968-3e72-43f6-86a5-634020d297e9"},{"Title":"Intercultural Consultancy Project","Description":"Working with an external collaborative partner, you will negotiate a 12 week consultancy project that demonstrates and builds upon theoretical and practical skills you have acquired on your course. The module will enable you to work contextually within the framework of work-based learning by facilitating knowledge exchange between the student and their external partner. The project will respond to the opportunities and needs of the external partner as applied to the field of intercultural communications. You will critically engage with how this professional sector operates in context of the wider business environments and how this can be applied to your career development. This module supports you in the development of key skills required in contemporary intercultural work environments, such as face-to-face and asynchronous communications, collaborative and cooperative decision making or intra-team conflict resolution.","Code":"MOD008998","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"828f471c-8924-483e-b522-4be3447c71d2"},{"Title":"Communication and Conflict","Description":"On this module you'll explore historical and thematic approaches to reporting on conflict and also how communication functions in a crisis. You'll examine the reciprocal relationships between the military, governments and the media, including how the media can be used to legitimise conflict, and the changing role of social media in building consensus and protest, including the use of Twitter and Facebook to organise demonstrations and undermine the power of state-dominated discourses. You’ll also consider more traditional forms of communication, including censorship and propaganda, and whether the state is ever able to retain control of the narrative, as well as the role of the war reporter, and the way in which governments can utilise the independent media and how independent it really is. Other areas of exploration include consent, public interest, ethics and the representation of suffering, looking at whether the dominance of media in the debate in the West means that public interest in conflict is limited by the limitations of the media, and what this means for winning hearts and minds during insurgencies, military interventions and peacekeeping operations. Finally, you'll look at the way war and conflict is portrayed in fictional accounts and the underlying assumptions of such portrayals, and will examine conflicting discourses about war in post-conflict environments and the way the media can contribute to or hamper the process of post-conflict reconstruction. Themes throughout the module will include the question of who owns, defines and propagates the truth, and the implications of this in the context of conflict and war.","Code":"MOD003644","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"a956aeb6-6c48-423b-b081-fb889035e622"},{"Title":"Terrorism: Crime, Justice and Historical Continuities","Description":"Terrorism is often presented as a uniquely modern threat shaped by globalisation, digital radicalisation and the so-called war on terror. This module challenges that assumption by situating contemporary terrorism within broader historical continuities of political violence, state response and criminal justice intervention. You'll examine terrorism through a criminological lens, gaining insight into how acts of political violence are defined, constructed and governed as crime. By interrogating contested concepts such as radicalisation and extremism, you will sharpen your analytical skills and learn to question taken-for-granted assumptions. You'll assess how media narratives, public fear and political rhetoric influence public understandings of threat and legitimacy, equipping you to engage more confidently in academic, professional and public debates. Through diverse case studies, you'll explore connections between terrorism and organised crime, the growth of emergency powers, suspect communities, punishment and prison management. You'll evaluate whether criminal justice responses reduce violence or risk prolonging conflict. By the end of the module, you'll have enhanced your research, evaluation and critical reasoning skills while gaining a nuanced understanding of prevention, legitimacy and how justice can be reimagined in response to political violence.","Code":"MOD000829","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"27d13061-b77c-4866-a0e8-2beb247f3cec"},{"Title":"Going Global: Making the Modern World, 1979-1999","Description":"This module examines the main themes in contemporary world history, focusing specifically on the 1980s and 1990s as the foundations of the modern, globalising, world were being laid down. You'll critically assess the breakdown of the state-led economic model adopted after the Second World War and consider the development of the more globalised system which replaced it. You'll examine what globalisation meant in reality as changes in technology drove the new consumerism but also contributed to deindustrialisation. In addition, you'll consider how the changes in capitalism influenced the political left as socialist and communist parties across the world turned to market-based ideas and policies. The module also focuses on the ‘third wave of democracy’ which saw apparently stable regimes such as Pinochet’s Chile and Botha’s South Africa fall, and it considers how these factors fed into and influenced the late Cold War years. You'll uncover the ways in which the 1980s was a transformative but incomplete decade as the new ideas introduced by New Right politicians were not completely established until the 1990s with the development of the ‘Third Way’ politics and the victory of neoliberalism at home and abroad. This module is taught through weekly sessions and the emphasis will be on building individual understanding of the key themes of the period as well as encouraging teamwork and oral skills through group discussion and group work. You will develop analytical skills through the investigation of documentary material (identified in the ‘accessible archives’ seminar) from the Thatcher, Kinnock, Reagan or Clinton papers (for example) and you will be expected to bring a relevant document to each class to discuss each week.","Code":"MOD006397","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"1839fd5b-1815-4e4d-b975-e5eae0b1035e"},{"Title":"Postgraduate Research Methods","Description":"In this module you'll gain the research skills and techniques needed both to critically evaluate the literature you'll be using in your course and to put into practice in your own dissertation. We'll explore the methodologies and methods applied in contemporary social science research to enable you to select an appropriate range for your own needs. You'll have the opportunity to experiment with a variety of methods so that you'll fully understood them and be able to adapt them creatively for your own projects. The module will place research methods in a wider framework of social research strategies at a postgraduate level. We'll examine the research design options available to you at Masters level and explore thoroughly the issues involved in planning a research project and formulating research questions. With the aid of library expertise, you'll have access to and understand current tools for reviewing and researching existing literature. Particular attention will be paid to ethical principles and the politics of social research. A central part of the module will address the practicalities of employing both qualitative and quantitative methodologies. Computer-assisted analysis methods will be introduced.","Code":"MOD000825","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"5b02c3ba-c947-4e80-93fc-9a64099bcba0"},{"Title":"Global Development: Policy and Practice","Description":"This module aims to critically examine the key policies, politics and practices in the field of international development. It explores the key policies undertaken by various actors in the development field, including international organisations, national governments, the private sector, non-governmental organisations, and grassroots movements. You'll learn about the politics of ‘doing’ development and the challenges encountered at each level of policy: global, national, and local levels. You'll also critically examine the key debates in the literature on ‘best practise’ and ‘what works’ drawing on a variety of case studies and examples. You'll cover a range of related topics such as social protection programmes, grassroots movements, advocacy and public action. You'll also gain several practical skills related to project design, project monitoring and evaluation and other themes related to development management especially in the NGO sector. Key development challenges from climate change, poverty, inequality, migration, conflict and human rights will be critically examined in vibrant class discussions, debates and presentations drawing on historical and current events and case studies. You are encouraged to critically examine these challenges in light of relevant theoretical and empirical literature as well as to think about practical solutions to address these challenges. You'll be also critically analysing the difficulties encountered during the implementation of these policies and collectively discuss ways to overcome these difficulties.","Code":"MOD009232","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"0831cea3-1be3-4c1b-928f-166d81bde741"}],"Id":"acd17e3c-abeb-4f58-a23d-6485f5ed5a73","SelectedModule":false}],"UcasCode":"","SITSCode":"AGTTINRL","AstraCode":"P0185","ModeOfStudy":{"KisCode":"PartTime","ModeOfStudyCode":"PT","ExcludeFromCourseSummary":false,"Name":"Part-time","Id":"77ee6eb5-cef9-4099-87c0-3c2819c645cd"},"CoreOption":false,"FoundationOption":false,"PlacementOption":false,"ProfessionalExperienceOption":false,"PartTimeOption":false,"Extra1":false,"Extra2":false,"Status":null,"StartDateDisclaimer":null,"DegreeApprenticeship":false,"Award":null,"Qualification":null,"LocationOverride":null,"EntryRequirementYears":[{"Name":"2026","Id":"b0de6795-6e13-4745-98d9-c1515ee46eae"}],"EntryRequirementsInformation":[{"HeadingTitle":"Standard entry requirements","RichTextContent":[{"RichTextTitle":"","RichTextContent":"
