Postgraduate Psychology MPhil, PhD Research ( full-time, part-time) Cambridge January 2027, April, September 2027 Apply online For application deadlines visit our how to apply page . Overview Students undertaking a PhD in Psychology at Anglia Ruskin become part of a newly established and rapidly expanding centre of research excellence. We have world-leading staff members in each of the core areas of Psychology, with particular strengths in cognitive neuroscience, cognition and emotion, social psychology and health psychology. Full description PhD students in the School of Psychology and Sports Science have a range of state-of-the-art research laboratories and equipment at their disposal. MSc-level training in quantitative and qualitative methods is available to upgrade students’ existing research skills and additional specialist training in software and equipment will allow students to develop new research abilities. Training is also available in research writing and presentation skills and all our students are expected to publish their results in high-impact peer-reviewed journals and are supported to present their work at leading international conferences in their subject areas. Each PhD student is supervised by a team of experts in their subject area who guide them through the design and implementation of their research project, while supporting students’ academic career development. We work within two main research centres in Psychology with each covering a number of research areas: ARU Centre for Mind and Behaviour : Cognition Development and Lifespan Body and Self Clinical and Wellbeing ARU Centre for Societies and Groups : Applied Social Change Empowerment and Social Justice Successful applicants to our doctoral programme will join a thriving community of PhD students with dedicated research study areas. Our Psychology PhD community is actively engaged in the research culture of our School, attending regular meetings within their research clusters as well as the School's fortnightly research seminar series which hosts talks by leading psychology researchers from across the UK and beyond. Students also organise their own activities, including social as well as research events and together they host an annual Psychology PhD student conference at which students present their work to an audience of staff and students from across the University. In addition to our Psychology PhD, we've also identified a range of innovative research project opportunities for you as a postgraduate researcher. Completion times MPhil: full-time 1-3 years, part-time 2-4 years. PhD via progression from MPhil, including that period: full-time 2.5-5 years, part-time 3.5-6 years. PhD: full-time 2-4 years, part-time 3-6 years. For further guidance on the duration of research degrees please refer to the Research Degrees Regulations . Psychology PhD project opportunities Read about our current research in 'First' Our faculty's quarterly newsletter World-leading research at ARU Application tips Supervision and support Our supervisors will meet you regularly to discuss your progress formally and are available any time for support or advice. There are also extensive study resources online. If your work is interdisciplinary we can involve relevant specialists from other schools and disciplines. Our supervisory staff are recognised experts in their field. Their research expertise includes: Dr Jane Aspell - Jane is a cognitive neuroscientist and her research focuses on the multisensory bodily basis for self-consciousness. Prof Peter Bright - Peter Bright is a Professor of Psychology and his research interests are in memory, cognitive control and intelligence. Dr Matt Bristow - Matt’s research concentrates on psycho-neuro-immunology and the psychophysiology of stress. Dr Flavia Cardini - Flavia’s research is focused on the study of the brain representation of one’s own body as a result of the interaction between information from different sensory modalities. Dr James Close - James is a cognitive and comparative psychologist interested in the development and evolution of cognition and prosociality. His research is focused on understanding the factors which drive the categorisation and prosocial behaviours of animals and humans. Dr Suzanna Forwood - Suzanna is a cognitive psychologist interested in food choice, the factors that determine food choice and the tools available to improve the healthiness of food choices. Dr Sharon Geva - Sharon is a cognitive neuroscientist, with an interest in language and memory across the lifespan. She is studying cognitive processing and impairments following brain damage, using neuropsychological testing and brain imaging techniques. Dr Nic Gibson - Nic is interested in Applied Psychology, particularly well-being, resilience, and pro-sociality as personal strengths that influence positive outcomes. Research areas include play and playfulness in adults, human-animal companionship, gaming, and individual differences. Dr Julia Gillard - Julia is a Senior Lecturer in Clinical Psychology and Clinical Psychologist working in a specialist mental health service for adults with a diagnosis of Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Her research interests include clinical psychology, cross-cultural psychology, and individual differences in risk and resilience in mental health. Dr Lewis Goodings - Lewis is a qualitative social psychologist who is interested in the way that self and identity are mediated via social media technologies. He also considers the use of these technologies in relation to mental distress and the possible advantages or disadvantages therein. Dr Mick Finlay - Mick is a social psychologist conducting research in two main areas: intellectual disabilities and political conflict between groups. Dr Ruth Ford - Ruth studies the cognitive and social development of young children, focusing on memory, cognitive control, and social cognition. Her research encompasses both theoretical and applied projects. Dr Annelie Harvey - Annelie is a social psychologist interested in the psychology of justice. Her research considers how people react to victims and instances of misfortune. Dr Cathrine Jansson-Boyd - Cathrine is a consumer psychologist with a particular interest in tactile perception and environmentally friendly consumption. Additionally, she is interested in how consumers aesthetically evaluate products and consumer environments. Dr Emma Kaminskiy - Emma undertakes health services research with a particular interest in involvement and collaboration with service users and carers in mental health research and service improvement. Dr Helen Keyes - Helen researches how experienced and novice drivers’ brains process the road environment, as well as how the brain processes our own face and other familiar faces. Dr Elizabeth Kirk - Elizabeth is a developmental psychologist and her research focuses on the role of gesture in language and thought. Dr Eimear Lee - Eimear is a lecturer in psychology, and her research interests include biological psychology, health psychology, personality and individual differences, and psychosocial influences on health. Dr Sharon Morein-Zamir - Sharon’s research investigates the control of actions and thoughts, as it relates to disorders of compulsivity and impulsivity. Dr Craig Owen - Craig is a Senior Lecturer in Psychology. His areas of interest include critical social psychology, critical health psychology, sociology of sport, gender studies and qualitative research methods. Dr Michael Pake - Michael is a Senior Lecturer in Psychology and also acts as our undergraduate Admissions Tutor. Dr David Pearson - David is a cognitive psychologist whose research examines the cognitive processes involved during memory, mental imagery and visuo-spatial thinking, with a particular focus on applications in the fields of clinical and environmental psychology. Dr Debora Sa - Debora is a chartered psychologist and senior lecturer in psychology. Her research focuses on family carers'; mental health and well-being. Dr Tamer Said - Tamer is a cognitive psychologist who is interested in studying the relations between cognitive and non-cognitive factors within educational settings, with a special interest in conceptual change research and science learning. Dr Elena Sakkalou - Elena specialises in typical infant and child development and neurodevelopmental disorders, focusing on cognitive and social-communicative development and how it is affected by neurodisability. Dr Jane Scott - Jane is a Senior Lecturer in Clinical Psychology. She is a registered clinical psychologist with extensive international experience in clinical and academic settings. Her main research interests are hoarding disorder, eating disorders, body image, mental health and vision loss, and self-reflective practice. Dr Lesley Storey - Lesley is a social psychologist with an interest in health issues and social justice. Her research looks at the psychosocial impact of cancer, particularly sarcoma. Her current focus is on fear of recurrence. Her political psychology research looks at issues of inter-group conflict and social group memberships. Prof Viren Swami - Viren is a social psychologist whose research focuses on the psychology of human appearance and body image and, separately, the psychology of conspiracy theories. Dr Magdalena Zawisza - Magdalena is a Reader in Consumer and Gender Psychology; her research interests fall into three general areas: consumer, gender and applied social psychology. Students on the PhD in Psychology programme can benefit from attending (subject to availability of space in the class) some of the School’s MSc lectures which relate to their research. These could include lectures within the MSc modules listed below. Attendance is not compulsory: Developmental Psychopathology Imaging and Diagnostics in Cognitive Neuroscience Current Theoretical Issues in Cognitive Neuroscience Issues in Scientific Research Quantitative Research methods Diagnosis and Treatment in Child Psychology Where you'll research Your faculty The Faculty of Science & Engineering is one of the largest of the four faculties at ARU. Whether you choose to study with us full-time or part-time, on campus or at a distance, there’s an option whatever your level – from a foundation degree, BSc, MSc, PhD or professional doctorate. Whichever course you pick, you’ll gain the theory and practical skills needed to progress with confidence. Join us and you could find yourself learning in the very latest laboratories or on field trips or work placements with well-known and respected companies. You may even have the opportunity to study abroad. Everything we do in the faculty has a singular purpose: to provide a world-class environment to create, share and advance knowledge in science, technology and engineering fields. This is key to all of our futures. Visit your faculty Where can I study? Cambridge Our campus is close to the centre of Cambridge, often described as the perfect student city. Explore our Cambridge campus Fees & funding Course fees UK students, 2026/27 (per year) £5,238 UK students, 2026/27 (part-time, per year) £2,619 International students, 2026/27 (per year) £17,500 International students, 2026/27 (part-time, per year) £8,750 Bench fees In some cases extra costs known as bench fees will be charged for a postgraduate research degree. These are to cover additional/exceptional costs directly related to a specific research project. Some examples of these costs are (the list is not exhaustive): equipment hire, access costs to specialist equipment/workshops, volunteer expenses, specialist tissue/cell culture, specialist reagents or materials, specialist software, access to specialist databases, data collection costs, specialist media, recording or digital storage needs. We charge bench fees in bands. They may apply for every year of your course. These bands are the same for full- and part-time students. If you have to pay bench fees this will be made clear at your interview, and stated in your offer letter. For 2026/27 the bench fee bands are: £500 £1,400 £2,400 £4,900 £9,800 PhD by Published Work Initial registration: £1,700 Full registration: £4,900 Writing up fees 2026/27 £1,400 How do I pay my fees? You can pay your fees upfront, in full or in instalments – though you won't need to pay until you've accepted an offer to study with us. Find out more about paying your fees . Funding For advice on the Doctoral Loan and other sources of funding, including ARU scholarships, visit our finance guide for postgraduate researchers . You might also find The Alternative Guide to Postgraduate Funding helpful. ARU research ARU's academic excellence was recognised in 2021, as part of the Research Excellence Framework (REF), an exercise which assesses the quality of academic research. Sixteen areas of our work were classed as generating world-leading research . The results showed that we're making a significant impact on the societies we live in. Careers We’ll provide comprehensive research training in areas such as academic writing and publishing, research methods, subject developments, data analysis, conference skills and presentation. You can also access the Epigeum Suite of online skills training modules. Contact details If you're interested in finding out more about research study opportunities, please email [email protected] Entry requirements MPhil or PhD with progression from MPhil: You’ll need a Bachelor degree or equivalent with first or upper second class honours, in a related subject area. PhD: You’ll need a Master degree or equivalent in a related subject area. Please note we consider candidates for PhD with progression from MPhil in the first instance. If you want to be considered for direct entry to the PhD route then this can be discussed at interview if you are shortlisted. Please note you’ll also need to provide academic justification for this request. If English is not your first language, you'll require a minimum IELTS score of 6.5, with a minimum of 5.5 in each component (or equivalent test). If you don't meet our English language requirements, we offer a range of courses which could help you achieve the level required for entry. Important additional notes Our published entry requirements are a guide only and our decision will be based on your overall suitability for the programme as well as whether you meet the minimum entry requirements. Contact our postgraduate research degree team for more information about studying a PhD, MPhil or Professional Doctorate at ARU. You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your research programme. Before starting, we recommend that you check our technical requirements for online learning . Course durations are 1 year full-time or 2 years part-time (September starts), or 16 months full-time or 29 months part-time (January starts). Course content and modules remain the same. Source: Graduate Outcomes Survey 2026 Develop a scientific understanding of the core areas of psychology, and the relations between them. You’ll learn how psychology is influenced by factors such as physiology and external influences; how different languages change the way you look at the world; and the importance of childhood development. You’ll also learn how to design research projects, before conducting your own. No psychology degree? No problem. We welcome all students to this conversion course, whether you've studied psychology before or you're new to the field. Study with us in Cambridge or by distance learning . British Psychological Society Our course is accredited by the British Psychological Society (BPS). It provides you with Graduate Basis for Chartered Membership of the BPS, which is essential for pursuing careers in a range of recognised psychology professions. Written by and starring British Psychological Society members, this short film shows what brings psychologists together in one profession and one BPS. Close full-screen gallery. Written by and starring British Psychological Society members, this short film shows what brings psychologists together in one profession and one BPS. Why ARU? Study in Cambridge or by distance learning ‐ achieving the same professionally recognised qualification Build the scientific understanding and practical skills to apply psychology to a range of careers Explore the biological, social and environmental factors that shape people’s lives Learn from academics whose teaching is informed by the latest discoveries in psychological science Develop practical research skills by designing and conducting your own psychology project Gain Graduate Basis for Chartered Membership of the British Psychological Society Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers I found this course a great balance of lectures, seminars and one-to-one tutor support, complemented by online learning materials, recordings and activities. Daniel Grimmer, MSc Psychology (Conversion) graduate Develop analytical, research and communication skills that employers value. Accredited by the British Psychological Society, this MSc gives you Graduate Basis for Chartered Membership, the essential first step towards many professional psychology careers. You'll also graduate with practical research experience, ready to apply your understanding of human behaviour in a range of roles. What can you do with an MSc Psychology (Conversion)? Your MSc Psychology can open doors to careers across health and social care, marketing and PR, management and human resources, education and the public sector. If you want to become a psychologist, this conversion course also provides the foundation for further training in areas such as clinical psychology. Graduation doesn’t have to be the end of your time with us. You could continue your academic career with an MPhil/PhD Psychology . Take advantage of our Alumni Scholarship and save £400 on your fees. How can ARU help with my employability and career development? We want you to be a step ahead when you graduate, so we offer: courses designed with employers tutors with professional industry knowledge hands-on learning which may include industry-led projects, placements or Professional Experience modules . Alongside your course, there are lots of other opportunities to build your skills and experience: add value to your CV with an ARU Certificate of Professional Development get involved in a thriving volunteering programme develop your brilliant business ideas work with businesses to make a social impact . We’re here to help you develop your CV and find that all-important role after graduation. Our Employability Service offers tailored career appointments, advice on writing your CV, help to complete job applications, and much more. You’ll have 24/7 access to an online Careers Centre too, which is packed with useful resources. The support continues after you graduate, with lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . Find out more about careers support at ARU . Teaching and modules I love working with our MSc conversion students. They bring fresh perspectives and an inspiring drive to succeed. Dr Matt Bristow Develop a scientific understanding of the core areas of psychology and how biological, cognitive, developmental and social factors shape human behaviour. You'll explore topics including mental health, language and childhood development. Throughout the course, you'll learn to evaluate evidence, think critically and conduct research ethically. You'll also build practical skills in research design, data collection and analysis. You'll bring everything together in your Psychology Dissertation, where you'll design, carry out and present your own independent research project. What will I study? MSc Part-time option(s) MSc Modules are subject to change and availability, and may vary by location. If you have the choice of optional modules, these are indicated with a *. Year 1 Research in Action: Statistical Thinking (15 credits) Social Psychology, Development and Difference (30 credits) Contemporary Issues in Psychology (15 credits) Research in Action: Qualitative Methods and Psychology in Practice (15 credits) Brain, Body and Mind (30 credits) Diagnosis and Formulation in Mental Health (Level 7) (15 credits) Psychology Dissertation (60 credits) Into ARU Module details Part-time option(s) It's possible to study this course part-time. You'll take the same modules as MSc/MA students, but sometimes in a different order or in different years. As a part-time student you'll typically study for twice as long as full-time students. For example if the MSc/MA course takes one year, you can expect to study over two years, though for some courses this may vary. Year 1 Research in Action: Qualitative Methods and Psychology in Practice (15 credits) Diagnosis and Formulation in Mental Health (Level 7) (15 credits) Into ARU Research in Action: Statistical Thinking (15 credits) Contemporary Issues in Psychology (15 credits) Year 2 Brain, Body and Mind (30 credits) Social Psychology, Development and Difference (30 credits) Psychology Dissertation (60 credits) Module details What are the teaching times? For this course you'll receive a personalised timetable when you enrol, and will be expected to attend campus multiple days in the week. How is MSc Psychology (Conversion) assessed? We'll assess your progress in a number of ways. These include traditional coursework essays and exams, as well as portfolios, case study reports, multiple choice questionnaires, book reviews, and your dissertation. Who teaches MSc Psychology (Conversion) at ARU? Read profiles of teaching and research staff on this course. Dr Lewis Goodings Senior Lecturer in Psychology Dr Lesley Storey Senior Lecturer Dr Matt Bristow Principal Lecturer Professor Mick Finlay Professor of Social and Applied Psychology Dr Débora Vasconcelos e Sá Senior Lecturer in Clinical Psychology Facilities Study at ARU in Cambridge and use our dedicated Science Centre , home to specialist teaching spaces and research facilities. Here, you'll find psychology labs for EEG, perception, neuroscience, biomarker analysis and social behaviour research. These facilities support practical learning and independent research, helping you develop the scientific skills for careers in psychology and related fields. You'll also benefit from extensive library and IT resources. Take a guided tour and meet our students . Study psychology in our state-of-the-art Science Centre in Cambridge. Find out more about careers support at ARU . Teaching and modules Prepare to meet public health needs in the UK, through community health and wellbeing initiatives. You’ll explore key topics from epidemiological research and communities of health, to healthcare financing and service commissioning. With a focus and local and regional health concerns, you’ll learn about creating and evaluating community-based public health programmes. Finally, you’ll plan, design and conduct a major piece of research work with your Postgraduate Research Project. This can be either research- or work-based. What will I study? Year 1 Essential Issues in Public Health and Practice Community Public Health and Evaluation Strategic Leadership, Management, and Commissioning in Public Health Year 2 Statistics and Epidemiology Postgraduate Research Project - Public Health Module details How is MSc Public Health and Community Wellbeing assessed? We'll assess both your theoretical knowledge and practical skills. Assessments have been developed to include skills you'll need in your career such as policy briefs, persuasive arguments, intervention development and written evaluations, debates, and outbreak management plans. Who teaches MSc Public Health and Community Wellbeing at ARU? Read profiles of teaching and research staff on this course. Dr Russell Kabir Associate Professor & Course Leader Dr Ali Davod Parsa Associate Professor Dr Richard Hayhoe Senior Lecturer Facilities Enjoy a range of facilities designed to support your studies and career development. Students who do not meet this criterion will be advised to seek support from ALS English language programme prior to commencement of the course. Selection Process Candidates should normally have a good first degree or equivalent and be working, or hope to work, within any area of the public health arena. They do not necessarily need a professional qualification for access to the course but do need to demonstrate a strong interest in public health and local health improvement. Candidates with a third class honours, or ordinary (pass) degree plus a minimum of one year of relevant post-graduate work experience, will be considered on an individual basis. Candidates who do not have a first degree, but have relevant work experience, may be able to gain access to the course by completing a Non Graduate Entry Profile demonstrating, and reflecting on, achievement of generic undergraduate learning outcomes through experiential learning. Careers We expect our graduates to be able to seek roles in a variety of sectors such as health, government, voluntary organisations and the wider community. Graduation doesn’t have to be the end of your time with us. You could choose to continue your academic career with a PhD programme at ARU. Part-time, from 3 to 6 years. For further guidance on the duration of Research Degrees please refer to the Research Degrees Regulations . Apply online For application deadlines visit our how to apply page . Overview Make a substantial and original contribution to knowledge in the fields of education or social care with this PhD programme. Our School of Education will provide you with a thriving environment as an education researcher &ndasj; we're committed to developing research in education, identities and inequalities , contributing to knowledge and making a difference to people’s lives and societies. Before applying for a PhD in Education, we strongly recommend that all applicants contact and meet to discuss their application with a potential supervisor. This will ensure that an appropriate supervisor is available to support your studies. Find out more about our supervisors and their expertise. If you work in a professional setting, such as a school, college or other education environment, you might also be interested in our Professional Doctorate in Education . Full description Research group overview Our school’s research activities are consistently underpinned by a dual concern for inclusion and excellence, yet are also diverse in terms of epistemological, theoretical and empirical foci. Alongside our staff and other PhD students, you can engage with a range of topics relating to identities and inequalities in education, including gender, sexuality, ethnicity, class, Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND), education for sustainability (including democracy, rights and participation), digital technology in education, arts in schools, and teachers' careers and identities. We also support research in curriculum, pedagogy and educational leadership. Completion times MPhil: full-time 1-3 years, part-time 2-4 years. PhD via progression from MPhil, including that period: full-time 2.5-5 years, part-time 3.5-6 years. PhD: full-time 2-4 years, part-time 3-6 years. Social care research: Marginalised communities (adult and young people), models of care, and community engagement. We invite applications towards a PhD or MPhil programmes on topics related to these broad themes. Established, world-leading academics offer sustained and high-quality supervision. Postgraduate MA Social Work Combine in-depth professional training with practice placements - and register as a social worker when you graduate. Our course pages need JavaScript enabled to work correctly. Previous Section Course Overview Next Section Jump to a section Course overview Careers Teaching and modules Facilities Entry requirements Fees and funding Apply Apply now Come to an Open Event Start date September 2027 Location Blended learning Chelmsford UCAS course code L506 Duration 2 years full-time 1st in the region for postgraduates progressing into senior roles. Source: Graduate Outcomes Survey 2026 Make a difference to people’s lives. If you have at least six months’ relevant work experience, this postgraduate degree will prepare you to become a registered social worker. It’s a practical course featuring 170 days on placement. Your placements will cover statutory work, children’s services and adult services. You’ll start by exploring theories and approaches to social work, and developing your practical skills ready for placement. You may be eligible for an NHS Social Work Bursary while studying. Social Work England Our MA Social Work degree course is validated by Social Work England, so when you graduate, you’ll be eligible to apply to register as a social worker. Why ARU? Qualify as a professional social worker Get hands-on experience, with placements in both years of your course Learn more about working with both adults and children Work directly with service users Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers Explore different areas of social work, build your skills on placement, and graduate ready to work as a social worker. Social workers are in demand in the statutory, private, voluntary and independent sectors. You could build a career in areas including: children’s or adult services mental health services youth offending residential social care advocacy and support for vulnerable groups. Whichever area interests you, this course will prepare you for your Assessed and Supported Year in Employment (ASYE). What can I do with a Social Work degree? Although this course is focussed on social work, you’ll also gain a number of transferable skills. Graduation doesn’t have to be the end of your time with us. You could choose to continue your academic career with a research programme at ARU, such as the Professional Doctorate in Health and Social Care . Take advantage of our Alumni Scholarship and save £400 on your fees. How can ARU help with my employability and career development? We want you to be a step ahead when you graduate, so we offer: courses designed with employers tutors with professional industry knowledge hands-on learning which may include industry-led projects, placements or Professional Experience modules . Alongside your course, there are lots of other opportunities to build your skills and experience: add value to your CV with an ARU Certificate of Professional Development get involved in a thriving volunteering programme develop your brilliant business ideas work with businesses to make a social impact . We’re here to help you develop your CV and find that all-important role after graduation. Our Employability Service offers tailored career appointments, advice on writing your CV, help to complete job applications, and much more. You’ll have 24/7 access to an online Careers Centre too, which is packed with useful resources. The support continues after you graduate, with lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . Find out more about careers support at ARU . Teaching and modules Learn about professional social work practice, safeguarding and interventions – and practice your skills before you go on placement. You’ll be assessed as ‘ready for direct practice’ before beginning your placements. In Year 1 you’ll spend 70 days on placement, followed by 100 days in Year 2. You’ll also continue with university-based study. Your dissertation, completed in Year 2, is an opportunity to explore a topic of particular interest to you. We encourage you to take account of service users’ expertise and appreciate the importance of research in social work practice. What will I study? Modules are subject to change and availability, and may vary by location. If you have the choice of optional modules, these are indicated with a *. Year 1 Standards and Skills for Social Work Practice 1 Applied Social Work Theories and Research Evaluation (online) Safeguarding in Context with Children and Families Safeguarding in Context with Adults Standards and Skills for Social Work Practice 2 Into ARU Year 2 Contemporary and Sustainable Social Work Understanding Professional Practice (blended learning) Masters Dissertation - Social Work Standards and Skills for Social Work Practice 3 Module details What happens during placements? Placements are an essential part of your Social Work degree. They’re a chance to put what you’ve learnt into practice. You’ll spend 70 days on placement in Year 1 and 100 days in Year 2. Placements include experience of statutory work, children’s services and adult services. You’ll be working directly with service users. In Year 1, there are opportunities to advocate for service users, promoting service user voice and encourage independent choices. You'll undertake tasks such as interviewing service users to gather information, reviewing care plans, undertaking home visits, and needs versus risk assessments to promote relationship-based practice. In Year 2, you’ll undertake more complex tasks which may include completing a single assessment or life story work if working in a children’s team or undertaking a Mental Capacity Act (2005) assessment if working in an adults' team. You'll develop an ability to manage and be accountable for your own social work practice, making use of supervision and support. Placement locations and travel It’s likely that you’ll have to travel as part of your placement. Most of our placement providers are within commutable distance of our campus in Chelmsford. This means your placement location shouldn’t be more than 1.5 hours of travel from your home. Our partners include Essex County Council, Southend-on-Sea Borough Council and Thurrock Council. We also place students regularly with Suffolk County Council and Norfolk County Council. There may be a very limited number of placements in the London area. If you live outside East Anglia, travel time to placement will be measured from the campus where you’re studying. You’ll need your own transport to visit service users in the community, where public transport may not be available. How much time will I spend on placement? You’ll spend 70 days on placement in Year 1 and 100 days in Year 2. Typically, in Year 1 you’ll have three days of lectures a week on campus, with the rest of your time spent in independent study or on placement. In Year 2, you’ll spend one day per week on campus, and 3-4 days per week on placement. Support on placement While on placement, you’ll be supported by a Practice Educator and a Placement Tutor. You’ll be assigned a Practice Educator (PE), a social worker who’s trained to teach and assess students on placements. They meet the Practice Educator Professional Standards (PEPS). Their role is to support you in integrating theory and knowledge from university into practice. They’re also responsible for assessing your practice. The Placement Tutor (PT) is also an important source of support while you’re on placement. They’re a member of staff at ARU – usually academics in the Social Work team, so you’ll know them. Your PT attends meetings to make sure placements are set up in a way that meets your learning needs, and the University’s requirements. They’re your first point of contact for all placement-related matters, and are here to support you if you have any difficulties during a placement. How is MA Social Work assessed? Assessments mirror real-world situations, guiding you to be open to feedback – and learning how to give feedback in a way that is supportive and helpful. We use case scenarios to expose you to real-life practice examples and simulate knowledge and skills required for the job, both during placements and once qualified. Assessments will foster literacy and use learning outcomes and criteria to guide preparation and self-assessment/evaluation of work. Who teaches MA Social Work at ARU? Read profiles of teaching and research staff on this course. Dr Vanessa Ferguson Associate Professor Dr Gavin Millar Senior Lecturer and Course Leader Dr Sally Pritchard Senior Lecturer Jas Sangha Associate Professor and Race Equality Lead Kofi Konadu-Amankwah Senior Lecturer Dr Joanna Fox Associate Professor (Social Work) Facilities Enjoy a range of facilities designed to support your studies and career development. These include extensive library and IT resources, and careers support through our Employability Service . After you graduate, you’ll have lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . You can also access support, should you need it, with study skills, health and wellbeing, and more. Please enable JavaScript for "Fees Information" section to function. Entry requirements Standard entry requirements Important additional notes Our published entry requirements are a guide only and our decision will be based on your overall suitability for the course as well as whether you meet the minimum entry requirements. Other equivalent qualifications may be accepted for entry to this course; please email [email protected] for further information. Applicants to undergraduate courses can also check our information about undergraduate entry qualifications . You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your course. Interviews If you apply to study Social Work at ARU, we'll invite you to attend an interview. Interviews for Social Work in Chelmsford take place online through Microsoft Teams. Interviews for Social Work in Peterborough take place in-person, on our campus . The interview will consist of a written task, group discussion and individual interview. We'll be interested in exploring your knowledge, skills and values in relation to social work. Interview invitations will be sent by email enabling you to book onto an interview slot and access further interview information including the task. Please keep a close eye on all emails from ARU once you have submitted your UCAS application. You can prepare by researching the knowledge and an understanding of the role of a social worker. We recommend you look at websites such as Social Work England (SWE) , British Association of Social Workers (BASW) and Point of entry to training | BASW . When you graduate, you'll be eligible to apply for registration with SWE. From early on in your degree course, as well as throughout your career, you’ll be working with people accessing services and will need to uphold SWE’s Professional Standards . On the interview day, there’s no need to feel anxious – all of our interviewers are relaxed, friendly and looking forward to seeing your potential. Above all, you need to be certain that this is the profession you want to join. Consider visiting us at an Open Day or Taster Day , if you haven't already. Then commit yourself to learning as much as you can around knowledge, skills and values in relation to social work before your interview day. International students We welcome applications from international and EU students, and accept a range of international qualifications. See international and EU entry requirements See information about application deadlines You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your course. English language requirements If English is not your first language, you'll need to make sure you meet our English language requirements for postgraduate courses . Check the section ' English language requirements ' for IELTS requirements. Please enable JavaScript for "Fees Information" section to function. Fees and funding UK students £10,800 UK students starting 2027/28 (full-time, per year) Fees are payable upfront, in full or in instalments, but there's no need to pay until you've accepted an offer to study with us. Find out more about paying your fees and about postgraduate loans and funding . International students £19,750 International students starting 2027/28 (full-time, per year) You can pay your fees upfront, in full or in two instalments. We will ask for a deposit of £4,000 or a sponsorship letter Find out about paying your fees . Paying for university There are several ways to fund postgraduate study, and we recommend finding out more before you apply. Explore: postgraduate loans and other funding scholarships and bursaries for UK and international students our Alumni Scholarship , worth 20% off fees for ARU graduates. Social Work Bursary You may be eligible for a Social Work Bursary in the first and second year of your degree. It can help with living and travel costs and doesn't have to be repaid. The Social Work Team nominates students for the bursary using our own nomination criteria, and you must also meet the separate eligibility criteria of the Department of Health and Social Care. There are a limited number of bursaries available each year and the process is competitive. We consider your score at interview and attendance from week 1 of the course. Postgraduate MA, PG Dip Social Work Train as a social worker - and create meaningful and positive change for both individuals and communities. Our course pages need JavaScript enabled to work correctly. Previous Section Course Overview Next Section Jump to a section Course overview Careers Teaching and modules Facilities Entry requirements Fees and funding Apply Apply now Come to an Open Event MA PGDip MA Start date September 2027 Location Peterborough UCAS course code L506 Duration 2 years full-time PGDip You can choose to study this course part-time, and start in September or January. The course durations vary slightly: 2 years (September starts) or 28 months (January starts). Course content and modules remain the same. 1st in the region for postgraduates progressing into senior roles. Source: Graduate Outcomes Survey 2026 Whether you have experience of health and social care, or you're looking to change direction in your career, this postgraduate degree will prepare you to become a registered social worker. It’s a practical course featuring two placements, one in a statutory social work setting. You’ll start by exploring the principles of social work, and preparing for placement with interactive skills days. Learn from experienced practitioners, and people with lived experience of social work services. You may be eligible for an NHS Social Work Bursary while studying. Social Work England Our MA Social Work degree course is validated by Social Work England, so when you graduate, you’ll be eligible to apply to register as a social worker. Why ARU? Get hands-on experience, with placements in both years of your course Learn more about working with both adults and children Work directly with service users Qualify as a professional social worker Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers Learn more about social work, get practical experience on placement, and graduate ready to register as a social worker. Most of our students go on to work in statutory settings, but you might also consider roles in the private, voluntary and independent sectors. Whichever sector you choose, you'll be ready to embark on your Assessed and Supported Year in Employment (ASYE). Supported by employers, the ASYE is specially designed for newly qualified social workers and helps you to establish yourself in the sector. What can you do with a Social Work degree? Although focused on social work, this postgraduate degree will also equip you with transferable skills that can be used in a range of graduate roles. These skills include communication, assessment and problem solving, and analytical thinking. Graduation doesn’t have to be the end of your time with us. You could choose to continue your academic career with a research programme at ARU, such as the Professional Doctorate in Health and Social Care . Take advantage of our Alumni Scholarship and save £400 on your fees. How can ARU help with my employability and career development? We want you to be a step ahead when you graduate, so we offer: courses designed with employers tutors with professional industry knowledge hands-on learning which may include industry-led projects, placements or Professional Experience modules . Alongside your course, there are lots of other opportunities to build your skills and experience: add value to your CV with an ARU Certificate of Professional Development get involved in a thriving volunteering programme develop your brilliant business ideas work with businesses to make a social impact . We’re here to help you develop your CV and find that all-important role after graduation. Our Employability Service offers tailored career appointments, advice on writing your CV, help to complete job applications, and much more. You’ll have 24/7 access to an online Careers Centre too, which is packed with useful resources. The support continues after you graduate, with lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . Find out more about careers support at ARU . Teaching and modules Develop your theoretical knowledge of social work – and put what you learn into practice. One of the features of this degree is its emphasis on real-world application. You’ll develop your skills through two placements, gaining experience of different settings and areas of social work practice. We'll help you prepare for your placements through interactive skills days. This course is offered as an MA and a PGDip. Both include placements, and cover social work with children, families, and adults. If you choose to study the MA Social Work, you'll also complete specialist modules in mental health, research, and leadership and management. What will I study? MA PGDip MA Modules are subject to change and availability, and may vary by location. If you have the choice of optional modules, these are indicated with a *. Year 1 Understanding Social Work: Principles and Practice Foundations of Social Work Practice: Theories and Evidence Statutory Social Work: Law, Safeguarding and Risk Human Development for Social Work: Biological, Psychological and Social Perspectives Practice Stage 1: Communication and Relationships Practice Stage 2: Assessment and Interventions Into ARU Year 2 Social Work Practice with Children and Families Social Work Practice with Adults and Carers Social Work with Mental Health Leadership and Management in Social Work Postgraduate Social Work Dissertation Practice Stage 3: Reflection, Development, and Transition to Qualified Social Work Practice Module details PGDip You can choose to study over 2 years and gain a PGDip. As a PGDip student, you'll complete the same modules as MA students in Year 1. See the MA tab for details. In Year 2, you'll complete three core modules. These are: Social Work Practice with Children and Families (15 credits) Social Work Practice with Adults and Carers (15 credits) Practice Stage 3: Reflection, Development and Transition to Qualified Social Work Practice (0 credits) View full module descriptions (please note this includes all MA modules). What happens during placements? Placements are an essential part of your Social Work degree. They’re a chance to put what you’ve learnt into practice. You’ll spend an average three days per week on placement during your studies. This may vary depending on, for example, when your lectures take place. Placement locations and travel It’s likely that you’ll have to travel as part of your placement. Most of our placement providers are within commutable distance of our campus in Peterborough. This means your placement location shouldn’t be more than 1.5 hours of travel from your home. Our partners include Peterborough City Council, Cambridge County Council, Northamptonshire County Council, Bedford Borough Council, and Lincolnshire County Council. We also place students regularly with Suffolk County Council and Norfolk County Council. There may be a very limited number of placements in the London area. If you live outside East Anglia, travel time to placement will be measured from the campus where you’re studying. You’ll need your own transport to visit service users in the community, where public transport may not be available. Support on placement While on placement, you’ll be supported by a Practice Educator and a Placement Tutor. You’ll be assigned a Practice Educator (PE), a social worker who’s trained to teach and assess students on placements. They meet the Practice Educator Professional Standards (PEPS). Their role is to support you in integrating theory and knowledge from university into practice. They’re also responsible for assessing your practice. The Placement Tutor (PT) is also an important source of support while you’re on placement. They’re a member of staff at ARU – usually academics in the Social Work team, so you’ll know them. Your PT attends meetings to make sure placements are set up in a way that meets your learning needs, and the University’s requirements. They’re your first point of contact for all placement-related matters, and are here to support you if you have any difficulties during a placement. How is the course assessed? We use a number of assessment methods including assignments, presentations, reports, poster design, role play, and placement portfolios. Our assessment methods promote both experiential and active learning, helping you to develop a range of transferable skills applicable to social work practice. Who teaches MA Social Work in Peterborough? Read profiles of teaching and research staff on this course. Sam Bonnett Senior lecturer in Social Work Irina Morosanu Principal Lecturer for Practice Learning and Faculty Academic Lead for Social Work Facilities Enjoy a range of facilities designed to support your studies and career development. These include extensive library and IT resources, and careers support through our Employability Service . After you graduate, you’ll have lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . You can also access support, should you need it, with study skills, health and wellbeing, and more. Please enable JavaScript for "Fees Information" section to function. Entry requirements Standard entry requirements MA PGDip MA Important additional notes Our published entry requirements are a guide only and our decision will be based on your overall suitability for the course as well as whether you meet the minimum entry requirements. Other equivalent qualifications may be accepted for entry to this course; please email [email protected] for further information. Applicants to undergraduate courses can also check our information about undergraduate entry qualifications . You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your course. PGDip See entry requirements for the MA or MSc Important additional notes Our published entry requirements are a guide only and our decision will be based on your overall suitability for the course as well as whether you meet the minimum entry requirements. Other equivalent qualifications may be accepted for entry to this course; please email [email protected] for further information. Applicants to undergraduate courses can also check our information about undergraduate entry qualifications . You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your course. Interviews If you apply to study Social Work at ARU, we'll invite you to attend an interview. Interviews for Social Work in Chelmsford take place online through Microsoft Teams. Interviews for Social Work in Peterborough take place in-person, on our campus . The interview will consist of a written task, group discussion and individual interview. We'll be interested in exploring your knowledge, skills and values in relation to social work. Interview invitations will be sent by email enabling you to book onto an interview slot and access further interview information including the task. Please keep a close eye on all emails from ARU once you have submitted your UCAS application. You can prepare by researching the knowledge and an understanding of the role of a social worker. We recommend you look at websites such as Social Work England (SWE) , British Association of Social Workers (BASW) and Point of entry to training | BASW . When you graduate, you'll be eligible to apply for registration with SWE. From early on in your degree course, as well as throughout your career, you’ll be working with people accessing services and will need to uphold SWE’s Professional Standards . On the interview day, there’s no need to feel anxious – all of our interviewers are relaxed, friendly and looking forward to seeing your potential. Above all, you need to be certain that this is the profession you want to join. Consider visiting us at an Open Day or Taster Day , if you haven't already. Then commit yourself to learning as much as you can around knowledge, skills and values in relation to social work before your interview day. Please enable JavaScript for "Fees Information" section to function. Fees and funding UK students MA PGDip MA £10,800 UK students starting 2027/28 (full-time, per year) Fees are payable upfront, in full or in instalments, but there's no need to pay until you've accepted an offer to study with us. Find out more about paying your fees and about postgraduate loans and funding . PGDip £10,800 UK students starting 2027/28 (full-time, per year) Fees are payable upfront, in full or in instalments, but there's no need to pay until you've accepted an offer to study with us. Find out more about paying your fees and about postgraduate loans and funding . Additional course costs You'll be required to register for the DBS online update service, for which there is an annual fee. For the current fee, please see Gov.UK . Paying for university There are several ways to fund postgraduate study, and we recommend finding out more before you apply. Explore: postgraduate loans and other funding scholarships and bursaries for UK and international students our Alumni Scholarship , worth 20% off fees for ARU graduates. Social Work Bursary You may be eligible for a Social Work Bursary in the first and second year of your degree. It can help with living and travel costs and doesn't have to be repaid. The Social Work Team nominates students for the bursary using our own nomination criteria, and you must also meet the separate eligibility criteria of the Department of Health and Social Care. There are a limited number of bursaries available each year and the process is competitive. We consider your score at interview and attendance from week 1 of the course. Jump to a section Introduction Course options Key facts Teaching and assessment Entry requirements Fees and paying for university Facilities and showcase Lecturers Careers Introduction Gain an in-depth understanding of the latest issues in sociology. Hone your research skills and develop expertise for a career in social policy, public service and more. Dr Mirna Guha “I don't restrict myself to a particular discipline. I call myself a political sociologist, but I am an interdisciplinary scholar. I believe in the power of the arts and the media in making social change, and I always try and draw on this as much as possible within my work.” Dr Mirna Guha Course Leader, MA Sociology Read Mirna's Spotlight interview Already have an ARU degree? You may be eligible for our Alumni Scholarship for students starting postgraduate courses. Our MA Sociology will help deepen your knowledge of the theoretical and substantive aspects of contemporary sociology. You’ll become skilled in the principles and application of social research methodology as you examine key debates and issues such as progress and reason, genetic structuralism and the role of modernity. Study in Cambridge, where you’ll be supported by our research-active staff, whose interests reflect the latest developments in sociology. Read more Teaching times 2025-26 (subject to change for 2026-27) Three contact hours a week per module, with about 15 hours for independent learning and research. Our academics are experts in a wide range of areas, which include gendered inequalities, intersectional feminism, social theory, race and racism, the social and political aspects of scientific and technological innovation, ‘race’ and ethnicity and urban sociology. You’ll have the chance to take optional modules in more specialist areas of sociology that are of particular interest to you. These could include modern crime control, nationalism or nature and society. As an MA Sociology student at ARU, you can choose to study part-time or while you work; our postgraduate courses fit into your life. You’ll be welcome to attend and contribute to our research seminar series, symposia and frequent conferences, where you can network and benefit from access to leading practitioners. We’ll help you gain the confidence to become an independent researcher and develop the research and analytical skills that will equip you for a career in social policy, social work, local government and public service. Find out more about our community, the difference we make, the stories we tell, and the things that inspire us. You can also explore the work of our graduating students in our digital graduate showcase. Careers Our MA Sociology will prepare you for work in many fields, including human resources, social policy, social work, educational development, community development, counselling, local government, the civil service, public services and charities. Graduation doesn’t have to be the end of your time with us. You could choose to continue your academic career with a research programme at ARU, such as our PhD Sociology . This Masters degree will give you the opportunity to explore in depth the topics that currently preoccupy scholars, thinkers and practitioners in sociology.

You’ll follow lecture-seminars that reflect cutting-edge issues in sociology and develop your sociological reading, analytical and writing skills.

Your Major Project is your opportunity to investigate a topic that reflects your particular academic interest. We’ll support you to gain the research skills and techniques needed to evaluate the literature you will use throughout this postgraduate course, and which you will put into practice in your Major Project.

You’ll also have a choice of optional modules. This could involve exploring notions of identity related to belonging, as you examine key concepts such as nationalism, transnationalism, diaspora and migration. Or you could examine globalisation and how this impacts on social welfare policy and provision in different countries and societal contexts.

A further four optional modules, of which you'll select one, focus on the history of globalisation; globalisation and welfare; how communication functions in a crisis and approaches to reporting on conflict; and why and how violence proliferates.

Modules are subject to change and availability.

Depending on the module, you’ll show your progress through a combination of essays, presentations, case studies and portfolio work, as well as a Major Project at the end of the course.

","CoreModules":[{"Title":"Contemporary Debates in Sociology","Description":"This module will address key debates in contemporary Sociology, through the in-depth exploration of exemplar topics that currently preoccupy sociological scholars, thinkers, and practitioners. The module will be delivered through lectures and seminars on various aspects of a broad, overarching topic. Topics covered will encompass global sociological debates on decolonisation, public health, and indigenous research ethics and methodologies, etc, with one main topic guiding the coursework per term. You will be assessed through a split written assessment which will assess understanding on interrelated aspects of the main topic each term.","Code":"MOD006941","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"09ce4c7b-7972-4d4c-9a63-24d4413ec343"},{"Title":"Postgraduate Research Methods","Description":"In this module you'll gain the research skills and techniques needed both to critically evaluate the literature you'll be using in your course and to put into practice in your own dissertation. We'll explore the methodologies and methods applied in contemporary social science research to enable you to select an appropriate range for your own needs. You'll have the opportunity to experiment with a variety of methods so that you'll fully understood them and be able to adapt them creatively for your own projects. The module will place research methods in a wider framework of social research strategies at a postgraduate level. We'll examine the research design options available to you at Masters level and explore thoroughly the issues involved in planning a research project and formulating research questions. With the aid of library expertise, you'll have access to and understand current tools for reviewing and researching existing literature. Particular attention will be paid to ethical principles and the politics of social research. A central part of the module will address the practicalities of employing both qualitative and quantitative methodologies. Computer-assisted analysis methods will be introduced.","Code":"MOD000825","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"5b02c3ba-c947-4e80-93fc-9a64099bcba0"},{"Title":"Postgraduate Major Project","Description":"This module is the final element of taught postgraduate programmes in the School of Humanities and Social Sciences. Successful completion of this module, following successful completion of the taught elements of postgraduate MA degrees in the School, will lead to an MA qualification. The research project is developed in conjunction with a specified supervisor and in the context of the area of study of the MA in question. You can work on any topic that the School agrees and is able to supervise. The major project should enable you to demonstrate the ability to explore important and relevant questions in the context of your specialist subject area. You should be able to show detailed knowledge of the research area, demonstrating depth and/or breadth as appropriate; a critical understanding of appropriate methodologies and theories; the ability to present well-argued conclusions from a range of different sources, using material that may be complex and challenging, as appropriate. You should be able to recognise and propose solutions to ethical issues raised in the course of the research. You should be able to communicate your research in coherent terms, both orally and in writing as required.","Code":"MOD000835","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"7f834145-536d-464f-92e0-dbde83f22baa"}],"OptionalModules":[{"Title":"Global Development: Policy and Practice","Description":"This module aims to critically examine the key policies, politics and practices in the field of international development. It explores the key policies undertaken by various actors in the development field, including international organisations, national governments, the private sector, non-governmental organisations, and grassroots movements. You'll learn about the politics of ‘doing’ development and the challenges encountered at each level of policy: global, national, and local levels. You'll also critically examine the key debates in the literature on ‘best practise’ and ‘what works’ drawing on a variety of case studies and examples. You'll cover a range of related topics such as social protection programmes, grassroots movements, advocacy and public action. You'll also gain several practical skills related to project design, project monitoring and evaluation and other themes related to development management especially in the NGO sector. Key development challenges from climate change, poverty, inequality, migration, conflict and human rights will be critically examined in vibrant class discussions, debates and presentations drawing on historical and current events and case studies. You are encouraged to critically examine these challenges in light of relevant theoretical and empirical literature as well as to think about practical solutions to address these challenges. You'll be also critically analysing the difficulties encountered during the implementation of these policies and collectively discuss ways to overcome these difficulties.","Code":"MOD009232","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"0831cea3-1be3-4c1b-928f-166d81bde741"},{"Title":"Communication and Conflict","Description":"On this module you'll explore historical and thematic approaches to reporting on conflict and also how communication functions in a crisis. You'll examine the reciprocal relationships between the military, governments and the media, including how the media can be used to legitimise conflict, and the changing role of social media in building consensus and protest, including the use of Twitter and Facebook to organise demonstrations and undermine the power of state-dominated discourses. You’ll also consider more traditional forms of communication, including censorship and propaganda, and whether the state is ever able to retain control of the narrative, as well as the role of the war reporter, and the way in which governments can utilise the independent media and how independent it really is. Other areas of exploration include consent, public interest, ethics and the representation of suffering, looking at whether the dominance of media in the debate in the West means that public interest in conflict is limited by the limitations of the media, and what this means for winning hearts and minds during insurgencies, military interventions and peacekeeping operations. Finally, you'll look at the way war and conflict is portrayed in fictional accounts and the underlying assumptions of such portrayals, and will examine conflicting discourses about war in post-conflict environments and the way the media can contribute to or hamper the process of post-conflict reconstruction. Themes throughout the module will include the question of who owns, defines and propagates the truth, and the implications of this in the context of conflict and war.","Code":"MOD003644","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"a956aeb6-6c48-423b-b081-fb889035e622"},{"Title":"The Politics of Violence: Context and Policy in Practice","Description":"Violence is everywhere — in news headlines, on our streets, behind closed doors, online and across global conflict zones. But what drives it? How is it framed, justified, resisted, or ignored? And what can be done about it? The Politics of Violence invites you to explore the complex and contested meanings of violence — from everyday acts to systemic forms such as war and state oppression. You'll examine how violence is shaped by culture, politics, identity, and ideology, and ask critical questions about how it's understood, represented, and responded to. This module offers a powerful interdisciplinary lens, drawing on sociology, criminology, political science, psychology, and cultural studies to unpack why violence happens and how it can be addressed. You'll engage with a range of theoretical frameworks and put them to the test through real-world case studies and policy analysis. Expect to tackle questions like: What makes violence legitimate or illegitimate? How do media, governments, and communities frame violent acts? What makes an effective response to violence? You'll critically analyse policy, practitioner responses and legal frameworks and reflect on what works in reducing harm. The module lends itself to future careers in criminal justice, policy development and analysis, NGO and charity work and beyond. By the end of this module, you’ll not only understand how violence operates in context — globally and locally — but also how to think critically about the politics behind it, and the practical efforts aimed at prevention, intervention, and justice.","Code":"MOD004443","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"f2bf6bb9-eadb-4940-90dd-ee0e87a5100a"},{"Title":"Going Global: Making the Modern World, 1979-1999","Description":"This module examines the main themes in contemporary world history, focusing specifically on the 1980s and 1990s as the foundations of the modern, globalising, world were being laid down. You'll critically assess the breakdown of the state-led economic model adopted after the Second World War and consider the development of the more globalised system which replaced it. You'll examine what globalisation meant in reality as changes in technology drove the new consumerism but also contributed to deindustrialisation. In addition, you'll consider how the changes in capitalism influenced the political left as socialist and communist parties across the world turned to market-based ideas and policies. The module also focuses on the ‘third wave of democracy’ which saw apparently stable regimes such as Pinochet’s Chile and Botha’s South Africa fall, and it considers how these factors fed into and influenced the late Cold War years. You'll uncover the ways in which the 1980s was a transformative but incomplete decade as the new ideas introduced by New Right politicians were not completely established until the 1990s with the development of the ‘Third Way’ politics and the victory of neoliberalism at home and abroad. This module is taught through weekly sessions and the emphasis will be on building individual understanding of the key themes of the period as well as encouraging teamwork and oral skills through group discussion and group work. You will develop analytical skills through the investigation of documentary material (identified in the ‘accessible archives’ seminar) from the Thatcher, Kinnock, Reagan or Clinton papers (for example) and you will be expected to bring a relevant document to each class to discuss each week.","Code":"MOD006397","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"1839fd5b-1815-4e4d-b975-e5eae0b1035e"},{"Title":"Beyond Borders Intercultural Communication Welfare and Policy","Description":"This module takes an interdisciplinary approach to introducing key topics and ways of working in the social sciences. You'll look at the development of relations, communicative styles and values between individuals and groups of different cultural backgrounds and delve into comparative issues concerning social policy and social welfare in the international and intercultural context. You'll do this by exploring areas such as gender equality, social housing, education and immigration and wider social concepts such as identity, intersectionality and inequality. You'll work with case studies to exemplify these concepts. In this way, you'll develop the foundation for a deeper understanding and appreciation of fundamental topics in the social sciences. You'll also receive guidance on study at Master’s level and the module will guide you towards the academic research and writing skills needed to work independently at this level.","Code":"MOD010759","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"bbb89968-3e72-43f6-86a5-634020d297e9"},{"Title":"Intercultural Consultancy Project","Description":"Working with an external collaborative partner, you will negotiate a 12 week consultancy project that demonstrates and builds upon theoretical and practical skills you have acquired on your course. The module will enable you to work contextually within the framework of work-based learning by facilitating knowledge exchange between the student and their external partner. The project will respond to the opportunities and needs of the external partner as applied to the field of intercultural communications. You will critically engage with how this professional sector operates in context of the wider business environments and how this can be applied to your career development. This module supports you in the development of key skills required in contemporary intercultural work environments, such as face-to-face and asynchronous communications, collaborative and cooperative decision making or intra-team conflict resolution.","Code":"MOD008998","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"828f471c-8924-483e-b522-4be3447c71d2"}],"Id":"dc568ffc-4901-4886-9ab5-305a63cda2c6","SelectedModule":false}],"UcasCode":"","SITSCode":"","AstraCode":"P0339","ModeOfStudy":{"KisCode":"FullTime","ModeOfStudyCode":"FT","ExcludeFromCourseSummary":false,"Name":"Full-time","Id":"3188d331-b419-4c02-bf25-30c84b6fff3d"},"CoreOption":false,"FoundationOption":false,"PlacementOption":false,"ProfessionalExperienceOption":false,"PartTimeOption":false,"Extra1":false,"Extra2":false,"Status":null,"StartDateDisclaimer":null,"DegreeApprenticeship":false,"Award":null,"Qualification":null,"LocationOverride":null,"EntryRequirementYears":[{"Name":"2026","Id":"b0de6795-6e13-4745-98d9-c1515ee46eae"}],"EntryRequirementsInformation":[{"HeadingTitle":"Standard entry requirements","RichTextContent":[{"RichTextTitle":"","RichTextContent":"

","CoreModules":[{"Title":"Postgraduate Major Project","Description":"In this module you’ll explore a topic of your choice in greater depth (on the condition that we have the expertise to supervise it). This format of this project is also flexible; you may choose the standard dissertation format to present your work. You may also, under the guidance of your supervisor, opt to undertake a project that, for example, involves the production of an artefact, staging of an exhibition or publishing on-line content that has a public education or community enrichment brief. You may also consider, again under the guidance of your supervisor, designing a project that tests an hypothesis you ultimately write up as a report but which you test through the production of material for public consumption. You can undertake some of this work in collaboration with other members of the course, conditional on a clear agreement is reached about the division of labour across this team. This project gives you the opportunity to use material and research methods from the rest of the course. It is an opportunity for you to demonstrate that you have the detailed knowledge and understanding of your chosen research area, a critical appreciation of the appropriate methodologies and theories, and the ability to locate, to critically engage with and evaluate an appropriate range of sources. You will also be expected to recognise and manage appropriately any ethical issues that arise in the completion of this project.
