This Masters degree will give you the opportunity to explore in depth the topics that currently preoccupy scholars, thinkers and practitioners in sociology.

In Year 1 you’ll follow lecture-seminars that reflect cutting-edge issues in sociology and develop your sociological reading, analytical and writing skills. We’ll also support you to gain the research skills and techniques needed to evaluate the literature you will use throughout this postgraduate course, and which you will put into practice in your Major Project in Year 2.

Modules are subject to change and availability.

Depending on the module, you’ll show your progress through a combination of essays, presentations, case studies and portfolio work, as well as a Major Project at the end of the course.

","CoreModules":[{"Title":"Contemporary Debates in Sociology","Description":"This module will address key debates in contemporary Sociology, through the in-depth exploration of exemplar topics that currently preoccupy sociological scholars, thinkers, and practitioners. The module will be delivered through lectures and seminars on various aspects of a broad, overarching topic. Topics covered will encompass global sociological debates on decolonisation, public health, and indigenous research ethics and methodologies, etc, with one main topic guiding the coursework per term. You will be assessed through a split written assessment which will assess understanding on interrelated aspects of the main topic each term.","Code":"MOD006941","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"09ce4c7b-7972-4d4c-9a63-24d4413ec343"},{"Title":"Postgraduate Research Methods","Description":"In this module you'll gain the research skills and techniques needed both to critically evaluate the literature you'll be using in your course and to put into practice in your own dissertation. We'll explore the methodologies and methods applied in contemporary social science research to enable you to select an appropriate range for your own needs. You'll have the opportunity to experiment with a variety of methods so that you'll fully understood them and be able to adapt them creatively for your own projects. The module will place research methods in a wider framework of social research strategies at a postgraduate level. We'll examine the research design options available to you at Masters level and explore thoroughly the issues involved in planning a research project and formulating research questions. With the aid of library expertise, you'll have access to and understand current tools for reviewing and researching existing literature. Particular attention will be paid to ethical principles and the politics of social research. A central part of the module will address the practicalities of employing both qualitative and quantitative methodologies. Computer-assisted analysis methods will be introduced.","Code":"MOD000825","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"5b02c3ba-c947-4e80-93fc-9a64099bcba0"}],"OptionalModules":[],"Id":"8d58bd77-4f5d-4385-82d9-654a4b97703e","SelectedModule":false},{"Title":"Year 2","CoreModuleSectionHeading":"Core modules","OptionModuleSectionHeading":"Optional modules","Summary":"

This Masters degree will give you the opportunity to explore in depth the topics that currently preoccupy scholars, thinkers and practitioners in sociology.

In Year 2, the Major Project is your opportunity to investigate a topic that reflects your particular academic interest.

You’ll also have a choice of optional modules. This could involve exploring notions of identity related to belonging, as you examine key concepts such as nationalism, transnationalism, diaspora and migration. Or you could examine globalisation and how this impacts on social welfare policy and provision in different countries and societal contexts.

A further four optional modules, of which you'll select one, focus on the history of globalisation; globalisation and welfare; how communication functions in a crisis and approaches to reporting on conflict; and why and how violence proliferates.

Modules are subject to change and availability.

Depending on the module, you’ll show your progress through a combination of essays, presentations, case studies and portfolio work, as well as a Major Project at the end of the course.

","CoreModules":[{"Title":"Postgraduate Major Project","Description":"This module is the final element of taught postgraduate programmes in the School of Humanities and Social Sciences. Successful completion of this module, following successful completion of the taught elements of postgraduate MA degrees in the School, will lead to an MA qualification. The research project is developed in conjunction with a specified supervisor and in the context of the area of study of the MA in question. You can work on any topic that the School agrees and is able to supervise. The major project should enable you to demonstrate the ability to explore important and relevant questions in the context of your specialist subject area. You should be able to show detailed knowledge of the research area, demonstrating depth and/or breadth as appropriate; a critical understanding of appropriate methodologies and theories; the ability to present well-argued conclusions from a range of different sources, using material that may be complex and challenging, as appropriate. You should be able to recognise and propose solutions to ethical issues raised in the course of the research. You should be able to communicate your research in coherent terms, both orally and in writing as required.","Code":"MOD000835","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"7f834145-536d-464f-92e0-dbde83f22baa"}],"OptionalModules":[{"Title":"Global Development: Policy and Practice","Description":"This module aims to critically examine the key policies, politics and practices in the field of international development. It explores the key policies undertaken by various actors in the development field, including international organisations, national governments, the private sector, non-governmental organisations, and grassroots movements. You'll learn about the politics of ‘doing’ development and the challenges encountered at each level of policy: global, national, and local levels. You'll also critically examine the key debates in the literature on ‘best practise’ and ‘what works’ drawing on a variety of case studies and examples. You'll cover a range of related topics such as social protection programmes, grassroots movements, advocacy and public action. You'll also gain several practical skills related to project design, project monitoring and evaluation and other themes related to development management especially in the NGO sector. Key development challenges from climate change, poverty, inequality, migration, conflict and human rights will be critically examined in vibrant class discussions, debates and presentations drawing on historical and current events and case studies. You are encouraged to critically examine these challenges in light of relevant theoretical and empirical literature as well as to think about practical solutions to address these challenges. You'll be also critically analysing the difficulties encountered during the implementation of these policies and collectively discuss ways to overcome these difficulties.","Code":"MOD009232","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"0831cea3-1be3-4c1b-928f-166d81bde741"},{"Title":"Communication and Conflict","Description":"On this module you'll explore historical and thematic approaches to reporting on conflict and also how communication functions in a crisis. You'll examine the reciprocal relationships between the military, governments and the media, including how the media can be used to legitimise conflict, and the changing role of social media in building consensus and protest, including the use of Twitter and Facebook to organise demonstrations and undermine the power of state-dominated discourses. You’ll also consider more traditional forms of communication, including censorship and propaganda, and whether the state is ever able to retain control of the narrative, as well as the role of the war reporter, and the way in which governments can utilise the independent media and how independent it really is. Other areas of exploration include consent, public interest, ethics and the representation of suffering, looking at whether the dominance of media in the debate in the West means that public interest in conflict is limited by the limitations of the media, and what this means for winning hearts and minds during insurgencies, military interventions and peacekeeping operations. Finally, you'll look at the way war and conflict is portrayed in fictional accounts and the underlying assumptions of such portrayals, and will examine conflicting discourses about war in post-conflict environments and the way the media can contribute to or hamper the process of post-conflict reconstruction. Themes throughout the module will include the question of who owns, defines and propagates the truth, and the implications of this in the context of conflict and war.","Code":"MOD003644","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"a956aeb6-6c48-423b-b081-fb889035e622"},{"Title":"The Politics of Violence: Context and Policy in Practice","Description":"Violence is everywhere — in news headlines, on our streets, behind closed doors, online and across global conflict zones. But what drives it? How is it framed, justified, resisted, or ignored? And what can be done about it? The Politics of Violence invites you to explore the complex and contested meanings of violence — from everyday acts to systemic forms such as war and state oppression. You'll examine how violence is shaped by culture, politics, identity, and ideology, and ask critical questions about how it's understood, represented, and responded to. This module offers a powerful interdisciplinary lens, drawing on sociology, criminology, political science, psychology, and cultural studies to unpack why violence happens and how it can be addressed. You'll engage with a range of theoretical frameworks and put them to the test through real-world case studies and policy analysis. Expect to tackle questions like: What makes violence legitimate or illegitimate? How do media, governments, and communities frame violent acts? What makes an effective response to violence? You'll critically analyse policy, practitioner responses and legal frameworks and reflect on what works in reducing harm. The module lends itself to future careers in criminal justice, policy development and analysis, NGO and charity work and beyond. By the end of this module, you’ll not only understand how violence operates in context — globally and locally — but also how to think critically about the politics behind it, and the practical efforts aimed at prevention, intervention, and justice.","Code":"MOD004443","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"f2bf6bb9-eadb-4940-90dd-ee0e87a5100a"},{"Title":"Going Global: Making the Modern World, 1979-1999","Description":"This module examines the main themes in contemporary world history, focusing specifically on the 1980s and 1990s as the foundations of the modern, globalising, world were being laid down. You'll critically assess the breakdown of the state-led economic model adopted after the Second World War and consider the development of the more globalised system which replaced it. You'll examine what globalisation meant in reality as changes in technology drove the new consumerism but also contributed to deindustrialisation. In addition, you'll consider how the changes in capitalism influenced the political left as socialist and communist parties across the world turned to market-based ideas and policies. The module also focuses on the ‘third wave of democracy’ which saw apparently stable regimes such as Pinochet’s Chile and Botha’s South Africa fall, and it considers how these factors fed into and influenced the late Cold War years. You'll uncover the ways in which the 1980s was a transformative but incomplete decade as the new ideas introduced by New Right politicians were not completely established until the 1990s with the development of the ‘Third Way’ politics and the victory of neoliberalism at home and abroad. This module is taught through weekly sessions and the emphasis will be on building individual understanding of the key themes of the period as well as encouraging teamwork and oral skills through group discussion and group work. You will develop analytical skills through the investigation of documentary material (identified in the ‘accessible archives’ seminar) from the Thatcher, Kinnock, Reagan or Clinton papers (for example) and you will be expected to bring a relevant document to each class to discuss each week.","Code":"MOD006397","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"1839fd5b-1815-4e4d-b975-e5eae0b1035e"},{"Title":"Beyond Borders Intercultural Communication Welfare and Policy","Description":"This module takes an interdisciplinary approach to introducing key topics and ways of working in the social sciences. You'll look at the development of relations, communicative styles and values between individuals and groups of different cultural backgrounds and delve into comparative issues concerning social policy and social welfare in the international and intercultural context. You'll do this by exploring areas such as gender equality, social housing, education and immigration and wider social concepts such as identity, intersectionality and inequality. You'll work with case studies to exemplify these concepts. In this way, you'll develop the foundation for a deeper understanding and appreciation of fundamental topics in the social sciences. You'll also receive guidance on study at Master’s level and the module will guide you towards the academic research and writing skills needed to work independently at this level.","Code":"MOD010759","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"bbb89968-3e72-43f6-86a5-634020d297e9"},{"Title":"Intercultural Consultancy Project","Description":"Working with an external collaborative partner, you will negotiate a 12 week consultancy project that demonstrates and builds upon theoretical and practical skills you have acquired on your course. You will critically engage with how this professional sector operates in context of the wider business environments and how this can be applied to your career development. This module supports you in the development of key skills required in contemporary intercultural work environments, such as face-to-face and asynchronous communications, collaborative and cooperative decision making or intra-team conflict resolution.","Code":"MOD008998","HideMdfLink":false,"MdfLinkText":"View the full module definition","Id":"828f471c-8924-483e-b522-4be3447c71d2"}],"Id":"1f9e2d15-42b9-48ff-a56e-b4e7313a97cd","SelectedModule":false}],"UcasCode":"","SITSCode":"","AstraCode":"P0339","ModeOfStudy":{"KisCode":"PartTime","ModeOfStudyCode":"PT","ExcludeFromCourseSummary":false,"Name":"Part-time","Id":"77ee6eb5-cef9-4099-87c0-3c2819c645cd"},"CoreOption":false,"FoundationOption":false,"PlacementOption":false,"ProfessionalExperienceOption":false,"PartTimeOption":false,"Extra1":false,"Extra2":false,"Status":null,"StartDateDisclaimer":null,"DegreeApprenticeship":false,"Award":null,"Qualification":null,"LocationOverride":null,"EntryRequirementYears":[{"Name":"2026","Id":"b0de6795-6e13-4745-98d9-c1515ee46eae"}],"EntryRequirementsInformation":[{"HeadingTitle":"Standard entry requirements","RichTextContent":[{"RichTextTitle":"","RichTextContent":"

Postgraduate Sociology MPhil, PhD Research ( full-time, part-time) Cambridge January 2027, April, September 2027 Distance-learning supervision available on this course. This course is located in the School of Humanities and Social Sciences. Find out more about our research . Apply online For application deadlines visit our how to apply page . Overview Our PhD research programmes will allow you to join one of our research projects or explore your own interests in Sociology, supported by the expertise of our staff. Full description You’ll be allocated two supervisors, with additional staff members available if necessary. Our supervisors are experienced in most areas of sociology, with particular strengths in social theory, gender studies, social studies of science and technology and diaspora and migration. We’ll provide you with a rich and stimulating research environment with strong links to research networks in Anglia Ruskin and the wider community, including the Citizens Advice Bureau and the University of Cambridge's Centre for Research into Arts, Social Sciences, and Humanities (CRASSH). We contribute to many of our Faculty’s research groups, including the International Policing and Public Protection Research Institute and the StoryLab Research Group . We also host and take part in many research events, including regular Faculty and departmental research seminars, which will allow you to present your research in a safe and supportive setting. These events, along with our online environment, will help you connect with other research students from a range of disciplines. All your subject-specific studies will be enhanced and supported by our University-wide training sessions, where you’ll gain important research expertise in areas like ethics, presentations, intellectual property and digital scholarship. PhD project opportunities in the Faculty of Arts, Humanities, Education and Social Sciences World-leading research at ARU International Policing and Public Protection Research Institute Humanities & Social Sciences research Supervision and support Our permanent supervisory staff are recognised as international experts in their fields, and have produced a large number of influential books, journal articles and edited collections, and won funding for a number of prestigious research projects. Our expertise in social sciences includes: Dr Liz Bradbury : classical and contemporary social theory, gender studies, psychoanalytic and psychosocial studies. Dr Mirna Guha : gendered inequalities; intersectional feminism; 'race', identity, and social relations; gender-based violence; sex work; social justice. Dr Shaun Le Boutillier : social theory and the structure versus agency debate, social emergence theory and the relationship between social wholes and individuals; social causation and the philosophy of the social sciences; agency and moral theory; the sociology of work and organisational life. Dr David Skinner : race and racism, the social and political aspects of scientific and technological innovation; the relationship between the natural and social sciences; forensics, databases and surveillance; the changing management of public services. Emma Brett: public service; learning and education; equality and cultural diversity; barriers to learning. Additional research expertise: Professor Bronwen Walter , Irish Diaspora Studies. Where you'll research Your department and faculty At the School of Humanities and Social Sciences, we believe in thinking critically about the past, present and future to challenge perceptions and better understand communities and people. With expertise from gender issues to literary analysis to exploring how the past has shaped our modern world, all our staff members are active researchers. This is reflected in our teaching, allowing us to support our students with the latest theories and practices, as well as essential employability advice. Visit your department Where can I study? Cambridge Our campus is close to the centre of Cambridge, often described as the perfect student city. Explore our Cambridge campus Specialist facilities You’ll have access to the world-famous University of Cambridge Library, our own campus library and other local archives. Our Faculty has a dedicated PhD room, where our doctoral students can all meet up to work and take an active part in our postgraduate student community. Fees & funding Course fees UK students, 2026/27 (per year) £5,238 UK students, 2026/27 (part-time, per year) £2,619 International students, 2026/27 (per year) £17,500 International students, 2026/27 (part-time, per year) £8,750 Bench fees In some cases extra costs known as bench fees will be charged for a postgraduate research degree. These are to cover additional/exceptional costs directly related to a specific research project. Some examples of these costs are (the list is not exhaustive): equipment hire, access costs to specialist equipment/workshops, volunteer expenses, specialist tissue/cell culture, specialist reagents or materials, specialist software, access to specialist databases, data collection costs, specialist media, recording or digital storage needs. We charge bench fees in bands. They may apply for every year of your course. These bands are the same for full- and part-time students. If you have to pay bench fees this will be made clear at your interview, and stated in your offer letter. For 2026/27 the bench fee bands are: £500 £1,400 £2,400 £4,900 £9,800 PhD by Published Work Initial registration: £1,700 Full registration: £4,900 Writing up fees 2026/27 £1,400 How do I pay my fees? You can pay your fees upfront, in full or in instalments – though you won't need to pay until you've accepted an offer to study with us. Find out more about paying your fees . Funding For advice on the Doctoral Loan and other sources of funding, including ARU scholarships, visit our finance guide for postgraduate researchers . You might also find The Alternative Guide to Postgraduate Funding helpful. ARU research ARU's academic excellence was recognised in 2021, as part of the Research Excellence Framework (REF), an exercise which assesses the quality of academic research. Sixteen areas of our work were classed as generating world-leading research . The results showed that we're making a significant impact on the societies we live in. Careers We’ll provide you with many opportunities for career development and training, in areas like writing up a paper for publication, placing an academic article, giving a conference paper, the doctoral writing style, updates on research methods and literature searches, internet training, editing skills for doctoral research, subsequent monograph publication and working with agents and publishers. You might also be able to take on teaching responsibilities in the department, or organise research events. In conjunction with the University’s research support, you can request specific support for writing-up, conference papers, general research methods and other research skills if you need it. Contact details If you're interested in finding out more about research study opportunities in this area, please email [email protected] Entry requirements MPhil or PhD with progression from MPhil: You’ll need a Bachelor degree or equivalent with first or upper second class honours, in a related subject area. PhD: You’ll need a Master degree or equivalent in a related subject area. Please note we consider candidates for PhD with progression from MPhil in the first instance. If you want to be considered for direct entry to the PhD route then this can be discussed at interview if you are shortlisted. Please note you’ll also need to provide academic justification for this request. If English is not your first language, you'll require a minimum IELTS score of 6.5, with a minimum of 5.5 in each component (or equivalent test). If you don't meet our English language requirements, we offer a range of courses which could help you achieve the level required for entry. Loading... Entry requirements are not currently available, please try again later. Important additional notes Our published entry requirements are a guide only and our decision will be based on your overall suitability for the programme as well as whether you meet the minimum entry requirements. Contact our postgraduate research degree team for more information about studying a PhD, MPhil or Professional Doctorate at ARU. You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your research programme. Postgraduate Sport and Exercise Sciences MPhil, PhD Research ( full-time, part-time) Cambridge January 2027, April, September 2027 Apply online For application deadlines visit our how to apply page . Overview Pursue original research in physiology, psychology, biomechanics or coaching/pedagogy, in highly-equipped surroundings with an innovative, expert team. Full description The Cambridge Centre for Sport and Exercise Sciences brings together expertise in physiology, psychology, biomechanics and coaching/pedagogy within the School of Psychology, Sport and Sensory Science . Specialists from these disciplines collaborate on projects within four broad categories: athlete performance; recreational-based sport and exercise; health-based exercise; judo-based research. Within this innovative and highly productive research environment we can provide you with supervision in a wide range of research topics, in well-equipped surroundings. We host research seminars, conferences and workshops to aid knowledge-sharing and you’ll be part of a supportive postgraduate community encompassing many specialisms. As an indication of activity within the department, here’s a brief overview of our current research projects: Nitrate and VO2 Bicarbonate and VO2 Stroke volume and menstrual function Visual search and anxiety in sport Visual impairment and adaptive gait Mobile multivariable physiological monitors and sporting performance Temporal analysis of lightweight women's Judo Understanding the coach-athlete relationship Specialist facilities You’ll be able to use specialist laboratories and equipment including: Dedicated human performance suite Exercise physiology laboratory Biomechanics Laboratory Learning Zone computer suite In addition to our Sport and Exercise Sciences PhD, we've also identified a range of innovative research project opportunities for you as a postgraduate researcher. Completion times MPhil: full-time 1-3 years, part-time 2-4 years. PhD via progression from MPhil, including that period: full-time 2.5-5 years, part-time 3.5-6 years. PhD: full-time 2-4 years, part-time 3-6 years. For further guidance on the duration of research degrees please refer to the Research Degrees Regulations . Sport & Exercise Sciences PhD project opportunities Read about our current research in 'First' Our faculty's quarterly newsletter World-leading research at ARU Application tips Supervision and support Our supervisory staff are recognised experts in their field. Their research expertise includes: Prof Dan Gordon - Exercise physiology. Dr James Johnstone - Strength and conditioning, talent identification and development of excellence, use of mobile monitoring technology in sport and performance. Adrian Scruton - Chronic changes in muscle activation (EMG) and walking gait with the use of unstable shoe design. Dr Matthew Timmis - Investigating visual search strategies in sports performance and how these patterns change as a function of task demand. Dr Katrina McDonald - Coaching and athlete education. Prof Lee Smith - Physical activity promotion and sedentary behaviour reduction. Prof Justin Roberts - Performance and functional nutrition in relation to sport, health and exercise physiology. Dr Francesca Cavallerio - Health and Wellbeing of athletes, psychology of sports injuries, athlete retirement. Dr Kjell van Paridon - The influence of psychological stress on visual attention, motor skill execution and performance. Dr Matt Jewiss - performance under pressure in a variety of performance domains, e.g., sport, education, aviation and the emergency services. Dr Ash Willmott - Sport and exercise physiology, extreme environments (heat stress and hypoxia), football performance and injury risk prediction. Dr Andrew Morrison - Biomechanics, specifically in golf and the coordination and control of human movement. Dr Sanjoy Deb - Nutrition and exercise, with diverse expertise that covers nutraceuticals, functional foods, nutritional physiology and behaviour change. Whichever course you pick, you’ll gain the theory and practical skills needed to progress with confidence. Join us and you could find yourself learning in the very latest laboratories or on field trips or work placements with well-known and respected companies. You may even have the opportunity to study abroad. Everything we do in the faculty has a singular purpose: to provide a world-class environment to create, share and advance knowledge in science, technology and engineering fields. Postgraduate MSc Sustainability LEARN, EXPERIENCE, APPLY, TRANSFORM. Develop your capabilities through this hybrid Master's programme, co-designed with the Eden Project. Gain the sustainability knowledge and applied skills to navigate complex, real-world issues. Our course pages need JavaScript enabled to work correctly. Source: Graduate Outcomes Survey 2026 This applied Master's degree, co‑designed by ARU and the Eden Project, offers a unique blend of academic and experiential learning. You can study full-time over 12 months , or part-time over 24 months providing the opportunity to study alongside your other responsibilities. Delivered predominantly online, the programme includes five immersive residential weeks at ARU in Cambridge and the Eden Project in Cornwall. These in‑person experiences allow you to build strong connections with a close‑knit cohort, enriching your learning experience with diverse perspectives and real‑world insights. You will learn from academics within our Global Sustainability Institute and engage directly with sustainability leaders from industry, civil society, government, and the third sector. You will apply your learning through your assignments and a professional placement, where you will also develop ‘Skills for Change’ – practical capabilities aligned with UNESCO’s Sustainability Competencies . The programme’s flexibility allows you to dive deeply into a specific sustainability area or build a broad foundation across multiple themes. With its focus on systems thinking, critical reflection, skills development and independent research this Master's equips you for a range of sustainability careers – whether you’re beginning your journey in the field, tackling sustainability challenges in your current role, or exploring a new professional direction. Discover some of the highlights of this Master's course. Close full-screen gallery. Discover some of the highlights of this Master's course. Why ARU? Experience a curated learning journey shaped by academic and industry perspectives Enjoy flexible online learning, full-time or part-time Develop a critical understanding of sustainability challenges aligned with industry needs, through this ISEP accredited Master's Strengthen your reflective practice and your capacity to drive change through a professional placement Learn from the Eden Project’s visionary approach to sustainability and a network of pioneering leaders Tailor assignments to explore one sustainability challenge or broaden your knowledge across diverse topics Accredited by ISEP This course is accredited by the Institute of Sustainability and Environmental Professionals (ISEP). This gives access to a global network of sustainability professionals, exclusive events, and toolkits and ensures that you graduate with industry-recognised skills in areas such as systems thinking, policy and legislation, environmental management tools, and leadership for change. Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers The course helped me realise my interests and led me to my new job [where] I am able to use the knowledge and skills gained from the MSc. Sophie Bowers, MSc Sustainability graduate People join the MSc Sustainability for many reasons, each leading to different career pathways. You may want to deepen your sustainability expertise to strengthen your current role, or tackle long‑standing challenges in your organisation or sector. Or you may be a recent graduate or early‑career professional who's eager to explore emerging opportunities in the sustainability field. What can you do with an MSc Sustainability? Examples of career roles after completing an MSc include: Sustainability education lead in a further education college Project manager Sustainability consultant Policy advisor Research manager Communications consultant CSR manager Further study, such as a research programme Moving into a meaningful career Since graduating from our MSc Sustainability degree, Sophie has moved sectors and now works in nature conservation with a wildlife trust. How can ARU help with my employability and career development? This Masters programme is structured around UNESCO Sustainability Competencies, allowing to develop your professional competences whilst learning about sustainability through a systems-thinking lens. It's I SEP-accredited, with core content designed to meet industry expectations for a sustainability qualification at this level. You will complete a supported professional placement – either in your current organisation or a new one – to build connections and grow as a sustainability leader. You will have access to employability services and an online Alumni Career Centre to support your next steps. Upon graduation you will become part of our MSc Sustainability Alumni Network Teaching and modules My favourite part has been the immersive experiences, whether at the Eden Project or the field trips at Cambridge. They bring all the learning to life in a really meaningful way. Develop a strong foundation of academic knowledge while building personal competencies in systems thinking, independent research, and professionalism. You'll start the course by establishing a solid grounding in sustainability from a systems perspective, helping you explore the interconnections between human and environmental systems and question prevailing societal assumptions. You will explore sustainability challenges using systems mapping techniques, whilst being introduced to academic methods and corporate sustainability tools that can support organisational decision making. You'll also consider what leadership means for individuals and sectors, through a module developed in collaboration with the Eden Project. This course includes a professional development placement – in your current workplace or a new organisation – where you'll reflect on your own capacity to lead and influence change. Finally, you'll undertake an independent research project on a topic of your choice, supported by an academic supervisor. You can explore examples of previous students’ dissertations here , which demonstrate the scope of topics that have been pursued. What will I study? If you have the choice of optional modules, these are indicated with a *. Year 1 Introduction to Sustainability and Systems (30 credits) Leading System Change (30 credits) Working Towards Change (30 credits) Year 2 Methods and Tools for Complex Systems (30 credits) Major Project (60 credits) Module details When does online teaching take place? This course is delivered predominantly online. Sessions take place from 12-1pm on set days, designed to fit around your schedule. There are also five residential weeks in Cambridge and Cornwall. What are the residential dates? Your course includes five residential sessions. Three sessions take place at ARU in Cambridge, and two at the Eden Project in Cornwall. Residential sessions are mandatory and dates are as follows. Full-time course You'll join five week-long residentials, two at the Eden Project and three in Cambridge. Your course lasts for 12 months and all residentials take place within that time. Trimester 1, Cambridge: 28 September- 2 October 2026 19-23 October 2026 23-27 November 2026 Trimester 2, Eden Project Cornwall: 8-12 February 2027 15-19 March 2027 Part-time course You'll join five week-long residentials, two at the Eden Project and three in Cambridge. The residentials are split over two years. Year 1, Trimester 1, Cambridge: 28 September - 2 October 2o26 23-27 November 2026 Year 1, Trimester 2, Eden Project Cornwall: 8-12 February 2027 15-19 March 2027 Year 2, Trimester 1, Cambridge: October 2027, week-long, dates to be confirmed How is MSc Sustainability assessed? Assessments take varied formats, providing the opportunity to develop a range of communication skills, including creating a sector specific future vision, producing a long-form academic essay, developing a business plan, writing reflective pieces, and completing an independent research dissertation. Who teaches MSc Sustainability at ARU? Read profiles of the core teaching team. Dr Davide Natalini Senior Research Fellow Dr Philippa Calver Lecturer in Sustainability Professor Rosie Robison Professor of Social Sustainability Professor Aled Jones Director, Global Sustainability Institute Other course contributors One of our key strengths is the range of experts from both academia and industry who contribute to the course. Each year we have over 30 contributors. Here are some of our programme contributors from recent years. Ian Trim (Visiting Fellow, ARU) Dan Ryan (Head of Nature Futures, Lost Gardens of Heligan) Prof Alison Greig (Emeritus Professor, ARU) Dr Jo Elworthy (Chief Science Engagement Officer, Eden Project) Dr Zareen Bharucha (Senior Research Fellow, ARU) Dr Lara Houston (Senior Research Fellow, ARU) Rev Canon Nigel Cooper (Visiting Professor, ARU) Imelda Phadtare (Principal Advisor, Climate Change, Save the Children) Sally Symons-Heard (Consultant and CEO of Cornwall School for Social Enterprises) Dr Pete Barbrook-Johnson (Lecturer in Social Economics at the Department of Arts and Sciences, UCL and Associate Fellow at the Institute for New Economic Thinking, University of Oxford) Chloë Fiddy (Honorary Research Fellow, ARU and Senior Policy and Engagement Lead, Institute of Sustainability and Environmental Professionals) Find out what MSc Sustainability alumni Abigail Blake learned on the course, and how it transformed her career. These include extensive library and IT resources, and careers support through our Employability Service . After you graduate, you’ll have lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . Postgraduate Sustainability PhD Research ( full-time, part-time) Cambridge January 2027, April, September 2027 Apply online For application deadlines visit our how to apply page . Overview Pursue your research degree with the Global Sustainability Institute, an internationally known institute that works with influential partners, including government and industry. Full description Established in early 2011, the Global Sustainability Institute's core research questions are based around personal motivations and systems change, in relation to sustainability. This translates into our key research areas: Complex Socio-Ecological Systems Creativity and Imagination Everyday Experiences and Emotion Participation and Community Engagement Policy, Governance and Institutions Reflexivity and Research Practices We collaborate with departments throughout Anglia Ruskin University, as well as with numerous external organisations, with recent PhDs including Swiss Re, Institute & Faculty of Actuaries, Essex County Council and the Cambridgeshire Planning Service. It’s an inspiring environment in which to conduct research and influence the world – and we can offer you high-quality supervision from influential figures in the sustainability field. Visit aru.ac.uk/gsi for further information about the Institute, and don’t hesitate to contact us if you’d like to discuss your research proposal. Completion times PhD via progression from MPhil, including that period: full-time 2.5-5 years, part-time 3.5-6 years. PhD: full-time 2-4 years, part-time 3-6 years. For further guidance on the duration of research degrees please refer to the Research Degrees Regulations . Exploring UK food system resilience Read more about the FoodSHINES PhD programme Global Sustainability Institute Sustainable Futures Research theme Supervision and support We can accommodate many research proposals. Our researchers come from a variety of backgrounds, including economics, geography, international relations, psychology, sociology, environmental social science, communications, mathematics and computer modelling. Our supervisory staff are recognised experts in their fields. Feel free to contact a member of our academic staff with an informal enquiry. The GSI staff are joined by visiting fellows – and we can call on the expertise of specialists throughout ARU to support the interdisciplinary aspects of your work. You can find out more about our postgraduate opportunities (MSc, PhD, ProfDoc), including links to PhD topics which would complement current research across our themes. Where you'll research Your faculty The Faculty of Science & Engineering is one of the largest of the four faculties at ARU. Whether you choose to study with us full-time or part-time, on campus or at a distance, there’s an option whatever your level – from a foundation degree, BSc, MSc, PhD or professional doctorate. Whichever course you pick, you’ll gain the theory and practical skills needed to progress with confidence. Join us and you could find yourself learning in the very latest laboratories or on field trips or work placements with well-known and respected companies. You may even have the opportunity to study abroad. Everything we do in the faculty has a singular purpose: to provide a world-class environment to create, share and advance knowledge in science, technology and engineering fields. This is key to all of our futures. Visit your faculty Where can I study? Cambridge Our campus is close to the centre of Cambridge, often described as the perfect student city. Explore our Cambridge campus Fees & funding Course fees UK students, 2026/27 (per year) £5,238 UK students, 2026/27 (part-time, per year) £2,619 International students, 2026/27 (per year) £17,500 International students, 2026/27 (part-time, per year) £8,750 Bench fees In some cases extra costs known as bench fees will be charged for a postgraduate research degree. These are to cover additional/exceptional costs directly related to a specific research project. Some examples of these costs are (the list is not exhaustive): equipment hire, access costs to specialist equipment/workshops, volunteer expenses, specialist tissue/cell culture, specialist reagents or materials, specialist software, access to specialist databases, data collection costs, specialist media, recording or digital storage needs. We charge bench fees in bands. They may apply for every year of your course. These bands are the same for full- and part-time students. If you have to pay bench fees this will be made clear at your interview, and stated in your offer letter. For 2026/27 the bench fee bands are: £500 £1,400 £2,400 £4,900 £9,800 PhD by Published Work Initial registration: £1,700 Full registration: £4,900 Writing up fees 2026/27 £1,400 How do I pay my fees? You can pay your fees upfront, in full or in instalments – though you won't need to pay until you've accepted an offer to study with us. Find out more about paying your fees . Funding For advice on the Doctoral Loan and other sources of funding, including ARU scholarships, visit our finance guide for postgraduate researchers . You might also find The Alternative Guide to Postgraduate Funding helpful. ARU research Visit aru.ac.uk/global-sustainability-institute-gsi/research for further information about current research at the Institute. Careers Our students are closely involved in the Institute’s activities, including team meetings, our annual summer away day and winter strategy day, contributing to our So What? magazine, and our own PhD support group. All of this training and engagement supports our PhDs in future career pathways, whether within academia or beyond. Previous PhD researchers in the GSI have worked for think tanks, consultancies, industry, and local government, and become lecturers and researchers at various universities including ARU, Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, Pan Atlantic University in Nigeria, and the Centre for Alternative Technology. Contact details If you're interested in finding out more about research study opportunities, please email [email protected] or visit the GSI postgraduate degrees page. Entry requirements MPhil or PhD with progression from MPhil: You’ll need a Bachelor degree or equivalent with first or upper second class honours, in a related subject area. PhD: You’ll need a Master degree or equivalent in a related subject area. Please note we consider candidates for PhD with progression from MPhil in the first instance. If you want to be considered for direct entry to the PhD route then this can be discussed at interview if you are shortlisted. Please note you’ll also need to provide academic justification for this request. If English is not your first language, you'll require a minimum IELTS score of 6.5, with a minimum of 5.5 in each component (or equivalent test). If you don't meet our English language requirements, we offer a range of courses which could help you achieve the level required for entry. Loading... Entry requirements are not currently available, please try again later. Important additional notes Our published entry requirements are a guide only and our decision will be based on your overall suitability for the programme as well as whether you meet the minimum entry requirements. Contact our postgraduate research degree team for more information about studying a PhD, MPhil or Professional Doctorate at ARU. You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your research programme. Postgraduate MSc Veterinary Physiotherapy Develop advanced veterinary physiotherapy skills to optimise performance, support rehabilitation, and improve animal welfare. Source: Graduate Outcomes Survey 2026 Advance your expertise in veterinary physiotherapy with this flexible, part-time MSc designed for graduates and animal health professionals. Delivered over three years through blended learning and residential weekends, you'll develop advanced clinical reasoning, rehabilitation and therapeutic skills for horses and dogs. You'll also gain valuable research, professional and business expertise, preparing you for a successful career in veterinary physiotherapy and animal rehabilitation. RAMP and AHPR This course is recognised by the Register of Animal Musculoskeletal Practitioners (RAMP), and pending accreditation by the Animal Health Professions’ Register (AHPR). It meets industry-recognised professional standards and competencies and prepares you to pursue professional registration and career opportunities in the animal rehabilitation sector. Why ARU? Study the anatomy and biomechanics of horses and dogs Learn through flexible blended delivery and residential practical weekends Develop hands-on skills in equine and canine rehabilitation Access specialist facilities, including commercial canine clinics Build confidence through real-world case studies and clinical placements Complete your MSc alongside your existing professional commitments Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers [This is] an outstanding course with substantial hands-on clinic time led by engaging lecturers. Drawing from their own veterinary physiotherapy practices, they add incredible depth to a rewarding course that means I now get to do my dream job! Claire Bidwell, MSc Veterinary Physiotherapy graduate Turn your passion for animal health and rehabilitation into a rewarding career. This MSc will equip you with advanced clinical, research and professional skills valued across the animal health, rehabilitation and welfare sectors. You might progress into veterinary physiotherapy practice, animal rehabilitation, clinical consultancy, education, research, product development, animal welfare organisations and related industries. The course also develops the business and communication skills needed to establish an independent practice or expand an existing professional role. Graduation doesn't have to be the end of your time with us. You might decide to continue your academic career and join a research programme at ARU. Take advantage of our Alumni Scholarship and save £400 on your fees. What can you do with a Veterinary Physiotherapy degree? Graduates can pursue a range of careers across animal health, rehabilitation and welfare. Many work as veterinary physiotherapists supporting the assessment, treatment and rehabilitation of horses and dogs, either independently or as part of multidisciplinary teams. The advanced clinical, research and professional skills developed on this course can also support careers in animal rehabilitation centres, education and training, research, consultancy, animal welfare organisations, product development and the wider animal health sector. The course is also well suited to professionals looking to enhance their existing roles or develop specialist expertise. Where have previous Veterinary Physiotherapy graduates worked? Our graduates have gone on to establish successful veterinary physiotherapy businesses, join multidisciplinary veterinary and rehabilitation practices, and work within the wider animal health sector. Career destinations include: veterinary physiotherapy and rehabilitation clinics veterinary practices hydrotherapy centres equine performance and rehabilitation facilities animal welfare organisations education and training research, consultancy, and product development technical and sales support insurance services clinical advisory roles. The advanced clinical, communication and business skills developed throughout the course will prepare you for a wide range of opportunities across the animal health and rehabilitation industries. How can ARU help with my employability and career development? We want you to be a step ahead when you graduate, so we offer: courses designed with employers tutors with professional industry knowledge hands-on learning which may include industry-led projects, placements or Professional Experience modules . Alongside your course, there are lots of other opportunities to build your skills and experience: add value to your CV with an ARU Certificate of Professional Development get involved in a thriving volunteering programme develop your brilliant business ideas work with businesses to make a social impact . We’re here to help you develop your CV and find that all-important role after graduation. Our Employability Service offers tailored career appointments, advice on writing your CV, help to complete job applications, and much more. You’ll have 24/7 access to an online Careers Centre too, which is packed with useful resources. The support continues after you graduate, with lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . Find out more about careers support at ARU . Teaching and modules Our students arrive from all sorts of pathways – seeing how far they develop is incredibly rewarding. Hope Jameson, Senior Lecturer Combine advanced scientific knowledge with practical clinical skills. You'll explore comparative anatomy, biomechanics, pathology and rehabilitation, developing the knowledge needed to assess and treat a range of equine and canine conditions. Throughout the course, you'll strengthen your clinical reasoning, communication and professional practice skills, while considering ethical, legal and sustainability issues within animal healthcare. Practical training, clinical experiences and case-based learning will help you apply theory to real-world situations. In your final year, you'll complete an independent research project, investigating a topic relevant to veterinary physiotherapy and animal rehabilitation. What will I study? Modules are subject to change and availability, and may vary by location. If you have the choice of optional modules, these are indicated with a *. Year 1 Animal Structure, Function and Pathology (45 credits) Academic and Professional Development for Future Success (15 credits) Year 2 Advancing Clinical Skills and Professional Development (30 credits) Advanced Therapy, Manual and Electrophysical Agents and Exercise Prescription (30 credits) Year 3 Major Project (60 credits) Module details What are the teaching times? This course is designed to fit around professional and personal commitments, with most face-to-face teaching taking place during residential weekends at our Writtle campus. Teaching days typically run from 9am to 5pm and include a mix of lectures, workshops and practical sessions. Alongside on-campus teaching, you'll engage with online learning materials and independent study throughout the programme. In Year 1, you'll attend approximately 12 teaching and assessment weekends, while Year 2 includes around 18 weekends, incorporating practical training and internal clinical placement days. How do placements work? Clinical experience is integrated throughout the course, allowing you to apply your learning in real-world settings while developing practical skills and professional confidence. You'll gain experience through internal placement opportunities, including access to our commercial canine clinics and specialist equine facilities. You'll also have opportunities to observe and work alongside practising clinicians, engaging with real cases and rehabilitation programmes. External visits and practical experiences further enhance your understanding of professional practice, helping you develop the clinical reasoning and hands-on skills required for a career in veterinary physiotherapy. How is Veterinary Physiotherapy assessed? Assessment methods are designed to reflect the knowledge, practical skills and professional competencies required in veterinary physiotherapy practice. You'll complete a variety of assessments throughout the course, including case studies, scientific reports, presentations, clinical portfolios, practical examinations, research evaluations and online activities. Practical skills are assessed through observed structured clinical examinations (OSCEs), while your final year culminates in an independent research project focused on a topic relevant to veterinary physiotherapy and animal rehabilitation. This diverse approach allows you to demonstrate both theoretical understanding and practical expertise while developing skills valued by employers and professional bodies. Entry requirements Standard entry requirements Important additional notes Our published entry requirements are a guide only and our decision will be based on your overall suitability for the course as well as whether you meet the minimum entry requirements. Other equivalent qualifications may be accepted for entry to this course; please email [email protected] for further information. Applicants to undergraduate courses can also check our information about undergraduate entry qualifications . You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your course. International students We welcome applications from international and EU students, and accept a range of international qualifications. See international and EU entry requirements See information about application deadlines You'll need a computer and reliable internet access to successfully engage with your course. English language requirements If English is not your first language, you'll need to make sure you meet our English language requirements for postgraduate courses . Check the section ' English language requirements ' for IELTS requirements. Interviews We conduct interviews for our MSc Veterinary Physiotherapy course. If invited to interview, you can sign up for a timeslot through our Applicant Portal (we'll send you details of how to access the Portal). All interviews will be held online, and relevant links will be shared closer to the interview date. You'll be required to submit any outstanding application material ahead of the interview. This includes copies of all qualifications, letters provided from referees, evidence of required equine and canine practical placements to include 50 hours in equine and 50 hours in canine settings. If you cannot provide evidence of completed placements, please provide evidence of secured, upcoming placements that will fulfil these requirements. You will also be required to provide video evidence of your equine handling skills, following the instructions below. This video should be under ten minutes. You will need to: 1) Introduce yourself to the camera wearing the appropriate PPE, please ensure we can see your face before you proceed to the following tasks. 2) Enter safely a stable where a horse is waiting for you. 3) Secure the horse using the head collar. 4) Put an adequate bridle on the horse safely. 5) Pick the left hind and clean the hoof. 6) Remove the equipment. 7) Exit the stable. The video must not be edited. Running commentaries are not necessary. Please send this video to [email protected] and ensure your student ID number is included in the email. The video should reach us by no later than one week before your selected interview date. Please enable JavaScript for "Fees Information" section to function. Fees and funding UK students £15,940 UK students starting 2027/28 (total cost) Fees for our MSc Veterinary Physiotherapy vary by year. For UK students starting in 2027-28 the fees are £6,380 in Year 1, £6,380 in Year 2, and £3,180 in Year 3. Fees are payable upfront, in full or in instalments, but there's no need to pay until you've accepted an offer to study with us. Find out more about paying your fees and about postgraduate loans and funding . Additional course costs For this course, you'll need access to a laptop and a reliable internet connection. Practical course equipment/uniform To take part in practical activities safely and comfortably, you’ll need a riding hat or skull cap that meets current BETA safety standards, riding gloves and sturdy yard boots, long or short. Clothing should be smart and practical, such as dark trousers, waterproofs, or plain jeans (no rips or embellishments). A warm, waterproof outdoor coat (no hood) is also important, plus a digital camera or phone can come in handy for recording your practical work. A lab coat will also be needed for practical sessions in the laboratory. Estimated: £15–£25 Estimated cost for basic yard wear and equipment: £150–£250. During canine hydrotherapy sessions we recommend students to have their own set of waders to ensure comfort and size. Estimated £27-45. Re-take fees for practical exams (OSPEs) may also be incurred. The fee is currently £20 each time. The following additional costs apply in your second year In your second year, you will need to arrange individual insurance as you’ll be treating patients. This will cover you during clinical placements. It is compulsory in order to practice and treat patients. We recommend that you use Balens which is £23.18 (2025). In your second year, you will be working alongside clients and members of the public and will need to dress professionally. The following equipment and uniform are a requirement. Equine: stool for equine practicals (Estimated: £10-20) Canine: wetsuit or waders for hydrotherapy (Estimated: £25-50) Indoor shoes: black trainers (no coloured logos) or boots (Estimated £10-60) T-shirt or long sleeve top (black or navy) (Estimated: £4-20) Fleece (black or navy) (Estimated: £15-50) Trousers: black jeggings or jeans; no blue rinse jeans, rips or embellishments (Estimated: £10-30) Black or brown boots for the yard (Estimated: £25-£150) All clothing must be free of large motifs or branding. Any logos should be small and discreet. No sleeveless tops, or shorts or hoodies are allowed. Paying for university There are several ways to fund postgraduate study, and we recommend finding out more before you apply. Explore: postgraduate loans and other funding scholarships and bursaries for UK and international students our Alumni Scholarship , worth 20% off fees for ARU graduates. This degree prepares you for a multitude of careers, including finance, banking, insurance and the charity sector. You could go on to become a practicing accountant or opt for a wide range of careers in the business sector. You may find yourself working in a global corporation, a small to medium-sized enterprise (SME) or even for yourself – it’s not unusual for company CEOs to come from an accounting or finance background. A foundation year prepares you for the rest of your course, and focuses on general skills such as researching and referencing, numeracy and ICT, and communication. We'll also start to look at some more subject-specific topics. What happens on a placement year? Your placement year is a chance to put everything you’ve learnt in Years 1 and 2 into practice. Spend typically 9-12 months working for an organisation, developing your skills and gaining valuable work experience. Our Placements Team is here to help you secure a placement. How is Accounting and Finance assessed? We'll assess your work in a number of ways including exams, coursework, essays and activity-based assignments. Expect, for example, problem-solving activities, consultancy projects, presentations, computer-based exams, a trading simulation portfolio, and group or individual reports. You'll also be able to access support materials through our learning management system, Canvas. Who teaches Accounting and Finance at ARU Read profiles of teaching and research staff on this course. Living costs Living at university We understand that affordability is an important issue when you’re thinking about studying at university. The overall cost of university can vary depending on where you’re studying and which course you’re taking. Costs may also be lower if you're living at home. However, some of the main costs you’ll want to think about include: accommodation bills internet, mobile phone and calls travel food and drink socialising and going out study materials. Most full-time UK students can apply for a Maintenance Loan to help cover living costs. More about maintenance loans . We also have a range of offers to help with the cost of living . Our Money Advice Service is on hand if you’d like to chat about living costs, budgets and managing your money. You can also find out more about student finance at one of our Open Days . Bursaries, scholarships and part-time work We offer a range of scholarships and bursaries for UK and international students , which provide extra financial support while you’re at university. If you're eligible for a scholarship, you'll generally receive it automatically – there's no need to apply. Our campus employment bureau, ARU Temps , can help you find part-time work that fits around your studies (including any time you may spend on placements). It's a great chance to enhance your CV and boost your income while you study. Undergraduate BSc (Hons) Agriculture Be part of the future of food and farming, build the skills for sustainable, resilient and innovative agricultural systems. Our course pages need JavaScript enabled to work correctly. Previous Section Course Overview Next Section Jump to a section Course overview Careers Teaching and modules Facilities Entry requirements Fees and funding Apply Apply now Come to an Open Day BSc (Hons) With placement With foundation year Part-time CertHE BSc (Hons) Start date September 2027 Location Writtle UCAS course code D401 Duration 3 years With placement Start date September 2027 Location Writtle UCAS course code D402 Duration 4 years with placement With foundation year Start date September 2027 Location Writtle UCAS course code DF02 Duration 4 years with foundation Part-time It's possible to study this course on either a four year or six year part-time basis. You'll take the same modules as BSc (Hons) students, but sometimes in a different order or in different years. CertHE UK students have the option to study Year 1 of this course, either for one year full-time or two years part-time, to achieve a CertHE. You can also choose to combine a foundation year with the CertHE. Contact us to discuss what you can do, or choose your preferred option when you apply. 1st in the region for undergraduates progressing into senior roles. Source: GOS 2026 Our course takes a progressive, future-focused approach to addressing the evolving needs of agriculture today. You'll explore how the industry must adapt to climate change, shifting policies and global food demands by integrating sustainable practices, innovation and systems thinking. Through real-world learning on our extensive working farm, you’ll examine the full agri-food supply chain, emerging technologies and the role of agriculture in delivering environmental and social value, preparing you to shape the future of a resilient, responsible industry. Learn more about studying Agriculture at ARU. Close full-screen gallery. Learn more about studying Agriculture at ARU. Why ARU? Immerse yourself in authentic, enquiry-led learning using our 150-hectare estate and working mixed farm Discover how technology, innovation and data can create sustainable farming systems that address climate change while ensuring food security Accelerate your career through placements, industry collaborations and a strong alumni network across agribusinesses Collaborate on real-world challenges through live briefs, research projects and industry events to shape tomorrow’s food systems Gain confidence and leadership skills from multidisciplinary experts to drive change in global agriculture Study at an award-winning university We were named Times Higher Education University of the Year 2023 . We've also been awarded a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework – a reflection of the outstanding education we offer our students. Careers My experience at Writtle has opened me up to realise there are a lot more jobs than working on a farm in agriculture, such as agronomy and land agency. Emily Keeble, BSc (Hons) Agriculture As a BSc (Hons) Agriculture graduate, you'll have a sound understanding of arable and livestock farming, as well as the wider environment in which production takes place. You’ll graduate equipped with real-life practical skills, industry insight and the ability to apply sustainable and innovative solutions, preparing you to drive innovation, influence policy and contribute to the future of food security and environmental stewardship in the UK and globally. What can you do with an Agriculture degree? You can pursue diverse career roles across the entire food supply chain as well as farm management, sustainability leadership, agricultural consulting, technology development, supply chain management and food science. Opportunities also exist in ESG and data analytics, agronomy, policy analysis, research science and precision agriculture, driving innovation and promoting sustainable practices in agriculture. Graduation doesn’t have to be the end of your time with us. You might decide to stay at ARU and study for a Masters, such as our MBA Agribusiness or MSc Crop Production . Take advantage of our Alumni Scholarship and get 20% off your fees. Where have other Agriculture graduates worked? Previous graduates have gone onto a variety of job roles, including: Agricultural Consultant Agronomist Animal Nutritionist Crop Specialist Estate Manager Farm Manager Land Agent Nutrition Company Sales Representative Postgraduate Qualification or Research Rural Practice Surveyor Soil Scientist Reggie Deakin – Assistant Farm Manager at 21 After graduating with a degree in Agriculture from ARU Writtle, Reggie Deakin stepped into a senior role at Wigborough Wick Farm in Essex. He now manages a 300-cow dairy herd and is leading improvements in livestock systems. “Being trusted with this responsibility straight out of university means a lot,” says Reggie, who’s already making a difference in cow welfare and farm efficiency. How can ARU help with my employability and career development? We want you to be a step ahead when you graduate, so we offer: courses designed with employers tutors with professional industry knowledge hands-on learning through Live Briefs , internships and placements Ruskin Modules that help develop the skills employers value. Alongside your course, there are lots of other opportunities to build your skills and experience: add value to your CV with an ARU Certificate of Professional Development get involved in a thriving volunteering programme develop your brilliant business ideas work with businesses to make a social impact . We’re here to help you develop your CV and find that all-important role after graduation. Our Employability Service offers tailored career appointments, advice on writing your CV, help to complete job applications, and much more. You’ll have 24/7 access to an online Careers Centre too, which is packed with useful resources. The support continues after you graduate, with lifelong access to our Alumni Career Centre . Find out more about careers support at ARU . Teaching and modules From soil to strawberries, spring wheat to sheep, and everything in between, students explore a diverse range of topics that are essential for shaping the future of farming and addressing the challenges of tomorrow's food systems. Harriet Wishart, Lecturer Study scientific, economic and managerial principles to support sustainable agriculture. You'll focus on real-world applications, using our own commercial farm and local businesses for hands-on learning. Your modules will cover areas such as ecosystems, agri-tech, net zero farming, animal welfare and agribusiness. You’ll explore supply chains, food systems and policy through both practical and theoretical approaches. In the final year, you’ll undertake a major research project, developing skills for your future career in agriculture. What will I study? BSc (Hons) With placement With foundation year Part-time CertHE BSc (Hons) Modules are subject to change and availability, and may vary by location. If you have the choice of optional modules, these are indicated with a *. Year 1 Into ARU Ecosystems and Sustainable Development (30 credits) Agricultural Systems in Action (45 credits) Transforming Agriculture (Towards Net Zero) (15 credits) Biological Processes (15 credits) Agribusiness Management for a Circular Economy (15 credits) Year 2 Farm Teams (30 credits) High Welfare Animal Production (15 credits) Research Methods (15 credits) Political and Economic Contexts of Value Chains (15 credits) Fresh Produce Production (15 credits) Ruskin Module (15 credits) Year 3 Dissertation (Agriculture) (30 credits) Business Consultancy Project (30 credits) Natural Resource Management (15 credits) Contemporary Issues in Food Production (15 credits) Science Innovative and Intelligent Agriculture (15 credits) Resilient Future Farming - Animal Production (15 credits) * Resilient Future Farming - Novel and Global Crops (15 credits) * Module details With placement Placement year Work Placement (120 credits) Module details With foundation year To prepare you for university study, you can take a foundation year at the start of this course. Find out more about foundation years . Year 1 Academic and Personal Management Skills (20 credits) Biological Concepts (Introduction to Laboratory Skills) (20 credits) Maths for IT and Science (15 credits) Chemistry for Life Sciences (15 credits) Applied Industry Techniques (30 credits) Independent (Themed) Project (20 credits) Module details Part-time It's possible to study this course on either a four year or six year part-time basis. You'll take the same modules as BSc (Hons) students, but sometimes in a different order or in different years. CertHE UK students have the option to study Year 1 of this course, either for one year full-time or two years part-time, to achieve a CertHE. You can also choose to combine a foundation year with the CertHE. Contact us to discuss what you can do, or choose your preferred option when you apply. What happens on a foundation year? A foundation year prepares you for the rest of your course, and focuses on general skills such as researching and referencing, numeracy and ICT, and communication. We'll also start to look at some more subject-specific topics. What happens on a placement year? Your placement year is a chance to put everything you’ve learnt in Years 1 and 2 into practice. Spend typically 9-12 months working for an organisation, developing your skills and gaining valuable work experience. Our Placements Team is here to help you secure a placement. How is this course assessed? We'll assess your progress in a number of ways including reports, examinations, presentations – both individually and in small groups, essays and technical reports, assessed roundtable discussions, case studies, experimental work and laboratory reports, poster presentations, debates, and your dissertation. Our assessments are designed to ensure you have the skills to make you employment ready. What equipment will I need? It’s advisable to have the following equipment: Technology : A laptop, a reliable internet connection and a phone capable of capturing digital images. Personal Protective Equipment : Safety wellingtons or safety boots (with steel toecaps), a hi-vis tabard and suitable waterproof clothing for outdoor fieldwork. Estimated cost: £100–£200. You’ll also need notebook and paper for note taking, pens, pencils folders and a scientific calculator. Lecturers Read profiles of teaching and research staff on this course.
